He has no existing health conditions and is not on any medication. On examination he has a petechial rash on his limbs. He has no focal neurology and no signs of meningism. Hb 100 g/l Platelets 80 * 109/l WBC 4.0 * 109/l Eosinophils 0.4 * 109/l What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Dengue fever
Retro-orbital headache, fever, facial flushing, rash, thrombocytopenia in returning traveller → ?dengue Dengue fever is found in South America (as well as South East Asia) and presents like this with sudden onset fever and arthralgia combined with low platelets and haemorrhage in the case of Dengue haemorrhagic fever.

Viral hepatitis
Viral hepatitis and malaria are less likely to present with a petechial rash.

Chagas disease
Chagas disease (American trypanosomiasis) is also found in this area but would usually present with mild features and you would expect to see raised eosinophils.

Malaria
Viral hepatitis and malaria are less likely to present with a petechial rash.

Bacterial meningitis
Bacterial meningitis is unlikely as there are no signs of meningism.

stem: A 65-year-old man who has recently move to the UK from India presents with multiple pale patches on his skin. He has no previous medical problems and is not taking any medications. On examination he has 10 hypopigmented patches with reduced sensation. You suspect lepromatous leprosy. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Rifampicin, dapsone and clofazimine for 12 months
Dapsone, ethambutol and pyrazinamide for 12 months
explanation:
Rifampicin, dapsone and clofazimine for 12 months
This man has multibacillary leprosy (>6 lesions) so should have triple therapy with rifampicin, dapsone and clofazimine for 12 months.

Dapsone, ethambutol and pyrazinamide for 12 months
Dapsone, ethambutol and pyrazinamide for 12 months is not the correct treatment for lepromatous leprosy.

Dapsone and ethambutol for 6 months
Dapsone and ethambutol for 6 months is not the correct treatment for lepromatous leprosy.

Rifampicin and isoniazid for 6 month
Rifampicin and isoniazid for 6 months is not the correct treatment for lepromatous leprosy.

Rifampicin and dapsone for 6 months
Rifampicin and dapsone for 6 months is the correct treatment for paucibacillary leprosy (5 or less lesions), not lepromatous leprosy.

stem: A 19-year-old female returns from Ghana. She presents with pyrexia (40°C). She complains of bloody stools preceding this. On examination, she has abdominal distension, hepatosplenomegaly and rose spots on her abdomen. Before empirical treatment has started she passes away due to bowel perforation, resulting in overwhelming sepsis. Which organism is responsible for this type of pathology?
explanation:
Salmonella typhi
Salmonella typhi infection can cause rose spots on the abdomen. Rose spots appear in Salmonella typhi infections. They also appear in C.psittaci infections although it is more associated with typhoid than psittacosis.

Giardia lamblia
Giardiasis would not present this severely and acutely.

Treponema pallidum
Syphilis would present with painless chancre.

Staphylococcus aureus
Staphylococcus aureus would present within hours following ingestion and it is associated with violent vomiting.

Streptococcus pneumoniae
Streptococcus pneumoniae does not usually cause gastroenteritis.

stem: A 37-year-old gentleman who is originally from Brazil is referred to the dermatology clinic due to a non-healing ulcer on his forearm. The ulcer has been there for the last eight months and started as a small painless papule when he was still living in Brazil. Since then it has ulcerated to form a lesion 2cm in diameter which is painless but sometimes itchy. The lesion is dry and has a slightly raised border. In Brazil he had worked as an administrator on a large scale farm and he now works in a small office in the centre of a Welsh town. He has no significant medical history and takes no medications. He has had a recent negative HIV test. Aside from the lesion described above he has no other findings on examination and his observations and basic blood work are all normal. A biopsy of the lesion is performed which shows: Skin biopsy normal skin architecture with numerous amastigotes of leishmania. PCR Leishmania braziliensis. Which element of the vignette would push you towards systemic treatment of their cutaneous leishmaniasis?
options: The number of amastigotes seen at biopsy
explanation:
The Leishmania species
Cutaneous leishmaniasis acquired in South or Central America merits treatment due to the risk of mucocutaneous leishmaniasis. This gentleman has acquired cutaneous leishmaniasis whilst living in Brazil. The disease is contracted from the bite of an infected sand fly and normally presents with a painless papule which then ulcerates. The duration of the lesion depends on the species of leishmania that has been acquired and the host immune response but is typically 6-12 months. Most lesions will self resolve, however where there is a risk of mucocutaneous leishmaniasis as a sequelae then systemic therapy is warranted. This is only of concern with cutaneous leishmaniasis acquired in South America and of the Viannia subgenus (principally L. braziliensis and L. guyanensis). None of the species of Leishmania found outside of the Americas can cause the mucocutaneous form.

The location of the lesion
The location of this man's lesion is fairly innocuous; lesions on the face, hands and genitals are typically considered for systemic therapy.

The number of amastigotes seen at biopsy
The number of amastigotes seen is normally more reflective of the quality of the sample rather than the severity of disease.

That the lesion is painless
Most lesions are painless and this does not have a bearing on prognosis.

The size of the lesion
The lesion described is relatively small; lesions greater than 5cm would be considered for systemic therapy.

stem: A 26-year-old woman has had 1 week of dysuria and increased vaginal discharge. During this time, she has had no fever or abdominal pain. In the last 3 months, she has had unprotected sexual intercourse with a new partner and is now 10 weeks pregnant. She has no other past medical history or allergies. Her vital signs are normal, her abdomen is non-tender, and she has no adnexal tenderness. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated so far. Urinary nucleic acid amplification testing is positive for Chlamydia trachomatis. Which option is the best antibiotic for this patient?
explanation:
Azithromycin
Azithromycin is the treatment of choice for Chlamydia in pregnancy - erythromycin or amoxicillin are alternatives. Azithromycin is correct. This 26-year-old pregnant woman has tested positive for Chlamydia trachomatis at 10 weeks’ gestation and has symptoms of dysuria and increased vaginal discharge without systemic signs. Azithromycin is the best treatment as it is effective against Chlamydia trachomatis and is safe in pregnancy with no known teratogenic effects. Doxycycline, the first-line in non-pregnant patients, is contraindicated in pregnancy due to the risk of fetal tooth discolouration and bone growth impairment. Alternatives like erythromycin or amoxicillin may be used if azithromycin is unsuitable.

Ceftriaxone
Ceftriaxone is incorrect because it is not used to treat Chlamydia trachomatis but is instead the first-line treatment for Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection, which this patient does not have. Her nucleic acid amplification test was positive for chlamydia alone, and there were no features suggestive of gonorrhoea, such as purulent discharge or pelvic pain. Ceftriaxone may be appropriate if this patient had confirmed or suspected gonorrhoea or co-infection with chlamydia and gonorrhoea, which is not indicated here.

Ciprofloxacin
Ciprofloxacin is incorrect because it is both contraindicated in pregnancy and not indicated for Chlamydia trachomatis. Fluoroquinolones like ciprofloxacin carry a risk of fetal cartilage toxicity. Additionally, ciprofloxacin is not used in chlamydia infections, which are better treated with macrolides or tetracyclines (in non-pregnant individuals). Ciprofloxacin could instead be used in a non-pregnant patient with a complicated urinary tract infection or pyelonephritis, which would typically present with systemic symptoms like fever and flank pain, which are not mentioned in this case.

Doxycycline
Doxycycline is incorrect because it is contraindicated in pregnancy due to risks of fetal bone growth impairment and tooth discolouration. Although doxycycline is a first-line treatment for Chlamydia trachomatis in non-pregnant adults, it should be avoided in this 10-week pregnant patient. If she were not pregnant, doxycycline would be a suitable and effective option.

Metronidazole
Metronidazole is incorrect because it does not treat Chlamydia trachomatis, which is an intracellular bacterium. Metronidazole is instead used for anaerobic infections and protozoal conditions like bacterial vaginosis or trichomoniasis. These typically present with fishy-smelling or frothy discharge and altered vaginal pH, which are not features of this patient’s presentation or test result. It may be appropriate if this patient had symptoms or test results suggestive of bacterial vaginosis or trichomoniasis instead.

stem: A 26-year-old man presents to your sexual health clinic with a history of swollen inguinal lymph nodes and fever 1 month after he had receptive anal intercourse with a casual male partner. He tells you his last HIV test was 2 months previously and this is the only sexual contact he has had in the last 6 months. What is the most appropriate course of action to determine his HIV status?
options: Advise the patient it is too early to test for HIV; ask him to return
Request a combined antigen (P24) and antibody test
Ask the patient to return in 2 months for an RNA PCR test
Perform a bedside 'Point of Care' antibody only test and reassure the patient if this is normal
Take a full blood count for CD4 count
explanation:
Request a combined antigen (P24) and antibody test
Combined HIV antibody/antigen tests are now the first-line test for HIV screening of asymptomatic individuals or patients with signs and symptoms of chronic infection. A combined p24/Antibody test is the most appropriate test used in clinical practice as this has a 4 week window period.

Advise the patient it is too early to test for HIV; ask him to return
Advise the patient it is too early to test for HIV; ask him to return. Bedside antibody only test may not be accurate for a recent risk less than 6 weeks ago.

Ask the patient to return in 2 months for an RNA PCR test
Ask the patient to return in 2 months for an RNA PCR test. RNA PCR is sometimes used as a screening test but there is no reason to delay testing.

Perform a bedside 'Point of Care' antibody only test and reassure the patient if this is normal
Perform a bedside 'Point of Care' antibody only test and reassure the patient if this is normal. Bedside antibody only test may not be accurate for a recent risk less than 6 weeks ago.

Take a full blood count for CD4 count
Take a full blood count for CD4 count. CD4 count needs to be checked should the patient be HIV positive but will not give you any information about his HIV status.

stem: A 32-year-old man has 2 months of worsening mouth and nose ulcers. He returned from a 6-month trip across South America, where he hiked in forests. He noticed a small, painless skin lesion on his cheek after being bitten by a fly, which gradually ulcerated and spread. His vital signs are normal. There are multiple mucocutaneous ulcers with raised, indurated borders on the nasal septum and soft palate. He has mild cervical lymphadenopathy, but no hepatosplenomegaly, scleral icterus, or conjunctival suffusion. A punch biopsy reveals amastigotes within macrophages. Which pathogen is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Leishmania braziliensis
Leishmania braziliensis is correct. This patient returned from forested areas in South America, where Leishmania braziliensis is endemic. He developed a painless cutaneous lesion after a suspected sandfly bite that ulcerated and spread to the nasal septum and soft palate, forming raised, indurated mucocutaneous ulcers—hallmarks of mucocutaneous leishmaniasis. The biopsy showing amastigotes within macrophages confirms Leishmania infection. The absence of systemic symptoms or hepatosplenomegaly rules out visceral disease. Other species like Leishmania tropica usually cause only cutaneous disease without mucosal involvement.

Leishmania donovani
Leishmania donovani is incorrect because it causes visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar), not mucocutaneous disease. It typically presents with systemic symptoms such as prolonged fever, hepatosplenomegaly—especially massive splenomegaly—pancytopenia, weight loss, and grey skin discolouration. This patient has no systemic signs, hepatosplenomegaly, or features of pancytopenia (e.g. bruising, anaemia, recurrent infections). His travel to South America, mucocutaneous ulcers, and punch biopsy showing amastigotes support mucocutaneous leishmaniasis caused by L. braziliensis instead.

Leptospira interrogans
Leptospira interrogans is incorrect because it causes leptospirosis, an acute spirochaetal infection presenting with fever, myalgia—especially calf tenderness—jaundice, conjunctival suffusion, and occasionally renal or hepatic failure. This patient has no fever, jaundice, or conjunctival suffusion, and the chronic, painless skin and mucosal ulcers after a fly bite do not fit leptospirosis. The presence of amastigotes on biopsy confirms a protozoal infection, not a bacterial one. L. interrogans is more commonly linked to water exposure or occupations like farming or sewage work, which do not apply here.

Leptospira weilii
Leptospira weilii is incorrect because it also causes leptospirosis, typically presenting with acute fever, conjunctival suffusion, jaundice, and renal impairment—none of which are seen in this patient. It is not associated with insect bites or the development of painless cutaneous lesions that spread to mucosal sites. The biopsy showing amastigotes rules out bacterial causes like leptospirosis. L. weilii infection is more commonly associated with rodent exposure or contaminated water, which is not relevant in this scenario.

Paracoccidioides brasiliensis
Paracoccidioides brasiliensis is incorrect because it causes paracoccidioidomycosis, a systemic fungal infection primarily affecting the lungs and mucosa. It presents with chronic respiratory symptoms like cough and dyspnoea, and typically causes painful mucosal ulcers. It is not spread by fly bites and does not cause a painless skin lesion that later involves the mucosa. The biopsy findings of amastigotes within macrophages confirm Leishmania, not fungal infection, which would show yeast with multiple budding in a “pilot wheel” pattern.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a fever and yellow skin and eyes. He has recently had an illness characterized by fever, chills, headache, and myalgia after returning from Angola. He seemed to recover from the illness and was well for a period of 48 hours before deteriorating. He has a past medical history of rheumatoid arthritis and is on tocilizumab. On examination, there is bleeding from his eyes and mucus membranes and he is visibly jaundiced. The temperature is 38.5ºC. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Yellow fever
Yellow fever typically presents with flu like illness → brief remission→ followed by jaundice and haematemesis. The patient presents with a flu-like illness after returning from Angola, followed by a brief period of remission with subsequent recrudescence of fever and the development of jaundice and haemorrhage from the eyes and mucus membranes. This presentation is typical of yellow fever (and the brief period of remission is characteristic). Tocilizumab treatment for rheumatoid arthritis means the yellow fever vaccine is contraindicated and would put the patient at increased risk of developing the illness.

Ebola
Ebola is incorrect. This is a cause of viral hemorrhagic fever and can cause flu-like symptoms and subsequent jaundice and hemorrhagic complications. However, a period of remission before the recrudescence of the disease is not typical. Furthermore, Angola has never had an ebola outbreak but yellow fever is endemic. In this context, this diagnosis is less likely.

Lassa fever
Lassa fever is incorrect. This is another viral hemorrhagic fever that can result in fever and bleeding from mucus membranes. However, it is mainly endemic in West Africa and unlikely to be found in Angola.

Malaria
Malaria is incorrect. This is of course the common cause of fever in the returning traveller. It is said that the three most common causes of fever in returning travellers are malaria, malaria, and malaria! However, this is unlikely to cause hemorrhagic complications in contrast to yellow fever and therefore is less likely in this case.

Typhoid
Typhoid is incorrect. This is another one of the three most common causes of fever in the returning traveller. It is typified by fever, myalgia, and constipation. Bleeding complications are not expected and so this is less likely.

stem: Which of the following types of viral meningitis may be characteristically associated with a low cerebrospinal fluid glucose level?
explanation:
Mumps
Mumps meningitis is associated with a low CSF glucose. Mumps meningitis is associated with a low glucose in up to a third of patients.

stem: A 63-year-old man presents to general practice with a 2 month history of progressively worsening back pain, made worse on bending over and lifting objects. He also reports a similar length history of 3kg weight loss, fevers and malaise. There is no history of injury or trauma. His past medical history includes only atrial fibrillation. He has no history of drug use, and has no recent travel, but was born in Bangladesh. His observations are as follows: Blood pressure = 152/94 mmHg, heart rate = 88 beats per minute, temperature = 38.1ºC, oxygen saturation= 98% on air, respiratory rate = 22/min. Examination reveals normal cardiac, respiratory systems and neurological systems. There is localised tenderness across the upper lumbar vertebrae, with pain reproduced by straight leg raise. Digital rectal examination was normal. Blood tests reveal: Hb 121 g/L Male: (135-180) Platelets 320 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 13.5 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) CRP 44 mg/L (< 5) Previous chest radiographs show a calcific peri-hilar nodularity, but otherwise clear lung fields. A spinal X-ray has been ordered. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Spinal tuberculosis
Pott's disease (spinal TB) is an important differential in the setting of chronic back pain, fevers and old TB. Spinal tuberculosis (TB)/Potts disease refers specifically to vertebral osteomyelitis secondary to TB. It is the most likely diagnosis given the systemic features in conjunction with the clinical examination and chest X-ray. The chest X-ray indicates a Ghon focus, a sign of primary TB infection. The patient has likely re-activated a previously dormant infection. Potts disease is most common in the lower thoracic and upper lumbar vertebrae, and is more common in those with risk factors for TB such as being from Africa/Asia, or those with HIV. Blood cultures and HIV testing are indicated in this setting. Moreover, spinal MRI is extremely useful in identifying vertebral osteomyelitis in such a circumstance as this, with suspected cord compression being an indication for urgent MRI and potential surgery.

Mechanical lumbar disc prolapse
Lumbar disc prolapse is a common differential in elderly patients presenting with back pain. However, in this circumstance, there is a likely infective process ongoing given the history, fever, and chest radiograph. Disc prolapse is usually accompanied by unilateral radiculopathy according to the nerve root level with either sensory and/or motor weakness.

Spinal metastasis
Spinal metastasis should not be missed as a differential in the first presentation of back pain >55, especially with systemic symptoms such as weight loss and fevers. The lack of primary source for the metastasis with his history, normal respiratory exam and radiograph, and normal digital rectal exam reduce the likelihood of secondary metastasis being the case.

Lumbar osteoarthritis
Lumbar osteoarthritis, also termed spondylosis/facet joint degeneration, causes localised pain with potential for radiation and neurological symptoms. In this case, it would not explain the weight loss, fevers, or ongoing systemic inflammatory process evidenced by the blood results.

Iliopsoas abscess
While it is logical to rule out an iliopsoas abscess given the history of likely TB and back pain, patients with such abscesses would more likely display inguinal tenderness and pain on hip flexion/extension, due to irritation of the muscle during contraction/relaxation respectively. It is less likely due to the local tenderness in the vertebrae themselves.

stem: An 18-year-old female is admitted with a headache, photophobia, fever and confusion. She is managed with empirical antibiotics. What is the mechanism of action of the most commonly used first line antibiotic class?
explanation:
Inhibition of cell wall synthesis
Cephalosporins act by inhibiting cell wall formation. The correct answer is inhibition of cell wall synthesis. The first line antibiotics for possible bacterial meningitis are cephalosporins. Penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems and monobactams all act via inhibition of cell wall synthesis.

stem: A nurse in a GUM clinic asks you to look at a rectal gram-stained slide for a symptomatic patient she has just seen. It shows pinkish/red stained intracellular diplococci. What is the most likely organism?
explanation:
Neisseria gonorrhoea
Gonorrhoea is a gram-negative diplococci that can be identified on gram staining. The stem describes a gram negative stain. Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a gram-negative intracellular diplococcus. While mixed organisms are often seen on rectal slides, this particular pattern would raise suspicion of Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

Neisseria Meningitidis
Neisseria meningitidis is another gram-negative diplococcus but this would not be classed as a commensal and is much less likely in this scenario.

Chlamydia trachomatis
Chlamydia trachomatis cannot be diagnosed on gram staining.

Escherichia coli
E Coli is a gram-negative rod.

stem: A 67 year patient with known emphysema presents to the Emergency Department with a two week history of cough productive of blood stained sputum. Chest X-Ray shows a circular area of dense right upper lobe consolidation. Despite seven days of intravenous antibiotics (piperacillin and tazobactam) his condition has not improved. An urgent inpatient bronchoscopy reveals no endobronchial lesion but bronchoalveolar lavage reveals an underlying pathogenic organism. Ziehl-Nielson staining is negative. What organism would you suspect?
explanation:
Aspergillus fumigatus
This patient is likely to have developed an aspergilloma in an emphysematous cavity, which explains the lack of improvement with broad spectrum intravenous antibiotics, haemoptysis and chest X-Ray findings.

Moraxella catarrhalis
Moraxella and pseudomonas are usually sensitive to piperacillin + tazobactam and do not classically cause clinical haemoptysis.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Moraxella and pseudomonas are usually sensitive to piperacillin + tazobactam and do not classically cause clinical haemoptysis.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis
M. tuberculosis is unlikely given the negative Ziehl-Nielson staining.

Burkholderia cepacia
Burkholderia is typically an infective organism in cystic fibrosis patients, not those with emphysema.

stem: Which one of the following vaccines uses a protein that attaches to the polysaccharide outer coat to make the pathogen more immunogenic?
explanation:
Meningococcus
The correct answer is Meningococcus. The Meningococcal vaccines, including the MenACWY and MenB vaccines, are examples of conjugate vaccines. Conjugate vaccines are those that use a protein that attaches to the polysaccharide outer coat of the pathogen to make it more immunogenic. This is because polysaccharides alone are not very immunogenic, especially in infants and young children. By linking these polysaccharides to a protein, the immune system can recognise and respond more effectively to the pathogen.

Rabies
The Rabies vaccine does not use a protein-polysaccharide conjugate. Instead, it uses inactivated virus particles to stimulate an immune response. Inactivated or killed vaccines use the dead virus, which cannot replicate but still has enough of its original structure intact for our immune system to recognise it.

Yellow fever
The Yellow fever vaccine is a live-attenuated vaccine. Live-attenuated vaccines contain a version of the living virus that has been weakened so that it cannot cause disease in people with healthy immune systems. These types of vaccines often provide lifelong immunity with only one or two doses.

Oral polio
The Oral polio vaccine also falls under the category of live-attenuated vaccines. It contains weakened poliovirus strains and stimulates an excellent immune response by mimicking natural infection without causing severe disease.

Measles
The Measles vaccine is part of MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) or MMRV (measles, mumps, rubella and varicella) vaccines which are also live-attenuated vaccines. They contain weakened forms of these viruses and stimulate an effective immune response providing long-lasting protection.

stem: A 42-year-old dentist is reviewed in the medical clinic complaining of persistent lethargy. Routine bloods show abnormal liver function tests so a hepatitis screen is sent. The results are shown below: Anti-HAV IgG negative HBsAg negative Anti-HBs positive Anti-HBc negative Anti-HCV positive What do these results most likely demonstrate?
options: Previous vaccination to hepatitis B and C
Hepatitis C infection with previous hepatitis B vaccination
explanation:
Hepatitis C infection with previous hepatitis B vaccination
Given the deranged liver function tests these results most likely indicate previous hepatitis B vaccination with active hepatitis C infection. However, around 15% of patients exposed to the hepatitis C virus clear the infection. It would therefore be necessary to perform a HCV PCR to see if the virus is still present There is currently no vaccination for hepatitis C

Hepatitis B infection
The results show Anti-HBs positive and Anti-HBc negative, indicating previous vaccination to hepatitis B, not active hepatitis B infection.

Hepatitis C infection
The results show Anti-HBs positive, indicating previous vaccination to hepatitis B, and Anti-HCV positive, indicating active hepatitis C infection. This combination is not consistent with only hepatitis C infection.

Previous vaccination to hepatitis B and C
The results show Anti-HCV positive, indicating active hepatitis C infection, not just previous vaccination to hepatitis B and C.

Hepatitis B and C infection
The results show Anti-HBs positive and Anti-HBc negative, indicating previous vaccination to hepatitis B, and Anti-HCV positive, indicating active hepatitis C infection. This combination is not consistent with both hepatitis B and C infection.

stem: A 58-year-old caucasian male originally from the United Kingdom (UK) now living in East Africa has returned to the UK on holiday. He has become unwell in the last two days, complaining of a headache, rigors, vomiting, fever, abdominal pain and passing little amounts of dark red urine. On examination, there is hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice and anaemia. Urinalysis reveals blood only and microscopy showed no red cells. Of the following options, what is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Blackwater fever
Blackwater fever is a rare complication of malaria which can be fatal. It is caused by large intravascular haemolysis resulting in haemoglobinuria, anaemia, jaundice and acute kidney injury. Urine is classically black or dark red in colour. The cause of the massive haemolysis is unknown. The treatment is with antimalarials, intravenous fluids and in some cases dialysis. Urinalysis reveals blood which is not seen on microscopy as it is haemoglobinuria.

Leptospirosis
Severe leptospirosis, known as Weil's disease, can result in renal failure and jaundice but also tends to cause pulmonary haemorrhage and shows signs of bleeding. Furthermore, there is usually a relevant occupational history resulting in exposure to infected rat urine.

Acute viral hepatitis
Acute hepatitis is a consideration but normally results in a prodromal phase of flu-like symptoms lasting 16 weeks before jaundice appears and would not usually cause oliguria.

Pyelonephritis
Pyelonephritis would cause leucocytes and nitrates to be positive on urinalysis and would not cause hepatosplenomegaly.

Schistosomiasis
Schistosomiasis has an acute onset which includes symptoms of fever, chills, headache and fatigue but symptoms of haematuria do not come till the chronic phase as a result of bladder fibrosis and calcification, this presents more insidiously. In addition, in schistosomiasis, urine microscopy would show red cell casts.

stem: A 32-year-old man, who has recently migrated from India to the United Kingdom, presents with a several-month history of haemoptysis, weight loss and fevers. On examination, generalised crackles are noted. After a chest X-ray, the patient is diagnosed with tuberculosis and started on a regime of several antibiotics, including rifampicin. What is the mechanism of action of this drug?
explanation:
Inhibition of RNA synthesis
Rifampicin inhibits RNA synthesis. It specifically inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase. In doing so, elongation is physically blocked and so, without adequate RNA, bacteria cannot translate proteins.

Inhibition of DNA synthesis
Examples of antibiotics that inhibit DNA synthesis include metronidazole, sulphonamides and quinolones - such as ciprofloxacin.

Inhibition of cell wall formation
Beta-lactam antibiotics inhibit cell wall formation, including cephalosporins and penicillins. The latter group blocks cross-linking of peptidoglycan cell walls.

Inhibition of folate synthesis
Trimethoprim is an example of a folate synthesis inhibitor. This antibiotic inhibits dihydrofolate reductase. In doing so, dihydrofolic acid is not reduced to tetrahydrofolic acid, which is an essential precursor in the thymidine synthesis pathway.

Inhibition of protein synthesis
A number of antibiotics work by inhibiting protein synthesis. These include aminoglycosides (such as gentamicin), macrolides (such as erythromycin), tetracyclines and fusidic acid.

stem: A 27-year-old man who has recently moved to the UK from Uganda presents complaining of fatigue and purple skin lesions all over his body. On examination he has multiple raised purple lesions on his trunk and arms. You also notice some smaller purple lesions in his mouth. He has recently started taking acyclovir for herpes zoster infection. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Kaposi's sarcoma
Raised purple lesions is a classic description of Kaposi's sarcoma suggesting he has underlying HIV infection. HIV has a high prevalence in Uganda and the recent herpes zoster infection suggests he may have underlying immunocompromise.

Dermatofibroma
Dermatofibromas are usually small pink/red nodules that are characteristically very firm and would not be found in the mouth.

Drug reaction to acyclovir
A drug reaction is unlikely to present like this.

Psoriasis
Psoriasis presents with red, scaly lesions and again is not seen on mucosal surfaces.

Haemangioma
A haemangioma can present with a purple raised lesion but again it would be unusual to see them in the mouth and Kaposi's sarcoma is much more likely in this case.

stem: A 56-year-old diabetic man was admitted with pyrexia and rigors secondary to an infected diabetic foot ulcer and commenced on IV Flucloxacillin. The wound swab grew methicillin resistant Staphylococcus Aureus (MRSA) and he was commenced on an alternative IV antibiotic. Within an hour of administration the patient developed an itchy, erythematous maculopapular rash, which became diffuse covering >80% of his body surface area. He also began to complain of hearing loss in his right ear. What antibiotic is likely to have been prescribed?
explanation:
Vancomycin
Vancomycin is a glycopeptide antibiotic, which works by blocking cell wall subunit assembly (separate from beta lactams). The antibiotic has extensive gram positive cover and is commonly used to treat MRSA and Clostridium difficile. The characteristic side effects include: Ototoxicity, nephrotoxicity and red man syndrome. Red man syndrome is associated with flushing or a maculopapular rash. The proposed mechanism is non IgE mediated mast cell degranulation. Red man syndrome is more common with higher flow rates of infusion. Treatment includes antihistamines.

stem: A 17-year-old girl presents with a sore throat. On examination she has inflamed tonsils covered in white patches. Tender cervical lymphadenopathy and a low grade pyrexia are also present. Which one of the following organisms is most likely to be responsible?
explanation:
Streptococcus pyogenes
The correct answer is Streptococcus pyogenes. This organism, also known as Group A Streptococcus (GAS), is the most common bacterial cause of pharyngitis (sore throat) in children and young adults. The clinical presentation of the patient, including inflamed tonsils with white patches (exudate), tender cervical lymphadenopathy, and low-grade pyrexia, are all characteristic features of acute streptococcal pharyngitis caused by Streptococcus pyogenes.

Streptococcus viridans
Streptococcus viridans is a group of alpha-hemolytic streptococci that are part of the normal flora in the oral cavity. They are generally considered to be less pathogenic than other Streptococcus species and are not a common cause of pharyngitis. Instead, they are more commonly associated with dental infections and infective endocarditis.

Streptococcus agalactiae
Streptococcus agalactiae, or Group B Streptococcus (GBS), is another species that typically does not cause pharyngitis. It is an important cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis but is rarely implicated in upper respiratory tract infections in older children or adults.

Streptococcus pneumoniae
Streptococcus pneumoniae is a leading cause of community-acquired pneumonia and can also cause otitis media and sinusitis. However, it is not a common cause of pharyngitis or tonsillitis.

Staphylococcus aureus
Staphylococcus aureus is a Gram-positive bacterium that can cause skin infections, abscesses, and pneumonia, among other conditions. While it can be implicated in cases of pharyngitis, it is far less common than Streptococcus pyogenes and would not be the most likely cause given the patient's presentation.

stem: A 42-year-old presents with a history of progressive yellow thickening of his toenails which have started to separate from the nail bed. The underlying skin around the nail is inflamed and painful. The patient reports having had multiple episodes of 'athletes foot'. Samples are sent and confirm the presence of Tinea unguium. He is commenced on a drug known to inhibit the fungal enzyme squalene epoxidase after topical medications failed. Two weeks later he represents with abdominal pain, nausea and blood tests showing raised liver enzyme levels. What antifungal has the patient been started on?
explanation:
Terbinafine
Terbinafine inhibits the fungal enzyme squalene epoxidase, causing cellular death. This patient has presented with the fungal nail infection onychomycosis which can result from several different types of fungi including dermatophytes and fusarium. Terbinafine in its oral form is commonly used as first-line management for onychomycosis as topical treatments are rarely effective. Terbinafine is normally reserved until a fungal infection is confirmed via investigation as significant adverse effects can occur with its use including haematological issues (such as pancytopenia and agranulocytosis) and, as in this case, hepatic derangement. The mechanism of action of terbinafine is to inhibit the enzyme squalene epoxidase, which results in inhibition of ergosterol synthesis required for several fungal cells progresses. A reduction in ergosterol production results in fungal cellular death.

Amphotericin B
Amphotericin B is normally used for significant systemic fungal infections such as cryptococcal meningitis etc. It binds with ergosterol found on the fungal cell membranes resulting in ion leakage and cell death. As with terbinafine, amphotericin B can have significant adverse effects including renal and hepatic failure.

Caspofungin
Caspofungin is one of the newer classes of antifungal agents, an echinocandin, which has broad-spectrum activity against candida and aspergillus fungal infections. This class of antifungals is known to inhibit the synthesis of beta-glucan, a major component of fungal cell walls.

Flucytosine
Flucytosine is commonly used with amphotericin B for significant candida and cryptococcosis infection. It is converted into 5-fluorouracil by fungal cells, which in turn inhibits and disrupts fungal protein synthesis.

Griseofulvin
Griseofulvin is an oral antifungal used only for the management of dermatophytosis. It is known to disrupt mitotic spindles within the fungus, during cell replication, via interacting with the microtubules.

stem: A 24-year-old woman is seen in a sexual health clinic complaining of 5 days of vaginal discharge and bleeding. She had her last menstrual period 2 weeks ago and she does not normally suffer from intermenstrual bleeding. She reports having unprotected sexual intercourse 3.5 weeks ago. A cervical swab is taken and a nuclear acid amplification test (NAAT) is positive for Chlamydia trachomatis. The patient has a negative pregnancy test. There are no concerns about pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). What antibiotic would you prescribe?
explanation:
Doxycycline oral - 7 days
Doxycycline orally - 7 days is the correct answer. Doxycycline is the preferred antibiotic as patients with Chlamydia are at higher risk of coinfection with Mycoplasma genitalium, which is often resistant to macrolide antibiotics. Note, doxycycline should be avoided in pregnant patients (can cause transient suppression of foetal bone growth), but this patient has had a negative pregnancy test.

Azithromycin oral - single dose
Azithromycin oral - single dose: azithromycin can be prescribed for Chlamydia, but is now second line due to macrolide resistance to Mycoplasma genitalium (as above). However, it is an option in pregnant patients.

Ceftriaxone IM - single dose
Ceftriaxone IM - single dose: this is the treatment for Gonorrhoea.

Erythromycin oral - 14 days
Erythromycin oral - 14 days: like azithromycin, erythromycin is second line due to macrolide resistance to Mycoplasma genitalium. It can also be used in pregnant patients.

Ofloxacin oral + metronidazole oral - 14 days
Ofloxacin oral + metronidazole oral - 14 days: this is the treatment for pelvic inflammatory disease.

stem: A 32-year-old HIV-positive gentleman has been on treatment for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia in the form of co-trimoxazole. He reported initially experiencing some improvement in his breathing but more recently became very breathless when walking short distances. He felt his breathing was quite noisy at times too. The patient reported taking his medication regularly and eventual persistence with treatment led to a resolution in his symptoms. He was reviewed at the HIV clinic where he was subsequently started on aerosolized pentamidine as prophylaxis treatment. Now having been on this treatment for 6 months he presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of difficulty in breathing. What is the likely cause of this acute presentation?
explanation:
Spontaneous pneumothorax
Aerosolized pentamidine is an alternative treatment for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia but is less effective with a risk of pneumothorax. Bullous changes and pulmonary cysts can form in lung apices from repetitive inflammation and cytotoxicity of HIV on the pulmonary macrophages. These changes persist in spite of prophylaxis against recurring pneumocystis infection with aerosolized pentamidine which increases the risk of spontaneous pneumothorax.

Flail chest
Flail chest occurs due to trauma where a rib cage segment is broken and becomes completely detached from the chest wall resulting in chest pain and difficulty in breathing.

Pulmonary tuberculosis (TB)
Whilst these patients can get reactivation of latent TB, this would present with other symptoms such as fevers, chills, night sweats, cough and even haemoptysis in severe cases.

Community-acquired pneumonia
Given the acute presentation, it is less likely to be community-acquired pneumonia.

Empyema
Given the acute presentation, it is less likely to be empyema. Empyema is a collection of pus in the pleural cavity which can result in fevers, chest pain, difficulty in breathing and productive coughing. This is most commonly caused by pneumonia but can be due to tuberculosis, bronchiectasis, chest surgery and trauma.

stem: A 30-year-old cat owner is investigated for persistent lymphadenopathy and is found to have positive toxoplasma serology. He is otherwise well, with no past medical history and no regular medications. What is the treatment of choice?
explanation:
No treatment required
No treatment is required for toxoplasmosis in immunocompetent individuals.

Atovaquone
Atovaquone can be used as an alternative to pyrimethamine or sulfadiazine in the treatment of immunocompromised patients.

Pyrimethamine
Pyrimethamine is not used in isolation to treat toxoplasmosis.

Pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + folinic acid
Pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + folinic acid in combination are the treatment of choice in immunocompromised patients.

Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole
Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole is used as prophylaxis in immunocompromised patients e.g. transplant recipients, and in the treatment of CNS toxoplasmosis in AIDS.

stem: You are asked to review a 29-year-old woman who has been experiencing lower urinary tract symptoms for the previous 48 hours. She was initially admitted for control of hyperemesis gravidarum but is now more troubled by the urinary symptoms. She states that she has been having pain when micturating, increased urgency, and frequency. A urinalysis was performed which was positive for nitrites and leucocytes. What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Nitrofurantoin
Nitrofurantoin is recommended for the first-line treatment in pregnant women for urinary tract infections and is the most appropriate option. In pregnant women presenting with features of a urinary tract infection, treatment should be commenced immediately. An MSU should be sent to guide the antibiotic choice but this should not delay the initial treatment.

Amoxicillin
Amoxicillin is a second-line choice, as is cefalexin.

Trimethoprim
Trimethoprim should be avoided as it interferes with folate metabolism (especially in the first 12 weeks).

Gentamicin
Gentamicin may be considered for pyelonephritis or other infections but is not first-line.

No treatment
No treatment is not a safe option.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with severe pain in bilateral shoulders, hips and knees and fevers which started 4 hours ago. The patient returned from India 5 days ago. She has no past medical history. When she is called from the waiting room, she looks distressed and is unable to ambulate due to the pain in her joints. On examination, she has a fever of 39.2ºC but observations are otherwise normal. She has a macular rash affecting the torso. She is not meningitic. There is no swelling, erythema or irritation of any joint. What is the most likely causative organism?
explanation:
Chikungunya
Chikungunya can present with debilitating joint pain. Chikungunya characteristically presents with severe bilateral polyarthralgia and fever. Macular rash may also be present. Symptoms can start 2-10 days after exposure and should be suspected in patients who have travelled to the Indian subcontinent. The degree of joint pain in this scenario makes Chikungunya the most likely diagnosis.

Leptospirosis
Leptospirosis should be considered in the returning traveller presenting with non-specific self-limiting flu-like illness (headache, cough, pruritic rash and myalgia), or as a more severe icteric syndrome. Myalgia and joint pains are common but not specifically severe joint pain as a presenting complaint.

Malaria
Malaria is also spread through mosquito bites and normally presents with flu-like features such as fevers, headache; or in severe cases with reduced consciousness, anaemia, renal failure and eventually multi-organ failure, but severe joint pain is not a typical feature.

Rickettsia
Rickettsia is caused by a tick, flea or lice bite and presents as fever, headache and petechial or maculopapular rash. Severe bilateral joint pain is not a recognised feature.

Zika
Zika is also spread by mosquitoes. Patients will normally be asymptomatic or have a flu-like illness with conjunctivitis or maculopapular rash. Joint pain is a feature of Zika, but debilitating joint pain is not normally seen. This specific feature makes Chikungunya more likely based on the information given, but Zika would remain a differential.

stem: A 34-year-old gentleman presented with severe abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea after returning from a business trip to Thailand. He is normally fit and takes no medications. Your lab calls to say that amoebic trophozoites have been identified in his stool. Which of the following combinations of medications would be the most appropriate?
options: 7 days of metronidazole followed by 10 days of dapsone
7 days of IV quinine and meropenem
7 days of ceftriaxone with a proton pump inhibitor
7 days of metronidazole followed by 10 days of diloxanide furoate
7 days of clarithromycin followed by 7 days of liposomal amphotericin B
explanation:
7 days of metronidazole followed by 10 days of diloxanide furoate
Treatment for invasive amoebiasis should be followed by a luminal amoebicide to eradicate the cystic stage which is resistant to metronidazole and tinidazole (which are used against the invasive stage). Amoebic colitis is a severe and occasionally life-threatening condition which requires a high index of suspicion and prompt management. It is caused by Entamoeba histolytica and trophozoite stage causes significant damage to the bowel mucosa and can metastasise to other organs (most commonly the liver causing an amoebic liver abscess). The trophozoite stage is responsive to metronidazole and tinidazole; however, once treated a dormant cystic stage remains and has the potential to cause further disease. This stage is resistant to both metronidazole and tinidazole but can be eradicated with ten days of diloxanide furoate. Paromomycin is considered a second line treatment for the cystic stage and is more commonly used in North America. In many low/middle income countries treatment of the cystic stage is not recommended as re-infection is common, but in returning travellers with low chance of re-infection it is invariably given if available.

7 days of metronidazole followed by 10 days of dapsone
Although metronidazole is the correct treatment, dapsone is used for leprosy and occasionally for other mycobacterial diseases.

7 days of IV quinine and meropenem
Quinine is a treatment for malaria and although in severe cases meropenem might be considered to prevent secondary bacterial translocation of bowel pathogens, it would not treat the trophozoites.

7 days of ceftriaxone with a proton pump inhibitor
Ceftriaxone again might be considered to prevent bowel pathogen translocation but is not effective against Entamoeba histolytica and the proton pump inhibitor would offer little benefit.

7 days of clarithromycin followed by 7 days of liposomal amphotericin B
Clarithromycin is used to cover for atypical pneumonia amongst others and liposomal amphotericin B is used to treat a variety of fungal infections and hence neither would be appropriate choices here.

stem: A 65-year-old homeless man is brought into the emergency department by his friend, who states he has suffered from worsening muscle spasms and headaches. On examination, he has global hypertonia and shallow breathing. He has a large, deep cut on his arm which he sustained 10 days before. His observations are as follows: Heart rate 121 bpm Blood pressure 152/97 mmHg Respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute Saturation 94% on air Temperature 38.1ocelsius What is the mechanism by which the most likely toxin causes these symptoms?
options: Inhibition of GABA and glycine release
explanation:
Inhibition of GABA and glycine release
Clostridium tetani - blocks the release of GABA and glycine. This patient, who is homeless, presents with a deep laceration on his arm that is likely to be the entry point for an infection with Clostridium tetani. The toxin produced by this bacterium leads to progressive muscle spasms which evolve into widespread, painful hypertonia and may affect chest wall movement. This occurs due to the inhibition of GABA and glycine release.

Inhibition of acetylcholine release
The mechanism of action for the toxin produced by Clostridium botulinum is the inhibition of acetylcholine release, resulting in flaccid paralysis as opposed to the spastic paralysis caused by the tetanus toxin.

Inhibition of the GABA receptor
Inhibition of the GABA receptor is not associated with the mechanism of tetanus toxin. Instead, this describes how certain pharmacological agents diminish inhibitory neurotransmission. A well-recognised example is flumazenil, used as an antidote in benzodiazepine overdoses.

Inhibition of the NMDA receptor
Autoantibodies that lead to inhibition of the NMDA receptor are implicated in certain types of autoimmune encephalitis, which can be part of a paraneoplastic syndrome. However, this process plays no role in the pathophysiology of toxicity from Clostridium tetani.

Inhibition of voltage-gated sodium channels
Inhibition of voltage-gated sodium channels is unrelated to the pathophysiology induced by tetanus toxin. This mechanism underlies the action of local anaesthetics such as lidocaine on nerve conduction.

stem: A 39-year-old man with HIV is admitted due to shortness of breath. Chest x-ray shows bilateral pulmonary infiltrates and Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia is suspected. What type of staining should be applied to the bronchoalveolar lavage to demonstrate the organism?
explanation:
Silver stain
The correct answer is silver stain, as it is the most appropriate staining method to demonstrate the presence of Pneumocystis carinii in bronchoalveolar lavage samples. Silver stains, such as Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) or Grocott's methenamine silver stain, are commonly used to visualize fungi and other pathogens in tissue samples. In the case of Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia, these stains provide excellent contrast between the organism's cysts and surrounding lung tissue, allowing for clear identification.

Rubeanic acid
Rubeanic acid is not the correct choice, as it is a reagent used to detect copper in tissues. It forms a green complex with copper ions and can be useful in diagnosing Wilson's disease or assessing copper levels in liver biopsies. However, it is not relevant for visualizing Pneumocystis carinii.

Pearl's stain
Pearl's stain, also known as Prussian blue staining, is incorrect because it is primarily used to identify iron deposits within tissues. This stain involves the reaction between potassium ferrocyanide and ferric ions, resulting in a bright blue color where iron accumulates. Pearl's stain has applications in diagnosing conditions such as hemochromatosis but does not help visualize Pneumocystis carinii.

Rose Bengal
Rose Bengal staining is not suitable for identifying Pneumocystis carinii. This technique uses a red dye that binds to chitin-containing structures such as fungal cell walls but does not specifically target Pneumocystis carinii. Rose Bengal can be applied to corneal scrapings to diagnose fungal keratitis or Acanthamoeba infections, but it is not the best choice for demonstrating Pneumocystis carinii in bronchoalveolar lavage samples.

Congo red
Congo red staining is also an incorrect option. This stain is used to identify amyloid deposits in tissues by binding to beta-pleated sheet structures present in amyloid fibrils. Congo red-stained amyloid appears as red-orange birefringent material under polarized light microscopy. While this stain is valuable in diagnosing conditions such as amyloidosis, it does not aid in the visualization of Pneumocystis carinii.

stem: A 32-year-old man returns from a three-month backpacking trip in Bolivia and Brazil and presents with persistent nasal congestion, nosebleeds, and progressive ulceration of the nasal septum. He reports that two months ago, he developed a painless skin ulcer on his right cheek that partially healed but left scarring. Over the past few weeks, he has noticed increasing nasal obstruction and disfigurement. On examination, there is mucosal destruction of the nasal septum with ulceration extending into the oropharynx. What is the most likely causative organism?
explanation:
Leishmania braziliensis
Leishmania braziliensis is correct because it is the primary cause of mucocutaneous leishmaniasis, a progressive disease that begins with cutaneous leishmaniasis and later leads to destructive mucosal involvement of the nose, pharynx, and larynx. It is transmitted by sandfly bites and is endemic in Brazil and other parts of South America. The initial painless ulcer on the cheek is characteristic of cutaneous leishmaniasis, and months later, the parasite spreads via lymphatics to the nasal and oropharyngeal mucosa, leading to progressive ulceration, disfigurement, and nasal septal destruction. Diagnosis is confirmed by PCR, microscopy of biopsy samples, or culture, and treatment includes liposomal amphotericin B or miltefosine for severe cases.

Bartonella bacilliformis
Bartonella bacilliformis is incorrect because it causes Carrion’s disease (Oroya fever and verruga peruana), which presents with vasoproliferative skin lesions rather than mucosal ulceration. It is transmitted by sandflies in the Andes region (Peru, Ecuador, Colombia), but it does not cause progressive nasal destruction.

Histoplasma capsulatum
Histoplasma capsulatum is incorrect because histoplasmosis can cause mucosal ulcers, but it typically presents as pulmonary or disseminated disease, especially in immunocompromised patients (e.g., HIV/AIDS). The lesions tend to be multiple painful oral or pharyngeal ulcers rather than progressive nasal destruction following a cutaneous ulcer.

Mycobacterium leprae
Mycobacterium leprae is incorrect because leprosy primarily affects the skin and peripheral nerves, leading to sensory loss, hypopigmented patches, and thickened nerves rather than ulceration of the nasal septum. Lepromatous leprosy can cause nasal involvement, but it does not start as a skin ulcer before progressing to mucosal destruction.

Paracoccidioides brasiliensis
Paracoccidioides brasiliensis is incorrect because it is a fungal infection endemic to Brazil and South America that can cause chronic mucocutaneous lesions and pulmonary involvement. However, it usually presents with multiple painful oral ulcers (‘mulberry-like’ stomatitis) rather than nasal septal destruction.

stem: A 36-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after being found acutely confused during a welfare check. His past medical history is significant for poorly controlled HIV due to medication noncompliance. On examination, the patient is confused and agitated. He walks with a broad-based gait. CD4 count 70 cells/mm^3 (500 - 1500 cells/mm^3) An MRI brain with gadolinium contrast demonstrates several nonenhancing, asymmetrical periventricular and subcortical lesions, consistent with demyelination. Which organism is most likely to have contributed to this patient's presentation?
explanation:
John Cunningham virus
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy is caused by the JC virus or BK virus. John Cunningham virus is the correct answer. Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, an AIDS-defining illness caused by the John Cunningham (JC) virus, should be suspected in patients with poorly controlled HIV presenting with neuropsychiatric deterioration. This patient's asymmetrical subcortical demyelinating lesions support the diagnosis of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. The risk of central nervous system infection rises with CD4 counts below 200 cells/mm^3.

Cryptococcus neoformans
Cryptococcus neoformans is incorrect. Cryptococcus may cause indolent fungal meningoencephalitis in severely immunocompromised patients. Radiological features are classically a 'soap bubble' appearance, rather than the periventricular demyelination seen in this patient.

Cytomegalovirus
Cytomegalovirus is incorrect. Although cytomegalovirus may cause encephalitis in severely immunocompromised patients, this patient's presentation and MRI findings are more suggestive of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, caused by the JC virus.

Toxoplasma gondii
Toxoplasma gondii is incorrect. Although this patient is at high risk of cerebral toxoplasmosis, MRI findings do not support this and there is typically no associated demyelination. Contrast MRI in patients with cerebral toxoplasmosis classically shows discrete ring-enhancing lesions.

Varicella zoster virus
Varicella zoster virus is incorrect. Although varicella zoster virus may cause encephalitis in severely immunocompromised patients, this patient's presentation and MRI findings are more suggestive of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, caused by the JC virus.

stem: A 34-year-old man from West Africa is admitted due to confusion associated with left-sided weakness and ataxia. He is known to be HIV positive but is not on anti-retroviral treatment. The following results are obtained: CD4 43 u/l CT head Low attenuation diffusely. No mass effect or enhancement What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy
The most likely diagnosis in this scenario is progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). PML is a rare and often fatal demyelinating disease caused by the JC virus. It typically affects immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV infection, especially when the CD4 count is below 200 u/l. In this case, the patient has a very low CD4 count of 43 u/l, which makes him susceptible to opportunistic infections like PML. The clinical presentation of confusion, left-sided weakness, and ataxia are also consistent with PML. Additionally, the CT head findings of low attenuation without mass effect or enhancement are characteristic of PML.

Toxoplasmosis
Toxoplasmosis is another opportunistic infection that can affect HIV-positive patients with low CD4 counts. However, it usually presents with focal neurological deficits and seizures due to brain abscesses. On imaging, toxoplasmosis typically shows ring-enhancing lesions with mass effect, which is not seen in this case.

Tuberculosis
Tuberculosis can also involve the central nervous system in HIV-positive patients but usually presents as tuberculous meningitis or tuberculoma. Tuberculous meningitis would cause meningeal signs and symptoms such as headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia rather than focal neurological deficits like those seen in this patient. A tuberculoma could cause focal neurological deficits but would be visible on imaging as a mass lesion with possible enhancement.

Cryptococcus
Cryptococcus, specifically Cryptococcus neoformans, can cause cryptococcal meningitis in immunocompromised patients. While it may present with confusion and neurological symptoms similar to what this patient is experiencing, it typically causes meningeal irritation signs (e.g., headache and neck stiffness) rather than focal neurological deficits. Additionally, imaging findings would be nonspecific or may show dilated perivascular spaces, which is not seen in this case.

Cerebral lymphoma
Cerebral lymphoma, particularly primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL), is another opportunistic infection that can affect HIV-positive patients with low CD4 counts. However, PCNSL usually presents as a solitary or multiple enhancing mass lesions on imaging, often with surrounding oedema and mass effect. This is not consistent with the CT head findings in this patient.

stem: A 42-year-old woman attends the hepatology clinic for review. She was an intravenous drug user 15 years ago but has been abstinent since. She feels well and has no symptoms. Liver function tests are normal. Hepatitis serology was requested by her GP. Anti-HCV antibody Positive HCV RNA Not detected HBsAg Negative Anti-HBc Negative What is the most appropriate interpretation of these results?
options: Previous hepatitis C infection that has cleared
explanation:
Previous hepatitis C infection that has cleared
Previous hepatitis C infection that has cleared is the correct interpretation. The presence of anti-HCV antibodies indicates exposure to hepatitis C virus, but these antibodies persist even after viral clearance. The key finding is the undetectable HCV RNA, which indicates there is no active viral replication. Approximately 15-45% of patients spontaneously clear hepatitis C after acute infection, and these individuals will continue to have positive anti-HCV antibodies indefinitely despite having cleared the virus. This patient's normal liver function tests and absence of symptoms support this interpretation. No further treatment is required, though she should be counselled about the results and reassured.

Chronic hepatitis C infection
Chronic hepatitis C infection would require the persistence of HCV RNA in the blood for 6 months. This patient has undetectable HCV RNA, which excludes chronic infection. Chronic infection affects 55-85% of those exposed to hepatitis C, but this patient is among those who have cleared the virus.

Acute hepatitis C infection
Acute hepatitis C infection is unlikely given the 15-year timeframe since her risk exposure and the absence of symptoms. Additionally, HCV RNA would be positive during acute infection as it is the investigation of choice for diagnosing acute hepatitis C.

False positive anti-HCV antibody result
False positive anti-HCV antibody result is possible but less likely given her clear risk factor of previous intravenous drug use. The negative HCV RNA makes this a true positive antibody result indicating previous exposure.

Occult hepatitis C infection
Occult hepatitis C infection refers to the presence of HCV RNA in hepatocytes despite undetectable serum HCV RNA, which is extremely rare and not supported by her normal liver function tests and clinical wellbeing.

stem: A 68-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 2-day history of fever, productive cough, and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. He has a temperature of 39.2°C, respiratory rate of 24 breaths/minute, and oxygen saturation of 92% on room air. Examination reveals decreased breath sounds and crackles in the right lower zone. You notice cold sores on his lips. Chest X-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation. What is the most likely causative organism?
explanation:
Streptococcus pneumoniae
Pneumonia caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae is associated with cold sores. Streptococcus pneumoniae is the correct answer. This patient presents with classic features of pneumococcal pneumonia, which is the most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), accounting for approximately 80% of cases. The clinical presentation strongly supports this diagnosis: acute onset of symptoms (2-day history), high fever (39.2°C), productive cough, and pleuritic chest pain. Importantly, the presence of herpes labialis (cold sores) is a characteristic feature associated with pneumococcal pneumonia. This association, while not fully understood, is thought to be related to the reactivation of latent herpes simplex virus during the acute inflammatory response to pneumococcal infection. The chest X-ray finding of lobar consolidation is also typical of pneumococcal pneumonia, which classically affects a single lobe (in this case, the right lower lobe).

Haemophilus influenzae
Haemophilus influenzae is an incorrect answer. While H. influenzae is a cause of CAP, it is less common than S. pneumoniae. H. influenzae pneumonia typically affects patients with underlying lung disease such as COPD or bronchiectasis. It does not have a specific association with herpes labialis. The presentation would be similar but would more likely show a patchy bronchopneumonic pattern on chest X-ray rather than the lobar consolidation described in this case.

Klebsiella pneumoniae
Klebsiella pneumoniae is an incorrect answer. K. pneumoniae pneumonia classically affects alcoholics, diabetics, and those with poor dental hygiene. It typically presents with 'currant jelly' sputum and has a predilection for the upper lobes. There is no association between K. pneumoniae pneumonia and herpes labialis. The patient in this scenario has no mentioned history of alcoholism or other risk factors for K. pneumoniae infection.

Mycoplasma pneumoniae
Mycoplasma pneumoniae is an incorrect answer. M. pneumoniae causes atypical pneumonia with a more gradual onset and less severe symptoms than seen in this case. It typically affects younger patients and is often associated with extra-pulmonary manifestations such as bullous myringitis, erythema multiforme, or hemolytic anemia. The chest X-ray in Mycoplasma pneumonia often shows an interstitial pattern rather than lobar consolidation, and there is no association with herpes labialis.

Staphylococcus aureus
Staphylococcus aureus is an incorrect answer. S. aureus pneumonia is often seen as a complication following influenza infection or in intravenous drug users. It typically presents with a rapidly progressive, severe pneumonia that may be complicated by lung abscess, empyema, or pneumatoceles. There is no specific association between S. aureus pneumonia and herpes labialis. The patient in this scenario does not have risk factors for staphylococcal pneumonia.

stem: A 57-year-old female presents with headache and fever to the Emergency Department. On examination neck stiffness is noted along with a positive Kernig's sign. A lumbar puncture is performed and reported as follows: CSF culture Gram positive bacilli What is the most likely causative organism?
explanation:
Listeria monocytogenes
Listeria monocytogenes - Gram-positive rod The correct answer is Listeria monocytogenes. The patient's presentation of headache, fever, neck stiffness, and positive Kernig's sign is suggestive of bacterial meningitis. The CSF culture result showing Gram-positive bacilli further supports this diagnosis. Among the given options, Listeria monocytogenes is a Gram-positive bacillus and a known cause of bacterial meningitis, particularly in older adults or immunocompromised individuals.

Cryptococcus
Cryptococcus is an incorrect option because it is a fungus, not a bacterium. It can cause cryptococcal meningitis, which typically occurs in immunocompromised patients such as those with HIV/AIDS. The CSF culture in this case would show encapsulated yeast cells rather than Gram-positive bacilli.

Haemophilus influenzae
Haemophilus influenzae is another incorrect option. While it can cause bacterial meningitis, it is a Gram-negative coccobacillus. Additionally, the incidence of H. influenzae-associated meningitis has significantly decreased due to widespread vaccination.

Streptococcus pneumoniae
Streptococcus pneumoniae is also an incorrect choice as it is a Gram-positive coccus and not a bacillus. However, it should be noted that S. pneumoniae is one of the most common causes of community-acquired bacterial meningitis in adults.

E. coli
E. coli is another incorrect option because it is a Gram-negative bacillus and not consistent with the CSF culture result in this scenario. Nonetheless, E. coli can cause bacterial meningitis particularly in neonates but would be less likely in this adult patient.

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents with lethargy, pyrexia and headaches. She is a student and returned from a holiday in Ibiza ten days ago. These symptoms have been present for the past six days and she is wondering whether she may need an antibiotic. She also has a history of menorrhagia and is concerned that she may be anaemic. Clinical examination reveals a temperature of 37.9ºC and marked cervical lymphadenopathy. You order a full blood count which is reported as follows: Hb 12.1 g/dl Platelets 189 * 109/l WCC 13.1 * 109/l Neutrophils 5.2 * 109/l Lymphocytes 6.2 * 109/l Film Atypical lymphocytes seen What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Septicaemia secondary to streptococcal throat infection
explanation:
Infectious mononucleosis
The correct answer is infectious mononucleosis. This patient presents with typical symptoms of infectious mononucleosis, including fever, fatigue, headache, and cervical lymphadenopathy. Additionally, the blood film shows atypical lymphocytes which can be seen in infectious mononucleosis. The disease is commonly caused by the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and often affects young adults.

Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia
While this condition may present with similar symptoms such as fever and fatigue, the blood count findings are not consistent with acute lymphoblastic leukemia. In this case, we would expect to see a higher white cell count with a predominance of blast cells.

Hashimoto's thyroiditis
This autoimmune thyroid disorder typically presents with hypothyroidism symptoms such as fatigue, weight gain and cold intolerance. Although Hashimoto's thyroiditis can cause an enlarged thyroid gland that could potentially lead to cervical lymphadenopathy, the presence of pyrexia and atypical lymphocytes on blood film make this diagnosis less likely.

HIV seroconversion
HIV seroconversion can present with flu-like symptoms including fever and lymphadenopathy; however, the presence of atypical lymphocytes in the blood film is more suggestive of infectious mononucleosis. Furthermore, there is no mention of any high-risk behaviour or recent unprotected sexual encounters that might suggest an increased risk for HIV infection.

Septicaemia secondary to streptococcal throat infection
Although streptococcal throat infections can cause fever and cervical lymphadenopathy, septicaemia would typically present with a much higher temperature and systemic signs of sepsis such as tachycardia or hypotension. Moreover, the presence of atypical lymphocytes on blood film is not typical for a streptococcal infection.

stem: A 27-year-old man presents to the genitourinary medicine clinic with several painless, soft lesions on the shaft of his penis. He first noticed them three weeks ago and they have gradually increased in number. On examination, there are five non-keratinised, fleshy papules measuring 3– 4 mm each. What is the most appropriate initial management?
explanation:
Topical podophyllum
Topical podophyllum is the correct answer because it is recommended as first-line therapy for multiple, non-keratinised genital warts according to UK guidelines. Podophyllum is a cytotoxic agent that can be applied topically and is effective for soft, moist lesions such as those described in this patient. This approach avoids more invasive or painful procedures and targets the type of lesion most likely to respond.

Cryotherapy
Cryotherapy is generally reserved for solitary or keratinised warts where topical agents may not penetrate effectively. In this scenario, the presence of multiple non-keratinised lesions makes cryotherapy less suitable as an initial choice due to practicality and efficacy.

Topical imiquimod
Topical imiquimod is usually considered a second-line option if first-line treatments such as podophyllum or cryotherapy fail or are contraindicated. While imiquimod can be used for external genital warts, it is not preferred initially when other options are available and appropriate.

Oral aciclovir
Oral aciclovir is an antiviral medication used primarily for herpes simplex virus infections rather than HPV-related genital warts. The clinical presentation here does not suggest herpes (which would typically present with painful vesicles), so aciclovir would not be beneficial.

Excisional biopsy
Excisional biopsy may be indicated if there was diagnostic uncertainty (for example suspicion of malignancy) or failure of standard therapies; however, typical features of benign genital warts are described here and excision would not be appropriate as a first-line intervention.

stem: A 68-year-old man is referred to the gastroenterology clinic with a 6-month history of intermittent abdominal bloating and loose stools. He spent 20 years working in rural Thailand before retiring to the UK. His examination is unremarkable. Stool microscopy for ova, cysts, and parasites is negative on three occasions. His blood results are shown below. Hb 138 g/L (135-180) Platelets 245 x 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 9.1 x 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Eosinophils 1.8 x 109/L (0.0 - 0.5) Which organism is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation:
Strongyloides stercoralis
Vague GI symptoms + eosinophilia + no ova/cysts on stool sample → ? Strongyloides stercoralis. This patient presents with a classic triad for chronic strongyloidiasis: vague, long-standing gastrointestinal symptoms, a significant peripheral eosinophilia, and a relevant travel history (prolonged residence in Southeast Asia). The key diagnostic clue that differentiates it from other common helminth infections is the repeatedly negative stool microscopy for ova and cysts. Strongyloides has a unique life cycle where larvae, not eggs, are passed in the stool. However, larval shedding is often intermittent and in low numbers, leading to a very low sensitivity (around 30%) for standard stool microscopy. Therefore, a negative result does not exclude the diagnosis. Given the high eosinophil count and clinical picture, the next most appropriate investigation would be Strongyloides serology (IgG ELISA), which has high sensitivity. It is crucial to diagnose and treat this infection due to the risk of life-threatening hyperinfection syndrome if the patient becomes immunosuppressed.

Ascaris lumbricoides
Ascaris lumbricoides (roundworm) is a plausible differential as it is a common helminth infection that can cause GI symptoms and eosinophilia, particularly during the larval migration phase through the lungs (Löffler's syndrome). However, in established intestinal infection, the diagnosis is typically made by identifying the characteristic large, bile-stained eggs on stool microscopy. Given that three stool samples were negative for ova, this diagnosis is less likely than strongyloidiasis.

Entamoeba histolytica
Entamoeba histolytica is a protozoan parasite that causes amoebiasis, which can range from asymptomatic carriage to severe dysentery and extra-intestinal disease like liver abscesses. While it can cause GI symptoms, it is not typically associated with a significant eosinophilia. The diagnosis is made by identifying cysts or trophozoites in the stool, or through stool antigen testing. The combination of marked eosinophilia and negative microscopy makes this diagnosis unlikely.

Giardia lamblia
Giardia lamblia is another protozoan parasite and a common cause of traveller's diarrhoea, often leading to bloating, flatulence, and malabsorption. However, like other protozoal infections, it does not cause a peripheral eosinophilia. Diagnosis is usually confirmed by stool microscopy for cysts and trophozoites or stool antigen detection tests. The presence of significant eosinophilia effectively rules out giardiasis as the primary cause.

Schistosoma mansoni
Schistosoma mansoni is a strong distractor. This trematode (fluke) can cause chronic intestinal schistosomiasis with vague abdominal symptoms and is well-known to cause a significant eosinophilia. The patient's travel history is also consistent. However, the diagnosis of intestinal schistosomiasis relies on the detection of characteristic eggs in stool samples. While egg excretion can be intermittent, three negative samples make this diagnosis less probable compared to Strongyloides, for which negative microscopy is the expected finding.

stem: A 24-year-old man presents to the sexual health clinic for review. He reports a two-day history of dysuria and yellow-green urethral discharge. He is normally fit and well, with no past medical history. He reports that he had unprotected sexual intercourse ten days before. Urethral swabs are taken and sent off for culture and sensitivities. Preliminary results are shown below: Urethral swab Gram-negative diplococci Based on the likely diagnosis, what is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
explanation:
Intramuscular ceftriaxone
Intramuscular ceftriaxone is the treatment of choice for Gonorrhoea. This patient has classic symptoms of gonorrhoeal infection: namely, dysuria and urethral discharge, which may be white, yellow or green in colour. The diagnosis of Gonorrhoea infection is favoured over other sexually transmitted infections such as Chlamydia trachomatis by the presence of gram-negative diplococci, suggestive of Neisseria gonorrhoeae. As of 2019, the recommended first-line treatment for Gonorrhoea infection without any information on microbiological sensitivities is a single dose of intramuscular ceftriaxone.

Intramuscular ceftriaxone and oral azithromycin
Intramuscular ceftriaxone and oral azithromycin is incorrect. This was previously advised by the British Society for Sexual Health and HIV (BASHH), but as of 2019, up-front azithromycin in the absence of any sensitivity data is not recommended.

Oral ceftriaxone
Oral ceftriaxone is incorrect. Oral ceftriaxone is not licensed for the treatment of gonorrhoeal infection.

Oral ciprofloxacin
Oral ciprofloxacin is incorrect. Due to high levels of ciprofloxacin resistance amongst gonorrhoeal infections in the UK, ciprofloxacin monotherapy is not recommended in the absence of sensitivity data suggesting that the causative organism is susceptible.

Oral doxycycline
Oral doxycycline is incorrect. This would be an appropriate first-line antibiotic regimen for Chlamydia trachomatis rather than gonorrhoeal infection.

stem: A 5-year-old child is admitted to the paediatric ward with a fever and a non-blanching rash. Both blood cultures and cerebrospinal fluid analysis show the presence of Neisseria meningitidis. The doctors recommend an antibiotic for the child's parents to take, given they were in contact with the child while unwell. Both parents are well, with no allergies or relevant medical history. What is the most appropriate antibiotic for the parents?
options: No antibiotic needed since they are asymptomatic
explanation:
Ciprofloxacin
Oral ciprofloxacin or rifampicin is used as prophylaxis for contacts of patients with meningococcal meningitis. Oral ciprofloxacin is used as prophylaxis for contacts of patients with meningococcal meningitis. Rifampicin is also used but is not on the list of options.

Amoxicillin
