Genitourinary clinic.
As part of his routine HIV work up his HLA B*5701 result is reported as
positive.
Which drug will not be included in his ART regimen as a result of this
information?
Tenofovir
Emtricitabine
Lamivudine
Stavudine
Abacavir
Question 27 of 287
A 45 year old man is diagnosed with HIV following attendance at
Genitourinary clinic.
As part of his routine HIV work up his HLA B*5701 result is reported as
positive.
Which drug will not be included in his ART regimen as a result of this
information?
explanation:
Abacavir can cause a severe and sometimes fatal hypersensitivity
reaction. It is a cell mediated delayed hypersensitivity reaction which
occurs around 6 weeks after starting treatment. Symptoms are of fever,
rash, malaise and gastrointestinal symptoms.
Patients without HLA B*5701 are highly unlikely to develop
hypersensitivity. Those with the HLA B*5701 allele have a 50% risk and
therefore in these individuals abacavir should be avoided.
It is therefore routine to test HLA B*5701 status on all newly diagnosed
patients with HIV.

A 28 year-old man presents to his doctor with a rash and bone pain.
Radiographs of the limbs revealed numerous osteolytic lesions. He was
successfully treated for secondary syphilis.
Which of the following tests is likely to remain positive in this patient
despite treatment?
Blood culture
Treponema pallidum particle agglutination (TPPA)
Venereal disease reference laboratory (VDRL)
Rapid plasmin reagin (RPR)
Wasserman test
Question 29 of 287
A 28 year-old man presents to his doctor with a rash and bone pain.
Radiographs of the limbs revealed numerous osteolytic lesions. He was
successfully treated for secondary syphilis.
Which of the following tests is likely to remain positive in this patient
despite treatment?
explanation:
Syphilis is a disease caused by infection with the spirochete Treponema
pallidum. The infection is systemic and the disease is characterized by
periods of latency. These features, together with the fact that Treponema
pallidum cannot be isolated in culture, mean that serologic techniques
play a major role in the diagnosis and follow-up of treatment for syphilis.
The Treponema pallidum particle agglutination assay (also called TPPA
test) is an indirect agglutination assay used for detection and titration of
antibodies against Treponema pallidum.
IgG antibodies to syphilis can remain elevated despite appropriate
antimicrobial treatment and a reactive result does not distinguish
between recent or past infection.

What investigation is most likely to be diagnostic?
explanation:
The correct answer is broncho-alveolar lavage which is most likely to be
able to demonstrate PCP characteristic cysts with silver staining. There
are several factors highly suggestive of PCP. This gentleman is poorly
compliant with his HIV medication and the other medication regime he is
describing is PCP prophylaxis, suggesting a low CD4 count. He also is
tachypnoeic with low saturations on mobilising and a clear chest X-ray.
All of these factors suggest PCP. In the case of a productive cough,
sputum could be obtained without the need for a broncho-alveolar
lavage. Imaging can be suggestive of PCP but is not as sensitive or
diagnostic as broncho-alveolar lavage. ECG and echocardiogram have
no role in PCP diagnosis.
Source:
Nelson, M., Dh Dockrell, and S. Edwards. 'British HIV Association and
British Infection Association Guidelines for the Treatment of
Opportunistic Infection in HIV-seropositive Individuals 2011.' HIV
Medicine 12 (2011): 1-5.

options: Admit to hospital for IV antibiotics
Advise that the risk of transmission is not significant
explanation:
This is a patient who has had a close contact with respiratory secretions
of a person with confirmed meningococcal meningitis. Despite the fact
that she has not had prolonged exposure, prophylaxis in the form of oral
ciprofloxacin is needed.
People who have been exposed to a patient with confirmed
bacterial meningitis should be given prophylactic antibiotics if they
been exposed to respiratory secretion, regardless of closeness of
contact
The risk of transmission by this route is sufficiently significant to make
monitoring for symptoms or not giving any treatment inappropriate.
A lumbar puncture is unlikely to be a helpful investigation for her as it
cannot exclude that she will develop meningitis.
IV antibiotics are used to treat meningitis, whilst oral antibiotics can be
used for prophylaxis of meningococcal meningitis.

Of note, he returned from Afghanistan two weeks ago. Examination
reveals a temperature of 38.1ºC, heart rate 89/min, blood pressure
123/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 17/min and oxygen saturations of 99%.
There is no evidence of no neck stiffness, objective photophobia,
jaundice or splenomegaly.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
Chikungunya
Zika virus
Plasmodium vivax
Plasmodium falciparum
Dengue fever
Question 34 of 287
A 19-year-old man attends the Emergency department with a fever for
the past one week. He notes that the fever comes on alternate days. He
reports also a co-existing headache, but no other particular symptoms.
Of note, he returned from Afghanistan two weeks ago. Examination
reveals a temperature of 38.1ºC, heart rate 89/min, blood pressure
123/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 17/min and oxygen saturations of 99%.
There is no evidence of no neck stiffness, objective photophobia,
jaundice or splenomegaly.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Fever in the returning traveller is a common presentation in the
Emergency department. A knowledge of the areas travelled and
incubation periods is essential to accurately diagnosing the potential
infectious disease.
Chikungunya is a viral disease transmitted to humans via infected
mosquitos. Fever and joint pain is the mos common presentation. The
incubation period is 2-12 days.
Zika virus is currently not present in Afghanistan.
Dengue fever has a incubation period of 4-10 days.
This leaves plasmodium falciparum, which has a usual incubation of 7-
14 days (but up to 3 months), and plasmodium vivax which has a typical
incubation of 12-17 days (but reported up to 12 months) following
exposure. Factors that point away from p. falciparum are the milder
presentation and the much lower prevalence of it in Afghanistan (p.
falciparum 5%, p. vivax 95%). Furthermore, fever due to malaria on
alternate days, known as benign tertian malaria, is suggestive of either p.
vivax or p. ovale. Comparatively, p. falciparum will typically cause more
of a continuous fever.

A 56-year-old woman with a history of type 2 diabetes and hypertension,
who is currently taking metformin and lisinopril, presents to the
Emergency Department with a one-week history of dysuria, increased
urinary frequency, and lower abdominal discomfort. She denies
experiencing flank pain, nausea, or vomiting. On examination, her
temperature is 38.2 ºC, and she exhibits suprapubic tenderness.
Initial urinalysis demonstrates pyuria, positive leukocyte esterase, and
nitrites. She was commenced on oral ciprofloxacin; however, her urinary
symptoms have persisted, and she has developed recurrent fevers.
Subsequent urine culture reveals an ESBL-producing E. coli infection.
What is the most appropriate next step in managing this woman's
condition?
Continue ciprofloxacin
Switch to aztreonam
Switch to ceftazidime
Switch to meropenem
Switch to piperacillin-tazobactam
Question 35 of 287
A 56-year-old woman with a history of type 2 diabetes and hypertension,
who is currently taking metformin and lisinopril, presents to the

experiencing flank pain, nausea, or vomiting. On examination, her
temperature is 38.2 ºC, and she exhibits suprapubic tenderness.
Initial urinalysis demonstrates pyuria, positive leukocyte esterase, and
nitrites. She was commenced on oral ciprofloxacin; however, her urinary
symptoms have persisted, and she has developed recurrent fevers.
Subsequent urine culture reveals an ESBL-producing E. coli infection.
What is the most appropriate next step in managing this woman's
condition?
explanation:
Switch to meropenem is the correct answer. The clinical presentation
and urine analysis indicate a urinary tract infection that has not
responded to ciprofloxacin therapy. The urine culture has confirmed the
presence of extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)-producing E.coli,
Carbapenems (e.g. meropenem) are useful in the management of
ESBL-producing bacteria
which demonstrates resistance to a range of antibiotics, including
quinolones such as ciprofloxacin, third-generation cephalosporins like
ceftazidime, and penicillins including amoxicillin and ampicillin. Among
the options provided, meropenem is the preferred treatment. This
antibiotic is part of the beta-lactam class within the carbapenems
subgroup and is effective against ESBL-producing organisms like ESBL-
producing E.coli.
Continue ciprofloxacin is unsuitable given that there has been no initial
response to this drug, coupled with emerging resistance in ESBL-
producing bacteria. Ciprofloxacin belongs to the fluoroquinolone family,
primarily targeting gram-negative and atypical bacteria, with some
activity against gram-positive species.
Switch to aztreonam is an incorrect option. Aztreonam, a monobactam,
is hydrolysed by extended-spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBLs), rendering
it ineffective against most ESBL-producing organisms unless combined
with a beta-lactamase inhibitor (BLI) such as avibactam. Studies have
shown that ESBL-producing E. coli exhibits high resistance to aztreonam
monotherapy, with resistance rates exceeding 90% in some reports.
Therefore, aztreonam alone is not suitable for treating infections caused
by ESBL-producing E. coli.
Switch to piperacillin-tazobactam is an incorrect choice. It falls under
the extended-spectrum penicillin antibiotic category (a part of beta-
lactams). While it may work for ESBL-producing E.coli, guidelines
generally prioritise carbapenems (such as meropenem) for complicated
or treatment-refractory ESBL infections to ensure a robust clinical cure.
Switch to ceftazidime is ineffective against ESBL-producing bacteria. It
is a third-generation cephalosporin with anti-pseudomonal properties.
Notably, ceftazidime-avibactam – a newer agent within this class – has
some efficacy against ESBL-producing pathogens.

and she is visibly coryzal. Her chest is clear to auscultation. Her chest X-

been closed to visitors due to an Influenza outbreak. Which of the

Empirical antibiotics for pneumonia
Zanamivir
Oseltamivir
Ribavirin
Salbutamol nebulisers
Question 37 of 287
An 81-year-old nursing home resident presents with a 48-hour history of
pyrexia, myalgia and coryza. On examination, her temperature is 37.9ºC
and she is visibly coryzal. Her chest is clear to auscultation. Her chest X-
ray is clear. Her relatives inform you that the nursing home has recently
been closed to visitors due to an Influenza outbreak. Which of the
following drugs should you also consider adding?
explanation:
Oseltamivir (Tamiflu) is the first-line treatment recommended for
patients with suspected or confirmed Influenza A. Ribavirin has not be
shown to be efficacious in the management of influenza. Zanamivir is
useful in patients with a poor swallow or in those with suspected or
confirmed exposure to oseltamivir-resistant influenza.
Her chest X-ray is clear and therefore there is no role for the addition of
antibiotic therapy at this stage.
Salbutamol nebulisers can be useful in patients with wheeze, however,
appropriate isolation precautions should be secured prior to the
administration of nebulisers in patients with Influenza infection.

explanation:
The correct answer is ivermectin. This patient is likely to have developed
strongyloidiasis, a parasitic infection caused by the nematode
Strongyloides stercoralis. This is a widely-distributed helminth but the
majority of cases are seen in sub-Saharan Africa and South America.
Infection is frequently asymptomatic and the first clue is peripheral
eosinophilia. In this case, the episode described in Malawi is consistent
with larva currens, a rash that develops when the worm penetrates the
skin before entering the bloodstream. From here they spread through the
lungs, over the epiglottis, are swallowed, and settle in the small intestine,
where they lay their eggs. Respiratory symptoms are rare but cough and
wheeze may develop during pulmonary migration. In chronic infection,
abdominal pain and diarrhoea may occur. In the context of
immunocompromise, Strongyloides hyperinfection syndrome can occur,
presenting with bloody colitis and pneumonitis, often with pleural
effusions. The treatment of choice in all cases is ivermectin, although
albendazole and thiabendazole are alternatives.
Artemisinin combination therapy is incorrect. This is the treatment of
choice for most cases of uncomplicated malaria. Malaria does not tend
to cause eosinophilia or skin lesions, and she has been compliant with
prophylaxis. These factors suggest this is very unlikely to be the
diagnosis.
Melarsoprol is incorrect. This is an arsenic-based treatment option for
East African sleeping sickness, caused by Trypanosoma brucei
rhodesiense. This is a rapidly progressive form of sleeping sickness,
initially causing an influenza-like illness with arthralgia and
lymphadenopathy but quickly progressing to altered mental status and
death. Melarsoprol is associated with significant toxicity and would not
be used for strongyloidiasis.
Nifurtimox/eflornithine combination therapy is incorrect. This is a
treatment option for West African sleeping sickness, caused by the
protozoan parasite Trypanosoma brucei gambiense. This causes a
slowly progressive illness characterised by behavioural change,
alterations to the sleep-wake cycle, and finally coma. There are no
symptoms here to suggest this and it is not typically associated with
Ivermectin is the drug of choice for treatment of strongyloidiasis
eosinophilia.
Praziquantel is incorrect. This is the treatment of choice for
schistosomiasis, a tapeworm infection caused by a variety of species of
schistosomes. The organism uses freshwater snails as an intermediate
host before being released into the water, where it penetrates human
skin and settles in the gastrointestinal or genito-urinary tract depending
on the species. There may be an itchy rash at the time of infection,
known as cercarial dermatitis, but this would not move up the limb or be
described as serpiginous. Schistosomiasis often presents with
eosinophilia, but in this case, the patient has been careful to avoid going
in the water, making this unlikely to be the cause.
Strongyloides stercoralis
Strongyloides stercoralis is a human parasitic nematode worm. The
larvae are present in soil and gain access to the body by penetrating the
skin. Infection with Strongyloides stercoralis causes strongyloidiasis.

history of fever, headache, and a rash. He describes the rash as initially
consisting of small red spots that have since coalesced into larger,
darker areas. He has recently returned from travelling in a rural region of
Southeast Asia. On physical examination, you note a black eschar on his
left ankle and a diffuse maculopapular rash across his trunk and
extremities.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
Leptospirosis
Malaria
Rocky mountain spotted fever
Scrub typhus
Typhoid fever
Question 39 of 287
A 32-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a five-day
history of fever, headache, and a rash. He describes the rash as initially
consisting of small red spots that have since coalesced into larger,
darker areas. He has recently returned from travelling in a rural region of
Southeast Asia. On physical examination, you note a black eschar on his
left ankle and a diffuse maculopapular rash across his trunk and
extremities.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Scrub typhus is the correct diagnosis. The clinical picture of a 5-day
history of fever, headache, and a diffuse maculopapular rash involving
the trunk and extremities, in conjunction with a distinctive black eschar
on the left ankle, strongly suggests scrub typhus. This condition is an
endemic rickettsial infection in Southeast Asia caused by Orientia
tsutsugamushi, transmitted by larval mites, and targets endothelial cells.
Notably, less than 50% of patients exhibit an eschar at the site of the
mite bite. Untreated scrub typhus can be fatal. Doxycycline is the
treatment of choice.

Exposure to bats/caves is a risk factor for Marburg virus, which

viral hemorrhagic fever. This condition typically presents with an abrupt
onset of fever, headache and malaise and progresses to include
gastrointestinal symptoms, arthralgia/myalgia and subsequently
haemorrhagic complications with multi-organ dysfunction as evidenced
in this case. The incubation period before the onset of symptoms is
typically 3-10 days. In addition to the geographic and zoonotic risk
factors, it is the only diagnosis listed that could account for the
haemorrhagic complications in this scenario (oozing from venepuncture
sites and bleeding from mucosal membranes). Treatment is supportive
and the condition is associated with a high mortality rate.
Hepatitis A is incorrect. While this could account for jaundice and
transaminitis, it is typically a self-limiting illness and associated with
fulminant liver failure only in very rare cases. It is not associated with
haemorrhagic complications.
Leptospirosis is incorrect. While this condition can present with fever,
headache and liver dysfunction, the traditional vectors for transmission
are mice, rats, cows and pigs. It is transmitted classically by coming into
contact with infected urine. While it is associated with subconjunctival
haemorrhage, it is not usually associated with more diffuse
haemorrhage as seen in this case. It is treated with antibiotics.
Malaria is incorrect. While this is the most common cause of the fever in
the returning traveller, the patient has taken malaria prophylaxis and has
had negative testing for malaria in addition to experiencing
haemorrhagic complications, all of which make a diagnosis of malaria
unlikely.
Typhoid is incorrect. While this is a common cause of fever in the
returning traveller and is associated with fever and diarrhoea, it would
not account for the haemorrhagic complications detailed in this
scenario.

complains of a chronic cough with night sweats for five weeks. On direct
questioning, he also admits coughing up small volumes of bright red
blood a few times. This has made him especially concerned as he his
father died from lung related problems following chronic coughs.
Following a chest X-ray and blood tests he is diagnosed with TB and
contact tracing is started. His 25-year-old male partner lives with him
and is identified as being at high risk of contracting TB. The partner
undergoes Mantoux testing and has a 2mm area of induration. He has
never had BCG vaccination as far as he is aware and has no vaccination
scar. What is the most appropriate management that should be offered
to the partner?
BCG vaccination
HIV testing and if negative then BCG vaccination
Prophylactic anti-TB treatment
Repeat TB screening in six weeks
No further management needed

A 27-year-old man who recently immigrated to the UK from Ethiopia
complains of a chronic cough with night sweats for five weeks. On direct
questioning, he also admits coughing up small volumes of bright red
blood a few times. This has made him especially concerned as he his
father died from lung related problems following chronic coughs.
Following a chest X-ray and blood tests he is diagnosed with TB and
contact tracing is started. His 25-year-old male partner lives with him
and is identified as being at high risk of contracting TB. The partner
undergoes Mantoux testing and has a 2mm area of induration. He has
never had BCG vaccination as far as he is aware and has no vaccination
scar. What is the most appropriate management that should be offered
to the partner?
options: HIV testing and if negative then BCG vaccination
Repeat TB screening in six weeks
explanation:
The correct answer is HIV testing and if negative then BCG vaccination.
The low area of response to the Mantoux testing indicates that he is
unlikely to have TB and has not been vaccinated. However, the test can
be a false negative result in an immunosuppressed patient. As the
partner is at increased risk of HIV, NICE advises that an HIV test should
be done prior to vaccination. BCG vaccination is a live vaccination and
therefore is contraindicated in an immunosuppressed patient. Of note,
previous vaccination can lead to a false positive result.
NICE advises that once a diagnosis of pulmonary TB has been made
then close contacts should be managed as follow:
If asymptomatic and younger than 65 years then test for latent TB. If
Mantoux-negative and unvaccinated then offer vaccination. If at risk
of HIV then test for HIV first.
If asymptomatic and older than 65 years then assess with a chest X-
ray.
Treatment for TB should be considered if TB is confirmed and not used
prophylactically. Repeat screening is generally not used.
Source:
'Tuberculosis NICE Guidelines.' The National Institute for Health and Care
Excellence, 13 Jan. 2016.

Yellow fever is endemic around the equator mainly in Africa. It is
transmitted by the Aedes mosquitoes there. Characteristically the
patient presents with fever and constitutional symptoms. Jaundice is a
main clinical sign associated most of the times with conjunctival
injection. Other important clinical signs are relative bradycardia, and
hemorrhagic diathesis. The cause of death is due to multi-organ failure.
Blood tests generally show leucopenia with predominant neutropenia
but this is not specific. Liver enzymes are elevated most of the time.
Diagnosis depends on a high degree of suspicion for the disease and but
also more important on serology which is highly specific for this lethal
condition.
Treatment is mainly supportive.
Primary sclerosing cholangitis could present with fever and jaundice.
This would happen in the context of ascending cholangitis (fever + pain
+ jaundice) with a long history of abdominal discomfort. Liver profile
would reflect obstructive changes.
Malaria should be excluded in any patient who had traveled to an
endemic area and developed fever. The picture in our patient was not
typical and the blood film had been negative for malaria parasites.
However one has to keep it in mind if the clinical picture fits. In that case
one needs to repeat the blood film and to order serology.
Leptospirosis is a consideration here. But it usually responds to
antibiotics. Liver enzymes would generally be more mildly elevated.
Dengue fever mainly presents with headache, fever and rash. It is mainly
endemic in South East Asia.

You are the medical basic specialist trainee on call and have been asked
to see a gentleman who has just been admitted for a bad chest
infection. According to the ward nurse, he has developed an allergic
reaction after five minutes of vancomycin i.v infusion.
On arrival you proceed to examine this young man who is febrile,
obviously unwell and receiving oxygen via nasal prongs. He claims he
had not developed any new symptoms since admission but felt sudden
warmth and flushing few minutes into his vancomycin drip. On
examination he has crepitations in his left base.
Apart from generalised erythema he appears to be stable and there is no
immediate danger to his airways. His blood pressure was 105/67mmHg,
pulse was 99b/min and oxygen saturation on 4L oxygen was 95% (all
observations are similar to previous readings). He has never taken
vancomycin but states he is allergic to penicillin and ciprofloxacin.
Given the likely diagnosis, what is the next step in your management?
Immediately stop vancomycin
Continue vancomycin but at a slower rate
Continue vancomycin rate unchanged
Administer i.v chlorphenamine maleate and stop vancomycin
Urgent i.m adrenaline
Question 45 of 287
You are the medical basic specialist trainee on call and have been asked
to see a gentleman who has just been admitted for a bad chest
infection. According to the ward nurse, he has developed an allergic
reaction after five minutes of vancomycin i.v infusion.
On arrival you proceed to examine this young man who is febrile,
obviously unwell and receiving oxygen via nasal prongs. He claims he
had not developed any new symptoms since admission but felt sudden
warmth and flushing few minutes into his vancomycin drip. On
examination he has crepitations in his left base.
Apart from generalised erythema he appears to be stable and there is no
immediate danger to his airways. His blood pressure was 105/67mmHg,
pulse was 99b/min and oxygen saturation on 4L oxygen was 95% (all
observations are similar to previous readings). He has never taken
vancomycin but states he is allergic to penicillin and ciprofloxacin.
Given the likely diagnosis, what is the next step in your management?
options: Continue vancomycin but at a slower rate
Administer i.v chlorphenamine maleate and stop vancomycin
explanation:
Answer: continue vancomycin but at a slower rate.
This is typical red man syndrome caused by rapid infusion of
vancomycin i.v. Vancomycin should be administered diluted and at a rate
of 10mg/minutes for doses over 500mg i.v.
It is an IgE independent mast cell degranulation reaction that occurs up
to 10 minutes into receiving vancomycin i.v at a fast rate. It is not a true
allergic reaction thus vancomycin should be continued but at a lower
rate of infusion.
Antihistamine prophylaxis, lower but frequent dosing and 2 hour infusion
rate have been found to reduce the incidence of red man syndrome.
This gentleman is obviously unwell but his vitals and chest findings are
more in keeping with his chest infection and possible sepsis.

A 25-year-old sexually active woman presents with abnormal vaginal
discharge and burning during urination. A nucleic acid amplification test
(NAAT) for sexually transmitted infections is performed.
NAAT
positive for Chlamydia trachomatis
She has no allergies, is using oral contraceptives, and is not pregnant or
breastfeeding.
What antibiotic is most appropriate in this case?
explanation:
National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidance states
that doxycycline is now the first-line treatment for anyone over the age
of 13 diagnosed with Chlamydia who is not pregnant or breastfeeding.
This is therefore the correct answer.
Azithromycin is the second-line treatment recommended by NICE for
treating Chlamydia in patients for whom doxycycline is contraindicated
or not tolerated.
Chlamydia - treat with doxycycline
Ceftriaxone is used in the treatment of Gonorrhoea but is not
recommended for treating Chlamydia.
Erythromycin is a third-line agent recommended by NICE for treating
Chlamydia in patients for whom both doxycycline and azithromycin are
contraindicated or not tolerated.
Trimethoprim is indicated in treating urinary tract infections in some
populations however is not used in the treatment of Chlamydia.

A 33-year-old male with a previous history of asthma and HIV presents
for review to HIV clinic. He has been noticing weight gain, marks on his
abdomen and his partner has noticed that his face has been looking
more heavy-set over the last two months. He was diagnosed as having
HIV at the age of 19 following needle sharing and use of heroin. He has
had good retroviral control following starting treatment at the age of 20
with tenofovir, emtricitabine, atazanavir and ritonavir. His asthma has
been well controlled with only salbutamol until six months ago when due
to recurrent exacerbation due to upper respiratory tract infection his
treatment was escalated to include regular fluticasone. Repeat blood
tests show an undetectable viral load and a CD4 count of 900
cells/microliter. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
Weight gain secondary to tenofovir use
Weight gain secondary to emtricitabine use
Weight gain due to reduced exercise tolerance
Endogenous Cushing's syndrome
Iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome
Question 48 of 287
A 33-year-old male with a previous history of asthma and HIV presents
for review to HIV clinic. He has been noticing weight gain, marks on his
abdomen and his partner has noticed that his face has been looking
more heavy-set over the last two months. He was diagnosed as having
HIV at the age of 19 following needle sharing and use of heroin. He has
had good retroviral control following starting treatment at the age of 20
with tenofovir, emtricitabine, atazanavir and ritonavir. His asthma has
been well controlled with only salbutamol until six months ago when due
to recurrent exacerbation due to upper respiratory tract infection his
treatment was escalated to include regular fluticasone. Repeat blood
tests show an undetectable viral load and a CD4 count of 900
cells/microliter. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
options: Weight gain secondary to tenofovir use
Weight gain secondary to emtricitabine use
Weight gain due to reduced exercise tolerance
explanation:
The correct answer is iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome. HIV protease
inhibitors are potent P450 inhibitors. This means that there are many
possible interactions that should be checked before starting treatment.
In this gentleman, hepatic enzyme inhibition has resulted in increased
steroid dose from his regular inhaler for his asthma. This also explains
the physical description showing standard Cushingoid features.
Endogenous Cushing's syndrome is possible but is less likely, and weight
gain from other causes would not explain all the physical changes
described.
Saberi, Parya, Tony Phengrasamy, and Dong Phuong Nguyen. Inhaled
Corticosteroid Use in HIV-Positive Individuals Taking Protease Inhibitors:
A Review of Pharmacokinetics, Case Reports, and Clinical Management.
HIV medicine 14.9 (2013): 519529. PMC. Web. 7 Mar. 2017.

A 22-year-old second generation British Pakistani is seen by the
Tuberculosis (TB) Specialist Nurse as part of the contact tracing service.
Her mother has recently been diagnosed with active TB after presenting
to the respiratory clinic with a 3-month history of night sweats, weight
loss, and haemoptysis.
The patient is clinically well and denies any focal symptomatology. Her
past medical history is unremarkable and she is a non-smoker. She
studies full-time at university but continues to live at home with her
extended family. She was fully immunised as a child.
On examination, she is afebrile. Her respiratory rate is 16/min and her
oxygen saturations are 97% breathing room air. There is no cervical
lymphadenopathy, her chest is clear and her abdomen is soft and non-
tender.
A Mantoux test is performed and read 72 hours later, at which time a
7mm area of induration is noted lying within a 16mm area of erythema.
An interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) is requested. What does a
positive IGRA indicate?
Latent TB or prior immunisation
Latent TB
Prior immunisation
Active or latent TB
Active TB or prior immunisation
Question 49 of 287
A 22-year-old second generation British Pakistani is seen by the
Tuberculosis (TB) Specialist Nurse as part of the contact tracing service.
Her mother has recently been diagnosed with active TB after presenting
to the respiratory clinic with a 3-month history of night sweats, weight
loss, and haemoptysis.
The patient is clinically well and denies any focal symptomatology. Her
past medical history is unremarkable and she is a non-smoker. She
studies full-time at university but continues to live at home with her
extended family. She was fully immunised as a child.
On examination, she is afebrile. Her respiratory rate is 16/min and her
oxygen saturations are 97% breathing room air. There is no cervical
lymphadenopathy, her chest is clear and her abdomen is soft and non-
tender.
A Mantoux test is performed and read 72 hours later, at which time a
7mm area of induration is noted lying within a 16mm area of erythema.
An interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) is requested. What does a
positive IGRA indicate?
explanation:
The area of induration described in the vignette constitutes a positive
Mantoux test. The area of surrounding erythema is not taken into
account.
We are told that the patient has been fully immunised as a child and she
may have therefore received the Bacille Calmette-Guerin (BCG)
vaccination; a cause of a falsely positive Mantoux test. The other
possibilities, in this case, are active or latent TB. An IGRA would be
advantageous in this setting as prior BCG vaccination does not produce
a false positive result. A positive test would, therefore, indicate prior
exposure to M. tuberculosis.
The main disadvantage of the IGRA is its inability to distinguish between
active and latent TB.

A 25-year-old man presents to the genitourinary medicine clinic with a
penile lesion which has been present for the last three weeks but is now
starting to reduce in size. He has had two sexual partners in the last 2
months, who were both men. There is no history of travel outside of the
UK in the last 3 years.
The lesion is a shallow ulcer with well-defined margins, which is not
tender to palpation. He has some non-tender enlarged lymph nodes on
both sides in the inguinal region.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
Chancroid
Donovanosis
Lymphogranuloma venereum
M-pox
Primary syphilis
Question 50 of 287
A 25-year-old man presents to the genitourinary medicine clinic with a
penile lesion which has been present for the last three weeks but is now
starting to reduce in size. He has had two sexual partners in the last 2
months, who were both men. There is no history of travel outside of the
UK in the last 3 years.
The lesion is a shallow ulcer with well-defined margins, which is not
tender to palpation. He has some non-tender enlarged lymph nodes on
both sides in the inguinal region.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The correct answer is primary syphilis , which is caused by Treponema
pallidum. This classically presents with a chancre at the site of entry of
infection. This usually starts as a painless papule, which evolves into a
painless ulcer. The lesion is usually single but multiple lesions can occur.
It generally heals over a few weeks.
Chancroid is incorrect. This is a sexually transmitted disease caused by
Haemophilus ducreyi. However, unlike in this patient, the ulcers are
Primary syphilis is associated with painless ulceration
commonly multiple and very painful. The inguinal lymphadenopathy in
chancroid is also generally painful. Chancroid is rare in the UK, and most
cases are acquired abroad in Africa or South East Asia.
Donovanosis is incorrect. This condition is also called granuloma
inguinale and is caused by Klebsiella granulomatis. The genital ulcers in
this condition are painless with a classically 'beefy red' base. This
diagnosis is less likely in this patient because the ulcers would not start
to heal without treatment but would continue to enlarge, and because it
is rarely seen in the UK. It is most commonly seen in tropical regions.
Lymphogranuloma venereum is incorrect. This is caused by serovars L1,
L2 and L3 of Chlamydia trachomatis . It is more common in tropical areas
but does occur in the UK, mainly in men who have sex with men. It can
cause painless ulceration in the primary stage, but unlike in this
scenario, the ulcers are small and heal within 1-3 days so this stage is
generally not noticed by patients. The secondary stage is characterised
by painful swollen inguinal lymph nodes or anal symptoms in patients
who have acquired an anal/rectal infection.
M-pox is incorrect. The M-pox virus classically causes painful vesicular
lesions, which usually start at the site of inoculation and are generally
multiple. The lesions may then spread to involve other areas of the body.

A 44-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with cough,
haemoptysis, and episodes of epistaxis. Additionally, she reports a two
week history of fatigue, fever and muscle aches.
On examination, she appears icteric. Coarse crackles are heard on her
chest and she has right upper quadrant tenderness. There is tenderness
in both her calves and in her lower back.
She is usually fit and well, working as a vet in a nearby town. She is a
non-smoker and consumes around 20 units of alcohol a week. At home,
she has a pet cat.
Which of the following is most appropriate for this patient?
Advise her to isolate for the course of her infection as she is at
risk of transmission to others
Advise serology testing is most likely to confirm the diagnosis
After recovery she should be offered a vaccine as she has
occupational risk
Offer a short course of oral ciprofloxacin
She should be warned that her cat was likely the source of her
infection
Question 51 of 287
A 44-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with cough,
haemoptysis, and episodes of epistaxis. Additionally, she reports a two
week history of fatigue, fever and muscle aches.
On examination, she appears icteric. Coarse crackles are heard on her
chest and she has right upper quadrant tenderness. There is tenderness
in both her calves and in her lower back.
She is usually fit and well, working as a vet in a nearby town. She is a
non-smoker and consumes around 20 units of alcohol a week. At home,
she has a pet cat.
Which of the following is most appropriate for this patient?
options: Advise her to isolate for the course of her infection as she is at risk of transmission to others
Advise serology testing is most likely to confirm the diagnosis
After recovery she should be offered a vaccine as she has occupational risk
Offer a short course of oral ciprofloxacin
She should be warned that her cat was likely the source of her infection
explanation:
Serology is the most commonly used test for the diagnosis of
leptospirosis, however, antibodies may not be present until after 7
days
This patient has occupational and social history that increase the risk of
zoonotic infections. She has presented with a febrile illness with
components which include liver involvement and a coagulopathy.
Together with myalgia classically affecting the calves and lower back
this is suggestive of leptospirosis.
The diagnosis is most commonly made by serological testing for
specific antibodies. It is difficult to isolate the organism by culture. The
greatest diagnostic yield for culture is if it is done in the first 10 days of
the illness. After this point, the organisms are only intermittently present
in the blood. This patient has had symptoms for at least 2 weeks and
therefore culture pick-up rates are now even lower.
An infected individual will shed leptospires in their urine for the period of
the illness and for a time afterwards. Hence there is in theory a
transmittable route to others but only in a specific way. Respiratory
droplet transmission does not occur and so normal social interactions
are safe.
There is no vaccine against leptospirosis available. Therefore, hand
hygiene is important in those with occupational risk.
Most cases of leptospirosis are mild and self-resolve without
pharmacological management. Where antibiotics are employed,
doxycycline or azithromycin are often used. Amoxicillin is also effective.
Leptospirosis is classically associated with rats, which are the most
common source of transmission, but other sources include dogs, cattle
and pigs.

This patient clearly has an infective process so much of the data

We're now left with more concrete findings: jaundice,
hepatosplenomegaly and a raised creatinine.
Now we take one of these findings, hepatosplenomegaly and consider

Causes of hepatosplenomegaly
chronic liver disease with portal hypertension

amyloidosis
This suggests that malaria is the most likely diagnosis. Jaundice and a
raised creatinine are consistent with this.

explanation:
The patient has PCP pneumonia, caused by Pneumocystis jirovecii - a
yeast-like fungus which is an opportunistic pathogen. The treatment for
this is co-trimoxazole.
Pneumocystis jiroveci penumonia is treated with co-trimoxazole,
which is a mix of trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole
All patients with dermatomyositis or polymyositis with pulmonary
fibrosis who are treated with glucocorticoids are advised to receive PCP
prophylaxis with co-trimoxazole. Stopping steroids would not be
appropriate in this scenario.
It is important to note that not all patients taking glucocorticoids for
rheumatological conditions require PCP prophylaxis. However, there is
evidence that in non-HIV cohorts, the greatest risk for developing PCP is
glucocorticoid use and deficiencies in innate and acquired immune
components. Therefore, although there are currently no formal
guidelines it is recommended that if an individual satisfies both these
criteria in rheumatological conditions, they should be considered for PCP
prophylaxis.
For example the following all should be considered for prophylaxis:
A patient on the equivalent of 20 mg prednisolone or greater for one
month plus the concomitant use of another immunosuppressive
drug
Dermatomyositis on high dose prednisolone for greater than one
month and pulmonary fibrosis
Allogenic or autogenic stem cell transplant or solid organ
transplantation

down the infusion of vancomycin and administration of anti-histamines.

explanation:
Typhoid or enteric fever is the commonest serious tropical disease
requiring treatment from Asia. Incubation period 7-18 days (range: 3-60
days). The highest incidence is found in south-central Asia and south-
east Asia.
Patients most commonly present with fever, headache,
constipation/diarrhoea, malaise, anorexia, dry cough, abdominal pain,
hepatosplenomegaly, Rose spot rash, bradycardia and potentially
misleading symptoms including meningism may occur.
Transmission is usually from contaminated food or water, occasionally
direct faecal-oral transmission, shellfish taken from sewage-polluted
areas, ingestion of contaminated milk and milk products and flies may
cause human infection through the transfer of infectious agents to
foods. Around 25% of those who contract typhoid fever become chronic
carriers, as bacteria persist in the biliary tract after symptoms have
resolved.
Investigations may reveal raised WCC, deranged LFTS. Blood cultures
have the highest yield within the first week of symptoms (sensitivity 40-
80%). Diagnosis can also be made from stool and urine cultures
(become positive after the first week) and bone marrow cultures.
Treatment is with quinolones most commonly ciprofloxacin. However,
there has been increasing reports of quinolones resistance in patients
returned from Asia and intravenous ceftriaxone may be used. If
quinolone resistance is confirmed azithromycin or cefixime are suitable
oral alternatives for uncomplicated disease. Treatment should be
continued for 14 days to reduce the risk of relapse. The addition of
steroids may be helpful in severe cases

The Salmonella group contains many members, most of which cause
diarrhoeal diseases. They are aerobic, Gram-negative rods which are not
normally present as commensals in the gut.
Typhoid and paratyphoid are caused by Salmonella typhi and Salmonella
paratyphi (types A, B & C) respectively. They are often termed enteric
fevers, producing systemic symptoms such as headache, fever,
arthralgia.

options: Metronidazole for 1 week, then diloxanide for 1 week
explanation:
Treatment for invasive amoebiasis should be followed by a luminal
amoebicide to eradicate the cystic stage which is resistant to
Metronidazole for 1 week, then diloxanide for 1 week is the correct
answer. This patient has amoebiasis, with the spherical cysts
representing Entamoeba histolytica cysts. The incubation period is from
days to years. Amoebiasis has a worldwide distribution but is more
common in tropical and subtropical regions. Metronidazole treats
Entamoeba trophozoites (but has insufficient activity against cysts).
Diloxanide or paromomycin are luminal agents that are active in the
bowel - they treat the Entamoeba cysts but are poorly absorbed, and so
are ineffective against organisms outside the bowel. Therefore a
combination of medications is required.
Abscess aspiration is the incorrect answer. Indications for abscess
aspiration in amoebiasis are:
Abscesses in the left liver lobe (possible rupture into pericardium)
Abscesses >10cm in diameter
Severe pain
Marked diaphragm elevation
Abscesses that fail to respond to medical management
Impending abscess rupture
Amoxicillin + ciprofloxacin + metronidazole is the incorrect answer. This
is the recommended treatment for bacterial liver abscesses, but this will
not treat amoebiasis. Patients with bacterial liver abscesses are likely to
be significantly more unwell (septic). They will also not have the
characteristic cysts or trophozoites on stool microscopy.
Metronidazole for 1 week is the incorrect answer. Metronidazole will
treat the Entamoeba trophozoites, but not the cysts.
Praziquantel is the incorrect answer. Praziquantel is an anti-helminthic
drug and will not treat Entamoeba histolytica, which is a protozoan.
Praziquantel (in combination with percutaneous aspiration) can be used
to treat hydatid liver cysts caused by Echinococcus granulosus. Hydatid
cysts tend to be multi-loculated and asymptomatic.

admitted for observation and immediately commenced on empirical

treatment should be commenced immediately and not withheld until the
results of swabs are available.

evidence of pneumonia on chest X-ray.

explanation:
Discussion of this case with microbiology would likely result in the
suggestion of imaging. In someone who has appropriate antimicrobial
treatment, regrowth of the same organism would not be expected so
soon. This may indicate there is a source of the bacteria that is not being
adequately treated - a renal abscess in this case, which may be identified
on ultrasound.
Escalation to meropenem should not be considered necessary if the
organism has been fully sensitive to the narrower spectrum antibiotics.
E. coli would be an unlikely source of hospital-acquired pneumonia.
Urology referral would be the next step should a renal abscess be
identified.
Imaging should first be carried out to determine whether a nephrostomy
is required.

Question 62 of 287
A 28-year-old man who has recently immigrated from Nigeria presents
with a penile ulcer. He reports that it initially started as a small lump but
then later progressed to a painful ulcer.
On examination, there is a 7mm diameter tender single ulcer with an
undermined ragged edge just proximal to the glans of the penis.
Examination of the testes and anal region is unremarkable. There is
tender inguinal lymphadenopathy.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Chancroid is a bacterial sexually transmitted infection characterised by
painful sores on the genitalia. It is caused by the gram-negative
coccobacillus Haemophilus ducreyi. It is a disease found primarily in
developing countries.
H. ducreyi enters the skin through microabrasions incurred during sexual
intercourse. A local tissue reaction leads to the development of an
erythematous papule, which progresses to a pustule in 4-7 days. It then
undergoes central necrosis to ulcerate.
The ulcer can range in size from 3 to 50 mm across. It is painful and has
sharply defined undermined borders
Other features include:
Irregular or ragged borders
A base that is covered with a grey or yellowish-gray material
A base that bleeds easily if traumatised or scraped
Painful lymphadenopathy in 30 to 60% of patients.
Dysuria and dyspareunia in females
About half of infected men have only a single ulcer. Women frequently
have four or more ulcers, with fewer symptoms.

A 25-year-old man presents to gastroenterology with a 6-month history
of unexplained chronic diarrhoea and unexplained chronic weight loss.
An HIV test is sent as part of his work-up and returns positive. His CD4
count is 150. He is started on anti-retroviral therapy.
Round oocysts measuring between 4 and 6 µm are seen during
microscopy of the patient's stool sample. They stain red using the
modified acid-fast stain. A diagnosis of Cryptosporidium is made. The
first-line treatment of nitazoxanide is not available.
What other medication could be a potential treatment option for this
patient?
explanation:
The oocysts described on stool microscopy are typical of
Cryptosporidium. Cyclospora and Isospora oocysts will also stain with the
modified acid-fast stain. The oocysts of Cyclospora look similar to those
of Cryptosporidium but are larger at 8-10 µm. Isospora oocysts are oval
shaped and are larger again at 10-20 x 20-30 µm.
Cryptosporidiosis is a protozoal infection that generally causes mild,
Rifaxamin is licensed for the treatment of cryptosporidiosis
watery diarrhoea in immune-competent patients, although symptoms
can persist for several weeks. It can cause chronic diarrhoea in immune
suppressed patients, especially those with HIV infection. Treatment is
not always required as the symptoms often improve once the immune
system starts to recover. If treatment is indicated the first line option is
nitazoxanide, followed by rifaximin.
Ciprofloxacin can be used for some causes of infectious diarrhoea, such
as Campylobacter and Salmonella but does not treat Cryptosporidium.
Metronidazole is effective against anaerobic bacteria and some
protozoa (including Giardia) but is not active against Cryptosporidium.
Nitrofurantoin is mainly used for the treatment of lower urinary tract
infections due to Gram negative rods and will not treat Cryptosporidium.
Prednisolone may worsen the patient's symptoms by increasing his level
of immune suppression so would not be a good treatment option in this
case.

comes to the emergency department with fever, non-productive cough
and shortness of breath for the past 2 days. He has also had a
headache, abdominal pain and diarrhoea since yesterday. The patient
has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, and a smoking history of 20
pack-years. He does not use alcohol or illicit drugs. His temperature is
39.2ºC, blood pressure is 110/65 mmHg, pulse is 80/min and
respirations are 18/min. Pulse oximetry shows 97% on room air.
Lung examination demonstrates crackles bilaterally. The abdomen is
soft and non-tender. The patient seems confused at times during the
examination. His serum glucose is normal; serum sodium is 128 mmol/l.
Chest x-ray demonstrates bilateral interstitial infiltrates. He is admitted
to the ward.
Which of the following antibiotics should be given to this patient?
explanation:
This patient has bilateral lung infiltrates, confusion and diarrhoea
following travel. Legionella pneumonia (Legionnaires' disease) must be
considered. Travel-associated Legionnaires' disease due to
contaminated water supplies is a well-documented condition linked to
cruise ships and hotels. Legionella pneumophila is a Gram-negative
bacilli that stains poorly as it is primarily intracellular; hence Gram stain
showing many neutrophils but no organisms is characteristic.
Legionnaires' disease is treated with antibiotics that achieve high
intracellular concentration, particularly macrolides or fluoroquinolones
(such as levofloxacin). The latter is favoured when the illness is severe
enough to warrant admission.
Choice 1: Co-amoxiclav is typically used in some cases of CAP, but not
Legionnaires' disease. It has activity against beta-lactamase-producing
Haemophilus and Moraxella species.
Choice 2: Ceftriaxone has good activity against pneumococcus as well
as Haemophilus and Moraxella. It does not have activity against
Legionella or other causes of atypical pneumonia.
Choice 3: Clindamycin is used primarily to treat infections with anaerobic
organisms; Legionella has aerobic activity.
Choice 5: Vancomycin has no activity against Legionella or most other
causes of atypical pneumonia.

which preceded Giemsa staining.

explanation:
The progressive neurological symptoms with demyelination on MRI
points to progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML).
PML is a demyelinating disease of the CNS due to the JC virus. It occurs
almost exclusively in immunosuppressed individuals with the majority of
cases being secondary to HIV infection. Patients typically experience
insidious onset of focal symptoms that include mainly behavior,
cognitive, speech, and motor functions. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)

psychiatric manifestation. But it would not explain the motor
deterioration nor the cognitive decline for this patient.

multifocal leukoencephalopathy

This lady of African background presents initially with fever after
travelling from Nigeria and goes on to develop chronic symptoms of
daytime somnolence, continuous headaches and behavioural changes.
These symptoms suggest African Sleeping Sickness or African
Trypanosomiasis. Trypanosoma gambiense is more common than
Trypanosoma rhodesiense in patients from West Africa, such as Nigeria.
Early stages of the disease tends to present about 3 weeks after being
bitten by an infected tsetse fly. Symptoms include fevers, arthralgia,
lethargy, drowsiness. Late stages include behavioural and mood
changes, headache and the pathognomonic daytime somnolence with
nocturnal insomnia.
Borrelia burgdorferi is transmitted by ticks (Ixodes spp.) and causes
Lyme disease. They occur in the USA, northern and central European
countries, and temperate forested areas of Asia.
Plasmodium vivax is one species of Plasmodium, the parasite that
causes malaria. It is spread by infected mosquitoes. It is an important
differential of fever in the returning traveller, however as the initial
malaria screens were negative, and the central nervous system
symptoms in the late stages are not consistent with a malarial infection.
Trypanosoma cruzi is responsible for American Trypanosomiasis (or
Chagas' disease). It is transmitted by contamination with infected faeces
of assassin bugs (reduviid bugs). It is found in South America and the
south USA. Chronic infection can lead to chronic congestive heart
failure, megaoesophagus and megacolon.

Leishmaniasis is caused by the protozoa parasite Leishmania tropica or
Leishmania mexicana which are transmitted via sandfly mainly in the
tropics and sub-tropics of Africa, Asia and the Americas. Cutaneous
leishmaniasis is the commonest form of leishmaniasis, which presents
an open sore at the bite sites. The lesions can develop over several
months or even years leaving unpleasant-looking scars.
African trypanosomiasis is caused by the protozoa parasite
Trypanosoma bruce which is transmitted via tsetse flies. The condition
causes systemic symptoms in the form initially of fevers, headaches and
joint pain, before progressing to cognitive impairment. Cutaneous
lesions are not commonly associated with the condition.
Chromoblastomycosis is normally found in rural region of tropical and
subtropical climates however it is a chronic fungal infection of the skin.
It can be caused by a number of different fungi that are implanted under
the skin, often by thorns or splinters. Analysis of skin scraping would
confirm the presence of muriform cells, indicative of the fungal infection.
Kaposi's sarcoma (KS) is a type of cancer that can form nodular, blotchy-
like lesions red, purple, brown, or black in colour on the skin of the lower
limbs, back, face and genitals, as well as mouth and organs lesions. KS
is a result of immune suppression and infection by human herpesvirus 8;
it is an aids defining condition and therefore is normally seen in
untreated HIV. Diagnosis is via confirming the presents of human
herpesvirus 8.

explanation:
Headache, fever, rash on the peripheries before spreading centrally,
tick bite → Rocky Mountain spotted fever (Rickettsia ricketsii)
Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever is the correct diagnosis. The clinical
presentation of fever, headache, and a rash that started on the
extremities and subsequently spread to the face and trunk, coupled with
a travel history to South America (specifically Bolivia) and a tick bite,
should prompt consideration of Rocky Mountain spotted fever. This
disease involves the proliferation of intracellular bacteria Rickettsia
rickettsii at the site of the tick bite, predominantly affecting the
endothelium of small vessels. Laboratory findings such as
thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, and raised liver enzymes further support
this diagnosis.
Babesiosis represents a tick-borne disease caused by protozoan
parasites of the Babesia genus. Transmission is primarily through Ixode
ticks. While it shares common features with Rocky Mountain spotted
fever, including fever, headache, thrombocytopenia, and increased liver
enzyme levels, Babesiosis characteristically does not present with a rash
and mainly infects erythrocytes.
Dengue Fever is an arboviral infection endemic in the Americas
transmitted by mosquitoes carrying dengue virus. Clinical
manifestations typically include fever, retro-orbital pain, severe myalgia,
and a distinctive rash which commences with facial flushing before
progressing to a second maculopapular rash on the back of hands and
feet extending to the torso. However, this type of rash differs from that
described in the scenario provided.
Lyme disease, another tick-borne illness caused by spirochetes of
Borrelia burgdorferi, is transmitted via hard ticks. It typically presents
with an expanding area of localised erythema with central clearing
(erythema migrans), often resembling a bull's-eye pattern at the tick bite
location. The rash does not match Lyme disease but suggests Rocky
Mountain spotted fever.
Tularemia is an uncommon zoonotic infection caused by Francisella
tularensis bacteria and transmitted by ticks. It can cause symptoms
such as fever, painful ulcerative lesions at inoculation sites with
associated regional lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and
potentially community-acquired pneumonia. The patient's clinical
features do not correspond with those commonly associated with
tularemia.

Question 212 of 287
A farmer presents with a tender lesion on his finger:
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The correct answer is Orf. Orf, also known as contagious ecthyma, is a
zoonotic disease caused by a parapoxvirus that primarily affects sheep
and goats. Humans can contract the disease through direct contact with
infected animals or via fomites. The typical presentation includes a
painful, red nodule on the hand or finger, often with central ulceration.
This aligns with the farmer's occupation and the clinical picture
presented.
Paronychia is an infection of the skin around the nail, typically caused by
staphylococci or streptococci bacteria. It presents with redness, swelling
and tenderness at the side of the nail bed. Although this could be
plausible given the patient's profession, it does not account for all his
symptoms nor does it match the image provided.
Tetanus, caused by Clostridium tetani, is characterised by muscle
stiffness and spasms due to neurotoxins produced by this bacterium
following wound contamination. While farmers are at an increased risk
due to potential exposure to soil and animal faeces where Clostridium
tetani spores reside, tetanus would not present as a single tender lesion
on a finger.
Anthrax is another zoonotic disease caused by Bacillus anthracis.
Cutaneous anthrax usually presents as a painless black eschar after an
incubation period of 1-7 days post-exposure. However, in this case, there
is no mention of exposure to livestock products such as hides or wool
which would increase suspicion of anthrax.
Finally, Hand, foot and mouth disease (HFMD), commonly caused by
coxsackievirus A16 or enterovirus 71, primarily affects children under 10
years old. It presents with fever and vesicular lesions in the mouth and
on hands/feet/buttocks. The age group affected and characteristic
distribution of lesions make HFMD less likely in this scenario.

explanation:

hemisphere. It is relatively rare in the UK, with risk being greatest in rural
forested areas such as the Scottish highlands, New Forest and Lake

of the spirochete phylum.
Clinical features of Lyme borreliosis include erythema migrans in 90% of
symptomatic individuals, which tends to occur to 2-40 days following
exposure. Erythema migrans has the classical appearance described in
the question but may be homogeneous in the early phase and can be
confused for cellulitis or a simple insect bite. Rarely, a non-specific
febrile illness without rash can occur. Neurological involvement
consisting of meningitis or cranial nerve palsy can occur in early
infection.
Erythema migrans is a clinical diagnosis and does not require
serological confirmation. Therefore, the patient should be treated
immediately with a 2-3 week course of oral doxycycline or amoxicillin,

Serological testing for pathogenic Borrelia species in 4 weeks (to allow for seroconversion)

explanation:
This patient has a convincing history for the attachment of ticks from a
region of the UK at high risk of Lyme borreliosis. When assessing the risk
of tick bites it is important to clarify for how long the tick was attached
and if it became engorged. Transmission of pathogenic Borrelia species
is unlikely if ticks are attached for less than 24 hours or do not become
engorged. Ticks should be removed gently using tweezers to minimise
irritation to the skin and the risk of rupturing the tick which can increase
the risk of infection.
Asymptomatic patients who report a tick bite should not undergo
serological testing or receive treatment. Testing can lead to false
positives secondary to previous infection or cross-reactive antibodies.
Prophylactic treatment of tick bites may be required if the patient is
immunosuppressed or in certain regions of the USA where the
prevalence of infected ticks is particularly high.
When serological testing is indicated paired blood samples should be
taken at four week intervals to allow seroconversion to take place.
Treatment with doxycycline or amoxicillin for 14 days is the appropriate
treatment for a patient presenting with erythema migrans after a tick
bite.

2012;344:e3124.

This patient presents with classic features of visceral leishmaniasis
(kala-azar) acquired during travel to Bihar, India, an endemic region. The
clinical presentation includes fever, night sweats, weight loss despite
preserved appetite, grey skin discolouration, massive splenomegaly, and
hepatomegaly. Laboratory findings show pancytopenia (reduced
haemoglobin, white cells, and platelets) and mildly deranged liver
function tests. The diagnosis is confirmed by the presence of Leishman-
Donovan bodies in bone marrow aspirate, which is the gold standard
diagnostic test for visceral leishmaniasis.
Sodium stibogluconate is the correct answer and the recommended
first-line treatment for visceral leishmaniasis in the UK according to
British National Formulary guidelines. It is an organic pentavalent
antimony compound that has been used for decades to treat
leishmaniasis. The drug works by inhibiting glycolytic enzymes and fatty
acid oxidation in the Leishmania parasite. A typical course lasts 28-30
days with daily intravenous or intramuscular administration. While
resistance has emerged in some regions, particularly in parts of India, it
remains an effective first-line agent in most cases. Side effects include
cardiotoxicity, hepatotoxicity, and pancreatitis, so monitoring is required
during treatment.
Amphotericin B is incorrect as first-line therapy according to UK
guidelines, although it is an important alternative treatment for visceral
leishmaniasis. Liposomal amphotericin B is particularly effective and
may be used when sodium stibogluconate fails or is contraindicated, or
in regions with high antimony resistance. It works by binding to
ergosterol in the parasite cell membrane, creating pores that lead to cell
death. While effective, it is generally reserved as second-line therapy or
used in combination with sodium stibogluconate in the UK setting.

Rifampicin and isoniazid (with pyridoxine) for 3 months is correct. This
patient has latent Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection: he has a
positive interferon-gamma release assay but negative sputum for acid-
fast bacilli and nucleic acid amplification tests as well as a normal chest
x-ray. Latent Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can either be treated
with 3 months of rifampicin and isoniazid or with 6 months of isoniazid.
No treatment required is incorrect. This patient has a positive interferon-
gamma release assay. This suggests either active or latent
Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. Given the negative nucleic acid
amplification test, sputum smear for acid-fast bacilli, and normal chest
x-ray, it is likely this patient has latent Mycobacterium tuberculosis
infection. This requires treatment with either 3 months of rifampicin and
isoniazid or 6 months of isoniazid alone.
Pyridoxine for 6 months is incorrect. Pyridoxine is a form of vitamin B6
and is used for the prevention of isoniazid-induced neuropathy. It is not
in itself used as part of the treatment of Mycobacterium tuberculosis
infection.
Rifampicin, isoniazid (with pyridoxine), pyrazinamide, and ethambutol
for 2 months, then rifampicin and isoniazid for 10 months is incorrect.
This is the treatment regimen for active Mycobacterium tuberculosis
infection with CNS involvement. It is also usually accompanied by a
course of steroids. The patient in this case, however, has latent
Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, evidenced by the positive
interferon-gamma release assay but negative sputum for acid-fast bacilli
and nucleic acid amplification tests as well as a normal chest x-ray.
Rifampicin, isoniazid (with pyridoxine), pyrazinamide, and ethambutol
for 2 months, then rifampicin and isoniazid for 4 months is incorrect.
This is the treatment regimen for active Mycobacterium tuberculosis
infection without CNS involvement. The patient in this question has
latent Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, so this answer is incorrect.
Positive IGRA, but asymptomatic and normal CXR → treat as for
latent tuberculosis

Reduced risk of AIDS and mortality
Reduced drug resistance

Question 76 of 287
A 24-year-old male patient is referred to HIV clinic following positive
testing on screening in a local GUM clinic. His CD4 count is 1020
cells/microlitre and viral load is 10,123 copies/ml. He is offered to start
antiretroviral treatment or monitoring. He has a past medical history of
depression and has emigrated from Nigeria three years ago. He is
planning to return abroad in two years. What benefit has been
established from starting early antiretroviral treatment as opposed to
deferring treatment?
options: Reduced risk of AIDS and mortality
explanation:
The correct answer is the reduced the risk of AIDS and mortality. BHIVA
has made the recommendation to offer antiviral therapy regardless of
the CD4 count. This is partly due to results of the SMART study which
demonstrated reduced chance of AIDS, a serious non-AIDS event or
death by 57% with similar results in high, middle and low-income
countries. Data on virological efficacy, drug resistance and toxicity is not
yet established. Reduced anxiety may also be a benefit but has not been
as definitively established.
Source:
'BHIVA Guidelines for the Treatment of HIV-1-positive Adults with
Antiretroviral Therapy 2015.' BHIVA. , Aug. 2016.

Heart rate 100 beats per minute

Respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute
Oxygen saturations 98%
Temperature 36.2 ºC
What is the most appropriate management option?
options: Test for IgM antibodies and if present start aciclovir
Test for serum measles DNA and if present provide immunoglobulin
explanation:
Providing immunoglobulin (Ig) is correct as the child is unvaccinated,
immunocompromised due to methotrexate and has had exposure to
measles. The MMR vaccination can also be offered to patients who are
unvaccinated and have exposure as vaccine-induced measles antibody
develops more rapidly than that following natural infection.
No treatment is incorrect. The child is unvaccinated,
immunocompromised and most likely had significant measles exposure
therefore immunoglobulin should be provided as a minimum.
Aciclovir is incorrect as it does not play a role in post-exposure
prophylaxis or the treatment of active measles.
Testing for serum measles DNA is incorrect as measles is an RNA
paramyxovirus and also this will have no impact on management.
IgM antibodies can be tested for, and are normally present within a few
days of rash onset however aciclovir is not indicated in measle post-
exposure prophylaxis.

making it a less likely diagnosis.

preceding phase of flu-like symptoms before the onset of respiratory
symptoms including shortness of breath and productive cough. Extra-
pulmonary symptoms are common in patients with Mycoplasma
pneumoniae and include erythema multiforme and haemolytic anaemia.
The absence of these extra-pulmonary symptoms and the occupational
history as a farmer make the diagnosis of Q fever more likely.

following infection with the influenza virus. Although this patient gives
an initial history of flu-like symptoms, it does not explain his

atrial fibrillation with a fast ventricular rate. She has no history of atrial

Bisoprolol
Digoxin
Intravenous fluids
Oral antibiotics
Flecainide
Question 82 of 287
A 53-year-old lady comes into the Emergency Department with a cough
productive of green sputum and palpitations. She feels very unwell,
feverish and lethargic. On examination, she has bronchial breathing at
her right base with respiratory rate 25/min, sats 95% on room air. Her
heart sounds are normal with an irregularly irregular heartbeat. Her heart
rate was 120/min and blood pressure 90/40 mmHg. An ECG shows
atrial fibrillation with a fast ventricular rate. She has no history of atrial
fibrillation. What is the first treatment that should be given for her atrial
fibrillation?
explanation:
This patient is clearly septic from pneumonia. This has tipped the patient
into atrial fibrillation (AF) given there is no previous history of atrial
fibrillation. It is important to treat the sepsis as the cause of the AF. To
do this it is imperative to give IV fluids and IV antibiotics. If the patients
AF does not settle following the resolution of the sepsis then other
options would be considered.

common in diabetic patients.

adequate coverage for streptococcal and staphylococcal skin and soft
tissue infections (gram-positive) but will not adequately treat gram-

an adjunct in severe skin and soft tissue infections but it does not

Necrotising fasciitis
Necrotising fasciitis is a medical emergency that is difficult to recognise
in the early stages.
It can be classified according to the causative organism:
type 1 is caused by mixed anaerobes and aerobes (often occurs
post-surgery in diabetics). This is the most common type
type 2 is caused by Streptococcus pyogenes
Risk factors
skin factors: recent trauma, burns or soft tissue infections
diabetes mellitus
the most common preexisting medical condition
particularly if the patient is treated with SGLT-2 inhibitors
intravenous drug use
immunosuppression
The most commonly affected site is the perineum (Fournier's gangrene).

A 17 year old girl presents to A&E accompanied by her anxious mother.
She was born in England, but both her parents were born in a rice
growing community in rural China. She has recently returned from a
holiday where she was visiting her family in China. They live on a farm
where she had close contact with dogs, sheep and pigs.
She arrived home one week ago. She was taking Mefloquine for malaria
prophylaxis.
She was complaining of fever and a headache yesterday. Today she has
been confused and disorientated.
She is previously fit and well, she has had all her immunisations
according to the UK immunisation schedule, with normal growth and
development. She does well at college and is a keen member of her
college canoe club. She has no allergies.
On examination she is febrile at 38.9°C but haemodynamically stable.
She appears confused and has an obvious difficultly walking.
Examination of her cranial nerves is difficult but unremarkable. She has
normal power and increased tone in her arms, which is more pronounced
on the left side, with hyperreflexia bilaterally. She has several writhing
involuntary movements of her upper limbs during the consultation.
A CT scan shows hypodensity in the thalami and basal ganglia
bilaterally, more pronounced on the left side.

A 17 year old girl presents to A&E accompanied by her anxious mother.
She was born in England, but both her parents were born in a rice
growing community in rural China. She has recently returned from a
holiday where she was visiting her family in China. They live on a farm
where she had close contact with dogs, sheep and pigs.
She arrived home one week ago. She was taking Mefloquine for malaria
prophylaxis.
She was complaining of fever and a headache yesterday. Today she has
been confused and disorientated.
She is previously fit and well, she has had all her immunisations
according to the UK immunisation schedule, with normal growth and
development. She does well at college and is a keen member of her
college canoe club. She has no allergies.
On examination she is febrile at 38.9°C but haemodynamically stable.
She appears confused and has an obvious difficultly walking.
Examination of her cranial nerves is difficult but unremarkable. She has
normal power and increased tone in her arms, which is more pronounced
on the left side, with hyperreflexia bilaterally. She has several writhing
involuntary movements of her upper limbs during the consultation.
A CT scan shows hypodensity in the thalami and basal ganglia
bilaterally, more pronounced on the left side.
A lumbar puncture reveals a lymphocytic CSF with a raised protein.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Finally, Mefloquine toxicity is an unlikely diagnosis because although mefloquine can cause neuropsychiatric side effects like dizziness or insomnia in some individuals, the patient's symptoms and investigation Alcohol consumption
explanation:
The most likely diagnosis in this case is Japanese Encephalitis. The
patient's history of travel to a rural area in China, where she had close
contact with animals, combined with her presenting symptoms of fever,
headache, confusion, and difficulty walking, as well as the CT scan
findings of hypodensity in the thalami and basal ganglia bilaterally are all
consistent with Japanese Encephalitis. This disease is a mosquito-borne
flavivirus infection that predominantly affects people living or travelling
to Asia.
Herpes Simplex Encephalitis is less likely due to the patient's travel
history and exposure to animals. Although Herpes Simplex Encephalitis
can also present with fever, headache, and confusion, it typically has a
more acute onset and would show different findings on imaging studies
(such as temporal lobe involvement on CT or MRI).
Alcohol consumption is an unlikely cause for this patient's presentation.
While excessive alcohol intake can lead to neurological symptoms such
as ataxia and confusion, there is no indication from the patient's history
that she has been consuming large amounts of alcohol. Furthermore,
her CT scan findings and lumbar puncture results do not support this
diagnosis.
Rabies could be considered given the patient's close contact with
animals during her trip; however, her clinical presentation does not fit the
classic signs of rabies. Rabies usually presents with hydrophobia (fear
of water), hypersalivation, and progressive paralysis. Additionally, while
rabies can affect the central nervous system leading to encephalitis-like
symptoms, it would not produce the specific CT scan findings seen in
this case.
results are much more consistent with Japanese Encephalitis.
Mefloquine toxicity would not typically cause the neurological findings
observed in this case, nor would it explain the CT scan and lumbar
puncture results.
Japanese encephalitis
Japanese encephalitis is the most common cause of viral encephalitis in
South East Asia, China the Western Pacific and India, with approx.
50,000 cases annually. It is a flavivirus transmitted by culex mosquitos
which breeds in rice paddy fields. The reservoir hosts are aquatic birds,
but pigs are an amplification host and therefore close domestic contact
with pigs is a risk factor.
The majority of infection is asymptomatic.
Clinical features are headache, fever, seizures and confusion.
Parkinsonian features indicate basal ganglia involvement. It can also
present with acute flaccid paralysis.
Diagnosis is by serology or PCR. Management is supportive.
Prevention is a vaccine and there are a variety of different types.

explanation:
Treatment for tick-borne encephalitis is supportive
A presentation of headache, neck stiffness, fever and reduced GCS is
suggestive of meningoencephalitis. The question revolves around
determining what is the most likely causative agent and therefore the
most appropriate treatment.
The history of recent travel should raise your suspicion for a potentially
uncommon aetiology. The camping history combined with a biphasic
illness is characteristic for tick-borne encephalitis. Ultimately, the finding
of a flavivirus in the CSF confirms the diagnosis. Management for this
condition is supportive.
Amphotericin B may be used in the treatment of primary amoebic
meningoencephalitis. This is a very rare cause of meningoencephalitis
caused by naegleria fowleri.
Aciclovir is used in the management of herpes simplex virus (HSV)
encephalitis. HSV, along with varicella-zoster virus and enteroviruses
make up 90% of cases of viral encephalitis. In this patient, the travel
history and biphasic illness suggest an alternate, atypical cause.
IV pyrimethamine/sulfadiazine and folinic acid are used in the
management of cerebral toxoplasmosis. Toxoplasmosis is usually
asymptomatic or mild in immunocompetent patients. The patient only
has a past medical history of asthma and is HIV negative, therefore this
is a less likely diagnosis.
IV quinine dihydrochloride may be used in severe or complicated
falciparum malaria. The patient has not come from a malaria-risk
country and does not have other features suggestive of malaria, such as
jaundice.
Tick-borne encephalitis

HIV and pregnancy
With the increased incidence of HIV infection amongst the heterosexual
population there are an increasing number of HIV positive women giving
birth in the UK. In London the incidence may be as high as 0.4% of
pregnant women. The aim of treating HIV positive women during
pregnancy is to minimise harm to both the mother and fetus, and to
reduce the chance of vertical transmission.
Guidelines regularly change on this subject and most recent guidelines
can be found using the links provided.
Factors which reduce vertical transmission (from 25-30% to 2%)
maternal antiretroviral therapy
mode of delivery (caesarean section)
