explanation:
Enterococci are gram positive gamma-haemolytic Streptococci. Most
important are E. faecalis and E. faecium. They are part of the normal
flora of the human intestine, the female genital tract, and urinary tract.
They are intrinsically of low pathogenicity however have a natural high
resistance to antibiotics.
Vancomycin Resistant Enterococcus (VRE) are important nosocomial
pathogens for which there are limited treatment options. Predisposing
Vancomycin Resistant Enterococcus (VRE) can be treated with
linezolid, daptomycin and tigecycline
factors for VREs include previous treatment with anti-microbials
(especially vancomycin, cephalosporins and broad-spectrum
antibiotics).
Most VRE have high-level resistance to β-lactams and aminoglycosides.
Management of VRE may include removal of catheters and drainage of
abscesses
If after clinical assessment and primary management, antimicrobial
treatment of VRE is considered necessary, a drug should be selected
based upon susceptibility testing of the organism involved. Nearly all
strains of E. faecalis, including VRE strains, are susceptible to ampicillin.
VREs also often remain sensitive to chloramphenicol, rifampicin and
tetracyclines. A number of newer agents include linezolid, daptomycin
and tigecycline.
Gentamicin can be used synergistically with another antibiotic, however
it should not be used alone.

A 45-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a 10-day
history of progressively worsening headaches. Despite regular analgesia,
the pain is not improving. He also complains of intermittent episodes of
dizziness associated with nausea and vomiting. His past medical history
includes human immunodeficiency virus for which he reports
compliance with highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART).
On examination, there is equal power and sensation in all 4 limbs. His
cranial nerve and cerebellar examinations are unremarkable.
Fundoscopic examination reveals bilateral papilloedema.
He is referred for neuroimaging, as shown below:
© Image used on license from Radiopaedia
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This patient's neuroimaging demonstrates 2 homogenous enhancing
lesions; 1 larger lesion in the right hemisphere with 1 smaller lesion in
the left hemisphere. Along with the history of worsening headaches
associated with red-flag features (e.g. dizziness, vomiting), the
presentation is in keeping with CNS lymphoma. CNS lymphoma
accounts for up to 30% of cerebral lesions in patients with HIV and is
associated with infection with the Ebstein-Barr virus. Like many cerebral
lesions, presenting symptoms vary depending on the structures involved
and include headache, nausea and vomiting, focal neurological signs
and signs of raised intracranial pressure (e.g. papilloedema), as seen
here.
Cryptococcus neoformans causes an opportunistic fungal infection that
causes headache, fevers, confusion and signs of raised intracranial
pressure. It is the most common fungal infection in patients with HIV.
Imaging studies show leptomeningeal enhancement, cryptococcomas,
hydrocephalus or dilated perivascular spaces. It does not account for
lesions seen in this patient's MRI.
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a viral infection that commonly causes illness
in patients with HIV, particularly in those with a CD4 count < 50 cells/mL.
The most common form of CMV is CMV retinitis. However, CMV
encephalitis is also common. On imaging, cerebral oedema may be
seen. Meningoencephalitis and ventriculitis are also features of infection
with CMV. These are not seen here, making CMV encephalitis unlikely.
Infection with JC virus is responsible for a condition known as
progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, a demyelinating disease of
the CNS. Symptoms include behavioural changes and alterations in
speech, vision and movement. On imaging, single or multiple lesions
may be seen, with demyelinating white matter lesions seen on MRI
studies.
Toxoplasmosis is an opportunistic infection caused by the parasite
Toxoplasma gondii. It is the most common cause of neurological brain
abscesses in patients with HIV with symptoms including headache, fever
and neurological changes including seizures, hemiplegia, cerebellar
signs, or an acute confusional state. Domestic cats are a common
source of transmission. Unlike CNS lymphoma, toxoplasmosis presents
as ring-enhancing lesions on neuroimaging. These are not seen on this
patient's scan, making it an unlikely diagnosis.

explanation:
The development of chickenpox in a pregnant woman is associated with
increased morbidity, including pneumonia, hepatitis and encephalitis.
Therefore, pregnant women who develop a chickenpox rash should see
their GP immediately.
Oral aciclovir should be prescribed in pregnant women with chickenpox,
if they present within 24 hours of the onset of the rash and are 20 weeks
gestation or beyond. (Use before 20 weeks can be considered).
Aciclovir reduces the duration of fever and symptomatology of varicella,
if commenced within 24 hours of developing the rash. Symptomatic
treatment can be used alongside aciclovir.
Pregnant women ≥ 20 weeks who develop chickenpox are generally
treated with oral aciclovir if they present within 24 hours of the rash
Pregnant women with severe chickenpox should be referred to hospital
for intravenous aciclovir. In addition, a referral to fetal medicine would be
necessary (in the above scenario), due to the small risk of fetal varicella
syndrome in the first 28 weeks of pregnancy.
It is important to advise anyone with chickenpox to avoid contact with
other potentially susceptible people, such a pregnant women and
neonates until the last lesions have crusted over (usually 5 days after the
onset of the rash).
VZIG has no therapeutic benefit once the rash has started. RCOG
Greentop guidelines, Chickepox in pregnancy.
Chickenpox exposure in pregnancy
Chickenpox is caused by primary infection with varicella-zoster virus.
Shingles is caused by the reactivation of dormant virus in dorsal root
ganglion. In pregnancy, there is a risk to both the mother and also the
fetus, a syndrome now termed fetal varicella syndrome
Risks to the mother
5 times greater risk of pneumonitis

risk of FVS following maternal varicella exposure is around 1% if

studies have shown a very small number of cases occurring

and mild leukopenia. Brucellosis is a zoonosis: an infectious disease
that jumps from a non-human animal to humans. It is caused by the
gram-negative, rod-shaped Brucella species of bacteria. It is more
common in the Middle East and in those that work with animals, such as
this man. It is spread by aerosol and considered a bioterrorism agent.
Rose Bengal plate test is used in suspected Brucellosis. One can
remember this as B-Rose in B-Ruce-losis.
Cryptosporidiosis is a protozoal disease that typically affects the
immunocompromised and causes diarrhoea.
Bartonella henselae is a bacteria that causes cat-scratch disease,
another disease that is more common in vets. Although it may present
with flu-like symptoms, it does not typically cause hepatosplenomegaly.
There is typically a history of a bite or scratch from a cat, with a lesion
developing over the area and painful lymphadenopathy. As a side note
Bartonella bacilliformis can cause Oroya fever, which may present with
hepatosplenomegaly and fever, but typically there is lymphadenopathy
also, with marked haemolysis.
Echinococcus granulosis is a tapeworm that causes hydatid disease,
another disease that is more common in vets. However, hydatid disease
causes cysts that typically affect the liver or lungs, and is more likely to
present with abdominal pain, jaundice, weight loss, and if affecting the
lungs then a cough and shortness of breath.
Leptospirosis is a possible diagnosis here, as it often presents in vets,
and can present with flu-like illness and hepatosplenomegaly. The sacral
tenderness, leukopenia and normal LFTs make this less likely.
Leptospirosis will typically cause leukocytosis, anaemia,
thrombocytopenia, even in the absence of DIC. Even when clinical
manifestations are mild, hyperbilirubinemia is often present and mild
elevations of serum transaminases are frequently seen. In exams,
leptospirosis will normally present with bilateral conjunctival suffusion,
Unwell vet with fever, malaise, arthralgia and lower back pain ?
Brucellosis
which is conjunctivitis without exudate. However, in reality, this occurs in
<60% of patients.

options: If no fever can become pregnant
Need to check Zika virus serology before becoming pregnant
Should avoid becoming pregnant for at least 2 weeks after travel
Should avoid becoming pregnant for at least 8 weeks after travel
explanation:
The latest advice as per Public Health England is that women who are
considering becoming pregnant should avoid becoming pregnant while
travelling in an area with active Zika virus transmission, and for 8 weeks
after their return.
Whilst folic acid is recommended to women trying for pregnancy, the
usual dose is 400 micrograms daily and there is currently no
recommendation to increase this after Zika exposure. The test for Zika
serology is only recommended for patients with a relevant travel history
and current symptoms.

A 42-year-old man attends the GP with a lesion on his left hand. He says
it first appeared as a red spot 2-3 weeks ago when he returned from Iraq.
However, since then the lesion has been progressively enlarging. There is
no history of pain or itch and he otherwise feels well. He is normally fit
and well and takes no regular medications.
On examination, his observations are all within the normal range. His
hand appears as shown below. On further inspection, there is sparing of
the mucous membranes and no further lesions are found on his body.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
Anthrax
Chagas disease
Leishmaniasis
Leprosy
Lyme disease
Question 96 of 287
A 42-year-old man attends the GP with a lesion on his left hand. He says
it first appeared as a red spot 2-3 weeks ago when he returned from Iraq.
However, since then the lesion has been progressively enlarging. There is
no history of pain or itch and he otherwise feels well. He is normally fit
and well and takes no regular medications.
On examination, his observations are all within the normal range. His
hand appears as shown below. On further inspection, there is sparing of
the mucous membranes and no further lesions are found on his body.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This patient has a superficial cutaneous lesion on his left hand with
central ulceration. The surrounding skin is not affected. Given the history
of rapid growth from a small red papule and a recent tour in Iraq, it is
likely that this patient has leishmaniasis, a parasitic disease spread by
sandflies. There are different species of leishmania that are responsible
for different manifestations of the disease, with cutaneous
leishmaniasis being the most common. Initially, a small red papule
appears at the site of the sandfly bite which gradually enlarges followed
by central ulceration before spontaneously resolving. The time to
resolution varies between 2 months and 1 year. The Middle East, North
Africa, and Asia are more common areas for contracting the disease.
Anthrax is a bacterial disease caused by Bacillus anthracis. Infection is
associated with exposure to infected carcasses and the introduction of
the organism into the body through a superficial wound. An initial
pustule appears at the site of infection which progresses to a black
eschar (a necrotic-looking ulcer with a black scab). The infection usually
resolves spontaneously, but in some can lead to death. The lesion shown
in this question is not that of a black eschar but rather a crusted ulcer
from a sandfly bite. This makes leishmaniasis the correct diagnosis.
Chagas disease is a parasitic disease spread by triatomine or 'kissing'
bugs. The disease is prevalent in Latin America and consists of an initial
acute phase and chronic phase. In the earlier stages of the disease,
symptoms include generalised malaise, fever, headaches, and myalgia
along with anorexia, nausea, and vomiting. In others, a chagoma (an
indurated, oedematous skin lesion) may be seen. In contrast, the patient
in this question has returned from the Middle East with a cutaneous
ulcerated lesion, making Chagas disease unlikely.
Leprosy is a granulomatous disease caused by Mycobacterium leprae
that affects the peripheral nerves and skin. Initial symptoms include
numbness, typically with loss of temperature followed by light touch,
pain, and finally deep pressure. Cutaneous lesions follow later in the
disease and appear as hypopigmented patches of skin with associated
sensory loss. This patient has a painless, crusted ulcer with no other
lesions or neurology making leprosy an unlikely diagnosis.
Ticks are well-known to spread Lyme disease, a bacterial infection
caused by Borrelia burgdorferi . The most common dermatological
manifestation of Lyme disease is a bulls-eye rash that appears at the site
of the tick bite. Other symptoms include fever, lethargy, and arthralgia
that are not described in this question.

co-amoxiclav with the addition of activity against Pseudomonas.

A 32-year-old lady of Ugandan origin presents to the HIV clinic.
She has been known to the HIV service since coming to the UK 10 years
ago. She currently takes tenofovir, emtricitabine, and dolutegravir. She is
extremely compliant with her current regime and is currently well.
She is 14 weeks pregnant and this is her first pregnancy. Despite some
vomiting earlier in the pregnancy, she is excited and feeling well.
Her blood tests show:

0.84x10^9/L
CD8 count
1.01x10^9/L
Viral load
<20RNA/ml
She has come to discuss the management of her HIV with you.
What is the most appropriate management for this lady?
options: Stop this patients current regime and change her onto zidovudine, lamivudine and nevirapine
Continue the current medications, but at a lower dose so that the medications do not cross the placental barrier and effect the foetus
Continue current regime and advise patient she will need to deliver by caesarean section to prevent transmission during birth
Continue current management and advise patient there is currently no reason why she should not have a vaginal delivery
Stop all HIV medications and advise this patient she will have to deliver by caesarean section
explanation:
It is recommended that women conceiving on an effective antiretroviral
(ART) regimen should continue this even if it contains efavirenz or does
not contain zidovudine.
Exceptions are: (1) Protease inhibitor (PI) monotherapy should be
intensified to include (depending on tolerability, resistance and prior
antiretroviral history) one or more agents that cross the placenta. (2) The
combination of stavudine and didanosine should not be prescribed in
pregnancy
Although there is most evidence and experience in pregnancy with
zidovudine plus lamivudine, tenofovir plus emtricitabine or abacavir plus
lamivudine are acceptable nucleoside backbones. In the absence of
specific contraindications, it is recommended that the third agent in ART
should be efavirenz or nevirapine (if the CD4 cell count is less than 250
cells/L) or a boosted PI.
No routine dose alterations are recommended for ARVs during
pregnancy if used at adult licensed doses.
With a viral load <50 at 36 weeks a vaginal delivery is recommended in
the absence of any obstetric complications. Since her viral load has
been undetectable for the last 6 years it is reasonable to assume this is
likely to continue throughout her pregnancy. She will continue to need
monitoring of her viral load throughout her pregnancy, particularly at 36
weeks.
In 2015 there were an estimated 1.5 million people living in Uganda with
HIV.
Pregnancy-guidelines-update-2014.pdf
HIV and pregnancy
With the increased incidence of HIV infection amongst the heterosexual
population there are an increasing number of HIV positive women giving
birth in the UK. In London the incidence may be as high as 0.4% of
pregnant women. The aim of treating HIV positive women during
pregnancy is to minimise harm to both the mother and fetus, and to
reduce the chance of vertical transmission.
Guidelines regularly change on this subject and most recent guidelines
can be found using the links provided.
Factors which reduce vertical transmission (from 25-30% to 2%)
maternal antiretroviral therapy
mode of delivery (caesarean section)
neonatal antiretroviral therapy
infant feeding (bottle feeding)

positive and has a CD4 count of 150 cells/µL.
He had been on a trip to Zimbabwe 10 months previously. Over the past
2 weeks, he had symptoms of anorexia and mild abdominal discomfort.
These had progressed on to severe abdominal cramps and bloody
diarrhoea.
He has a temperature of 37.8ºC, a blood pressure of 100/60 and a pulse
of 111/min. On examination, he looks unwell, is emaciated and has
generalised tenderness on examination of his abdomen. There is no
guarding or peritonitis.
What is the most likely causative organism?
Giardia lamblia
Toxoplasma gondii
Entamoeba histolytica
Cytomegalovirus
Strongyloides stercoralis
Question 99 of 287
A 43-year-old gentleman presents with bloody diarrhoea. He is HIV
positive and has a CD4 count of 150 cells/µL.
He had been on a trip to Zimbabwe 10 months previously. Over the past
2 weeks, he had symptoms of anorexia and mild abdominal discomfort.
These had progressed on to severe abdominal cramps and bloody
diarrhoea.
He has a temperature of 37.8ºC, a blood pressure of 100/60 and a pulse
of 111/min. On examination, he looks unwell, is emaciated and has
generalised tenderness on examination of his abdomen. There is no
guarding or peritonitis.
What is the most likely causative organism?
explanation:
Entamoeba histolytica is the only pathogen here which typically causes
bloody diarrhoea in an immunocompromised individual and hence is the
correct answer. Giardia typically causes steatorrhoea, Toxoplasma gondii
is more likely to cause a central nervous system infection, and while
CMV can cause diarrhoea it is rarely a presenting feature of the
infection. While Strongyloides stercoralis can cause diarrhoea, it is
usually watery rather than bloody.

clinic for review. She has been volunteering in India for the last 12
months and has been living with a local family. She first noticed a small
lesion on her lower leg around 6 weeks ago. It has since progressed
significantly, so she has returned to the UK to seek medical attention.
The lesion is painless. She has no other lesions elsewhere on the body.
There is no past medical history of note but her brother has ulcerative
colitis.
Her skin is examined, as shown below:
What is the most likely cause of this skin lesion?
Buruli ulcer
Cutaneous leishmaniasis
Fish tank granuloma
Pyoderma gangrenosum
Yaws
Question 126 of 287
A 25-year-old woman of Caucasian origin presents to the dermatology
clinic for review. She has been volunteering in India for the last 12
months and has been living with a local family. She first noticed a small
lesion on her lower leg around 6 weeks ago. It has since progressed
significantly, so she has returned to the UK to seek medical attention.
The lesion is painless. She has no other lesions elsewhere on the body.
There is no past medical history of note but her brother has ulcerative
colitis.
Her skin is examined, as shown below:
What is the most likely cause of this skin lesion?
explanation:
The image shows a large shallow ulcerating lesion on the lower leg, with
a moist surface. It is on an exposed area of the body and is a solitary
lesion. Combined with her travel history, the most likely cause is
cutaneous leishmaniasis . Lesions in cutaneous leishmaniasis can also
be dry or covered with a crust or scab. Leishmaniasis is transmitted by
bites of the sandfly and is due to a number of species of the protozoan
parasite Leishmania . The main species causing cutaneous
leishmaniasis in Asia, Africa, the Mediterranean and the Middle East are
Leishmania major, Leishmania tropica and Leishmania aethiopica.
Cutaneous leishmaniasis in Central and South America is caused mainly
by Leishmania braziliensis and Leishmania mexicana.
Buruli ulcer is incorrect. This is another tropical ulcerating disease
caused by Mycobacterium ulcerans . However, most cases occur in sub-
Saharan Africa and tropical parts of Australia, and it is rare in Asia. It is
also less likely in this patient because it tends to affect children under
the age of 15, and affects people living in poverty in rural areas. It is not
commonly seen in travellers.
Fish tank granuloma is incorrect. This condition is caused by
Mycobacterium marinum and can be seen in people who have had
exposure to fish tanks or are involved in fish or shellfish preparation.
However, unlike the lesion seen in this patient, skin lesions are generally
plaque-like or nodular, rather than ulcerating. Lesions can occur on the
legs but are more common on the hands and arms.
Pyoderma gangrenosum is incorrect. This diagnosis is less likely in this
patient because the ulcers of pyoderma gangrenosum are generally very
painful, and have a blue or purple undermined edge, neither of which are
present in this case. The patient also has no personal history of an
underlying condition associated with pyoderma gangrenosum.
Yaws is incorrect. This condition is one caused by Treponema pallidum
subspecies pertenue. It is endemic in a small number of countries in
Africa, Asia and the South Pacific, but is most common in Papua New
Guinea. The primary stage presents with a papule that can later ulcerate.
It is most common in children between 5 and 10. It is unlikely as a
diagnosis in this patient because it is extremely unusual in returning
travellers as it requires close skin contact (non-sexual contact) with
open skin lesions for transmission. It has also been eradicated from
India.

A 45-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department. He told the
admitting doctor that he had fallen onto his left hip last night while he
had been drinking at home. He had extensive bruising around his hip and
some bony tenderness which resulted in a hip x-ray being taken.
His x-ray shows no fracture nor bony abnormality, but several 2x4mm
specs of calcification are visible in his psoas and thigh muscles.
Later on, his wife asks to speak to you in confidence. She states that
over the last year her husband's personality has gradually changed and
he is sometimes forgetful. He lost his job 3 months ago as an engineer.
He had worked for 8 years in Peru on an engineering project in his
thirties. He drinks 8 units of alcohol per day and seems to have had a
low mood for several years.
Yesterday he had fallen, lost consciousness, and had a jerking of his
arms and legs lasting 1 minute. He had hit his hip on a coffee table and
had wet himself. Afterwards, he felt tired and lethargic but had refused
to go to hospital.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
HIV dementia
Alcohol withdrawal seizure

options: Emboli secondary to calcified aortic value
explanation:
This is neurocysticercosis. It is the most common cause of epilepsy
worldwide. Eggs of the Taenia Solium tapeworm are ingested,
oncospheres hatch and migrate to peripheral sites (classically muscles
and brain) and become cysticerci. They may remain asymptomatic or
cause inflammatory pathology when the cysticerci die. They eventually
become calcified.
Diagnosis is made with MRI or CT imaging. Calcified cysts in skeletal
muscle may be found incidentally on x-ray. Serology may be helpful.
Management is with praziquantel or albendazole and prednisolone.

A 23-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital with acute-onset fever,
neck stiffness, headache and photophobia. She has no significant past
medical history. A CT scan of the head is normal. The patient
subsequently undergoes a lumbar puncture which confirms a diagnosis
of bacterial meningitis.
She lives with a group of flatmates, including her partner, with whom she
has had close contact up until 2 days ago. The patient visited her
parents' house and had close contact with them 9 days ago; she visited
her grandparents' house 16 days ago and had close contact with them.
What is the most appropriate next step?
No prophylaxis required for contacts
Prophylaxis required for all flatmates
Prophylaxis required for all flatmates and parents
Prophylaxis required for flatmates, parents and grandparents
Prophylaxis required for partner only
Question 103 of 287
A 23-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital with acute-onset fever,
neck stiffness, headache and photophobia. She has no significant past
medical history. A CT scan of the head is normal. The patient
subsequently undergoes a lumbar puncture which confirms a diagnosis
of bacterial meningitis.
She lives with a group of flatmates, including her partner, with whom she
has had close contact up until 2 days ago. The patient visited her
parents' house and had close contact with them 9 days ago; she visited
her grandparents' house 16 days ago and had close contact with them.
What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Prophylaxis required for all flatmates and parents
Prophylaxis required for flatmates, parents and grandparents
explanation:
Guidance around meningitis prophylaxis is quite clear. Prophylaxis
should be offered to household members and those in close contact
within the past 7 days. As such, it should be given to all flatmates as
they have been in close contact up until 2 days prior. Oral ciprofloxacin
or rifampicin may be used. Ciprofloxacin is now the drug of choice.
People who have been exposed to a patient with confirmed
bacterial meningitis should be given prophylactic antibiotics if they
have close contact within the seven days before onset
Advising no prophylaxis is therefore incorrect.
Similarly, advising both flatmates and parents to have prophylaxis is
incorrect. Whilst the flatmates should be offered prophylaxis, the parents
last had contact over 7 days ago.
Prophylaxis for flatmates, parents and grandparents is unwarranted. The
parents and grandparents last had contact with the patient more than 7
days ago and so it is not needed for them.
Only advising the partner to have prophylactic antibiotics is incorrect.
The entire household has had close contact with her and so all
flatmates, not just her partner, should be offered them.

On examination, he appears pale and cachectic. There are audible
crackles bilaterally. His heart rate is regular and heart sounds are
normal. He has a soft and non-tender abdomen.
Laboratory tests:
CD4 count
< 200/mm³
Which of the following complications is most commonly associated with
the likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
This patient has a diagnosis of pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (or
PCP), a fungal pneumonia that is most commonly seen in
immunocompromised individuals, particularly those with HIV. Symptoms
of infection include fever, dry cough and shortness of breath (especially
on exertion) as seen in this patient. Given his lack of compliance with his
medications, most importantly the highly active antiretroviral therapy,
combined with the CD4 count < 200/mm³, this patient is at high risk of
developing PCP. The most common complication associated with PCP is
a pneumothorax secondary to rupture of pulmonary cysts.
Extrapulmonary manifestations of PCP include hepatosplenomegaly and
lymphadenopathy. However, these are rare and less likely. Encephalitis is
a complication of several viral infections including measles, herpes
simplex and varicella-zoster virus. It is not a complication of PCP.
Hepatitis has multiple causes such as inflammatory, ischaemic and
infective (e.g. hepatitis A,B,C,D and E). PCP is not a cause of hepatitis.
Pancreatitis is a complication of mumps and coxsackie B virus, but not
PCP.
Along with pneumothorax, other respiratory complications of PCP
include acute respiratory distress syndrome. However, a pleural effusion
is a less likely complication compared to a pneumothorax, making it
incorrect.

Observations:

Respiratory rate 18/minute
Oxygen saturations 98% on room air
Temperature 37ºC
On examination, there are white patches on the gums, tongue and
extending past the pharynx. The examination is otherwise unremarkable.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Fluconazole is the correct answer. The description of the lesions is
typical of candidiasis. Given the patient has oesophageal symptoms in
Candidiasis in immunocompromised patients should be treated
using high dose fluconazole
the form of dysphagia and odynophagia, we can assume that the
oesophagus is involved, in addition to the oro-pharynx. The patient is not
compliant with treatment for HIV and is therefore at risk of developing
AIDS. Oesophageal candidiasis is an AIDS-defining illness. In
immunocompromised patients, the treatment of candidiasis is with high
dose fluconazole.
Amphotericin is incorrect. This is an intravenous treatment associated
with significant toxicity. It is reserved for life-threatening, disseminated
fungal infections.
Lansoprazole is incorrect. The dysphagia and odynophagia are not likely
a result of gastro-oesophageal reflux.
Nystatin is incorrect. This would be suitable to treat oral thrush in an
immunocompetent patient but would not be sufficient in this case.
Surgical excision is incorrect. A differential for a single white patch in the
mouth or tongue might be oral leucoplakia, which is a pre-malignant
condition and which could be surgically excised. However, in this
context, multiple white patches in multiple locations is more likely to
reflect candida.

On examination, he has neck stiffness but no rash. He has a temperature
of 38.6 ºC and is confused. A CT head is unremarkable. A lumbar
puncture is performed. Examination of CSF with India ink is positive.
CD4 count
60 cells per mm
(500 - 1500)

Normal glucose
Normal protein
Opening pressure of 28 cm H2O
Presence of organism-specific antibodies in the CSF
Raised white cell count with predominantly neutrophils
Question 106 of 287
A 45-year-old man is known to be HIV positive but has a long history of
poor compliance with anti-retroviral medication. He presents to the
Emergency Department with a 4-day history of headache and vomiting.
On examination, he has neck stiffness but no rash. He has a temperature
of 38.6 ºC and is confused. A CT head is unremarkable. A lumbar
puncture is performed. Examination of CSF with India ink is positive.
CD4 count
60 cells per mm
(500 - 1500)
What additional finding from the lumbar puncture would be most in
keeping with the diagnosis?
options: Presence of organism-specific antibodies in the CSF
Raised white cell count with predominantly neutrophils
explanation:
This patient has cryptococcal meningitis. Cryptococcus neoformans is
an encapsulated yeast that is found in the environment and is a common
cause of meningitis in patients with HIV with a CD4 count of less than
100. Examination of the CSF with India ink is positive in 70-90% of cases
of HIV-related cryptococcal meningitis.
In cryptococcal meningitis, CSF shows high opening pressure and
elevated protein. The white cell count may vary according to HIV
status
Opening pressure of 28 cm H2O is correct. All patients with suspected
cryptococcal meningitis should have manometry performed as
intracranial pressure is often significantly raised. Patients can require
serial lumbar punctures to lower intracranial pressure, or may even
require neurosurgical devices such as extra-ventricular drains or
ventriculoperitoneal shunts to manage their intracranial pressure.
Normal glucose is incorrect. CSF glucose is generally low in
cryptococcal meningitis, although it can sometimes be normal.
Normal protein is incorrect. CSF protein is usually elevated in
cryptococcal meningitis.
Presence of organism-specific antibodies in the CSF is incorrect.
Antibodies to Cryptococcus neoformans are not used in diagnosis, either
in the blood or CSF. Cryptococcal antigen (CrAg), however, is a useful
test and can be carried out on both blood and CSF. A positive CSF CrAg
has a 98% sensitivity for cryptococcal meningitis. High CSF CrAg is a
poor prognostic marker.
Raised white cell count with predominantly neutrophils is incorrect. The
white cell count is usually elevated, but the predominant cell type would
be lymphocytes. Patients with HIV may not have an elevated CSF white
cell count, and this is a poor prognostic marker.

Question 107 of 287
A 26-year-old man presents with an intensely itchy rash which he thinks
is spreading rapidly. He has recently returned from a holiday in Brazil,
and mentions having seen many stray cats around the hotel resort.
Symptoms began approximately 1 week after returning from the holiday.
He denies having had any similar rashes previously, has no significant
past medical history and is systemically well.
On examination, the rash appears as follows:
Given the most likely diagnosis, which of the following is the most
appropriate management?
explanation:
The rash above has the appearance of cutaneous larva migrans, most
commonly caused by infection with the cat hookworm Ancyclostoma
braziliense. It is found in tropical regions throughout the world, including
Brazil, from where this patient has recently returned, having mentioned a
resort with many stray cats. The rash creeps due to the migration of the
larvae. The photo above demonstrates this creeping, serpiginous
eruption. Management involves the use of ivermectin, which is the
correct answer here, or albendazole.
Doxycycline is incorrect. This is an antibiotic that would be used for the
management of Lyme disease. This would instead present with
erythema chronicum migrans - annular, bulls-eye lesions, rather than the
tortuous lesions seen here.
Hydrocortisone is a topical steroid and is not involved in the
management of cutaneous larva migrans. Ivermectin or albendazole
should be given.
Malathion is a second-line option for the management of scabies. Whilst
also presenting with intense pruritus, scabies lesions would instead
appear as small, discrete burrows, particularly in the web spaces
between fingers, as well as the palms and wrists. The serpiginous
lesions seen here are more indicative of cutaneous larva migrans.
Permethrin is generally the first-line treatment used for scabies. Again,
the lesions seen above are more associated with cutaneous larva
migrans, not scabies.

The most appropriate treatment option is oral pyrimethamine-

diagnosis of cerebral toxoplasmosis. A 3-month treatment with
pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine is the most appropriate management
option.
Cerebral toxoplasmosis is not treated with intravenous amphotericin B .
Amphotericin B treats cryptococcal meningoencephalitis, which is
another important neuro-complication of HIV. The MRI scan in
cryptococcal meningitis shows cryptococcomas, meningeal
enhancement, abscesses, and gelatinous pseudocysts.
Methotrexate with whole brain irradiation is the most appropriate
treatment for primary CNS lymphoma which is sometimes
indistinguishable from cerebral toxoplasmosis in HIV patients. In this
scenario, an important differentiating feature of primary CNS lymphoma
and cerebral toxoplasmosis is the presence of a ring-enhancing lesion
on MRI. Primary CNS lymphoma is characterised by a single mass lesion
on an MRI scan that enhances homogeneously. When there is diagnostic
uncertainty, a 3-month treatment with pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine is
given.

he has already developed cerebral toxoplasmosis, and has a CD4 count

Low-grade primary CNS lymphoma in HIV can be treated by surgical
excision . Surgical excision has no role in treating cerebral
toxoplasmosis, which is the case here. Primary CNS lymphoma is the
most common HIV-associated brain tumour. The treatment of choice for
primary CNS lymphoma is high-dose methotrexate with radiotherapy.
Surgical excision can be considered for low-grade tumours.

answer here. Ticks that transmit Lyme disease can be found in the
United Kingdom as well as the USA.
American trypanosomiasis causes Chagas' disease which can manifest
as myocarditis and, ultimately, arrhythmias including complete
atrioventricular block. Despite the name, this disease is mainly found in
Southern and Central America, whereas the main source of transmission
throughout the USA is via immigration and blood transfusions.
Coxsackie A is not associated with ECG changes and therefore this
answer is incorrect.
Coxsackie B can cause viral myocarditis for which the most common
ECG change is sinus tachycardia. Fulminant Coxsackie myocarditis can
result in complete heart block however this would likely present with
gastrointestinal symptoms and more severe signs of cardiogenic shock.
Group A streptococci can cause rheumatic fever which in turn can cause
first-degree heart block however complete heart block is a far rarer
observation.

options: This patient's bile acids are well below that threshold at 5 µmol/L, and Hepatitis E
explanation:
Hepatitis E is the most likely cause of this patient's presentation. For any
pregnant with features of hepatitis, all pregnancy-related (acute fatty
liver of pregnancy, HELLP and intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy)
and non-pregnancy-related (such as viral and autoimmune hepatitis)
causes should be considered. She is in the 2nd trimester and has
marked elevations of transaminases (ALT and AST) in the thousands,
alongside mild jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, and negative testing
for hepatitis A (HAV IgM), which raises suspicion for hepatitis E infection
(HEV). It is particularly important in pregnancy, given the high risk of
maternal mortality and acute liver failure.
Acute fatty liver of pregnancy (AFLP) is generally seen in the late third
trimester and is characterised by hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy, and
elevated bilirubin—features not present here. This patient's normal blood
glucose and coagulation parameters (INR 1.1) argue against AFLP, and
the markedly elevated transaminases without severe derangements in
coagulation or hypoglycaemia make this diagnosis unlikely.
HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelet
count) typically includes thrombocytopenia and signs of pre-eclampsia
(e.g., high blood pressure), which are absent here. The mild anaemia
seen here can be due to pregnancy itself.
Hepatitis A remains a significant differential diagnosis due to its
symptomatology mirroring that seen in hepatitis E infection.
Nonetheless, given that hepatitis A IgM antibodies are absent in this
patient's serum analysis, we can exclude hepatitis A as the diagnosis.
Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy typically occurs during the third
trimester and presents with intense pruritus, especially on the palms and
soles, and significantly raised serum bile acids (often above 10 µmol/L).
Severe hepatitis in a pregnant woman - think hepatitis E
the transaminase elevations (ALT, AST) are far higher than usually seen
in cholestasis, making this diagnosis unlikely.

of feeling tired, cough, fevers and general lethargy. He becomes quite
tearful during the consultation as he has never felt like this.
On examination, he has tenderness over both trapezium muscles, his
temperature is 38.6 ºC and his throat is red without any collections of

A 21-year-old man presents to the emergency department with five days
of feeling tired, cough, fevers and general lethargy. He becomes quite
tearful during the consultation as he has never felt like this.
On examination, he has tenderness over both trapezium muscles, his
temperature is 38.6 ºC and his throat is red without any collections of
pus.
A rapid point of care test shows that he is influenza positive.
What is your next management step?
explanation:
This is a simple case of influenza of which most people who are low risk
will recover with supportive treatment. In high risk groups e.g.
immunosuppression or pregnancy, oseltamivir or zanamivir can be
considered. The duration of symptoms is important as those who
present within 48 hours of symptoms are more likely to derive benefit.
Oral antibiotics are not usually recommended though bacterial
superinfection can occur in influenza.
Low-risk patients with influenza who present 48 hours after
symptoms are recommended for supportive treatment

organisms they tend to present with a shorter history. The longer
duration of symptoms and unusual features of abdominal pain, dry
cough and hyponatraemia should alert you to an atypical organism of
which Mycoplasma pneumoniae is one of the commonest. The patient
also describes erythema multiforme which is seen with Mycoplasma
pneumonia.
Mycoplasma pneumoniae occurs in epidemics every three to four years
and typically affects younger people. It tends to have an insidious onset
with flu-like symptoms and atypical features. Hyponatraemia is often
seen. Cold agglutinins can cause an autoimmune haemolytic anaemia.
Diagnosis is confined with Mycoplasma serology. Treatment is with
clarithromycin or a tetracycline or fluoroquinolone.
Staphylococcal pneumonia may complicate influenza infection and is
seen most frequently in the elderly and in intravenous drug users or
patients with underlying disease. It can result in a cavitating pneumonia.
Pneumocystis jirovecii is seen in immunocompromised patients. It
typically presents with exertional breathlessness and patients are seen
to desaturate on walking. Whilst a HIV test should be considered in the
diagnostic workup of this patient, it is not the most likely diagnosis in
this case.
Mycoplasma pneumoniae
Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a cause of atypical pneumonia that often
affects younger patients. It is associated with a number of characteristic
complications such as erythema multiforme and cold autoimmune

explanation:
The plague is caused by the gram-negative bacterium Yersinia
pestis. Three clinical presentations can occur: bubonic (most
common), pneumonic and septicaemic
This patient has a diagnosis of the bubonic plague, caused by the gram-
negative bacterium Yersinia pestis. It is transmitted by fleas and is
endemic to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Madagascar, and
Peru. Symptoms typically include flu-like symptoms from 3-7 days post-
exposure followed by the eruption of inflamed, tense and painful lymph
nodes. The disease carries a significantly high mortality rate if not
treated and prompt recognition and antibiotic administration (i.e.
Streptomycin) can reduce the mortality from 60% to 15%.
Melioidosis is a bacterial illness caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei. It
is a tropical disease seen in South-East Asia, Africa, the Middle East and
the South Pacific. Some may present with a localised skin infection from
exposure to the bacterium as it enters the skin (e.g. nodule or ulcer
formation) whereas other patient's progress to septicaemia and abscess
formation. Melioidosis is not associated with inflamed and painful lymph
nodes making it an unlikely diagnosis.
Leprosy is a granulomatous disease caused by Mycobacterium leprae
which affects the peripheral nerves and skin causing symptoms such as
loss of temperature and light touch followed by loss of pain sensation.
Associated cutaneous lesions follow later in the disease and appear as
hypopigmented patches of skin. These symptoms are not seen in the
above patient and leprosy is not associated with painful
lymphadenopathy.
Yaws is a chronic skin infection caused by the bacterium Treponema
pallidum pertenue. There are several stages of illness with the disease
initially presenting as a papule from the site of infection that later
ulcerates. As the disease progresses, more widespread papules appear
over the rest of the body. These lesions are not seen with this patient,
making Yaws incorrect.
Ebola virus disease is an extremely deadly disease caused by multiple
different viruses including Zaire ebolavirus. The disease causes flu-like
symptoms including fever, myalgia and sore throat along with
gastrointestinal symptoms such as abdominal pain and vomiting. Zaire
ebolavirus causes a haemorrhagic illness and as the disease
progresses, patients develop unexplained bleeding and bruising.
Although this patient has flown from a high-risk area for the Ebola virus,
she has no gastrointestinal symptoms or haemorrhagic symptoms.
Bubonic plague
Bubonic plague is the commonest form of plague in humans. Fleas
transmit the bacteria from rodents to humans via their bite. The bacteria
can also be spread from one infected human to another if it develops
into pneumonic plague (in the lungs) via aerosolized particles.
Bubonic plague is still endemic in many countries. Yersinia pestis is
recognised as the causative organism.
Typically flu-like symptoms develop 3-7 days after exposure; High
temperature, headache, weakness. The lymph nodes exposed then
becomes inflamed, tense and painful.
Treatment reduces mortality from 60% to 15% and is typically with
antibiotics such as streptomycin.

automatically think of compliance issues given that the patients has
defaulted from treatment and is therefore unlikely to have been
controlling his HIV. The CD4 count of 400 is therefore not going to be
representative of his current immune system.
This leads us to the differential diagnosis of a intra-cerebral ring
enhancing lesion in a severely immunocompromised host. This includes
tuberculosis, lymphoma, toxoplasmosis and cryptococcus amongst
others.
Amphotericin and fluconazole is used in the initial 2 week phase of
treatment for cryptococcal meningitis. However we are told that the
cryptococcal antigen test is negative. This test has a relatively high
sensitivity and specificity is therefore reassuring.
We are also told that the patient has papilloedema and a 5cm lesion with
oedema, as a result attempting a lumbar puncture at this early stage is
fraught with risk. Although vital to diagnosis it would be prudent to
reduce the intra-cerebral swelling first by which time the patient may
have seriously deteriorated, therefore empirical treatment becomes a
priority.
Diagnosis of CNS tuberculosis is notoriously difficult and without access
to CSF it is likely that empirical treatment will be required in the interim.
When CSF is available culture, staining and PCR can be used to help
detect the organism. Toxoplasmosis is treated with pyrimethamine and
sulfadiazine as a first line. Again, empirical treatment may be required
before access to CSF is available. As a result the correct answer is
treatment of TB and Toxoplasmosis with steroids to reduce oedema.

The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction is a known phenomenon following
syphilis treatment that does not require any specific treatment or
This patient has syphilis and is experiencing a Jarisch-Herxheimer
reaction, the mechanism of which remains poorly understood, but is felt
to be related to the immune response triggered by the killed organisms.
Doxycycline is the treatment of choice in patients with a penicillin allergy
and, given the reported allergy described by the patient, a cephalosporin
would not be advised.
The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction is usually self-limiting and best
managed conservatively with antipyretics and good hydration unless
there is evidence of organ compromise. Hospital admission is
unnecessary unless there is evidence of organ compromise.
HIV seroconversion is possible given the recent unprotected intercourse,
but this patient would be considered low risk given his exposure and a
Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction is much more likely.

The history of travel to Africa and India with hints that the patient may
not have engaged with adequate mosquito protection places him at risk
for mosquito-borne illness. The combination of rash, fevers and
significant joint pains makes chikungunya fever the most likely culprit.
Its vector is the Aedes mosquito and is endemic within Africa and Asia. It
can cause issues like lymphopenia and thrombocytopenia on blood
tests. Treatment is supportive.
Dengue fever is less likely as it is not commonly associated with
significant joint pains. Instead, it is usually associated with myalgic
pains. It will also cause a circulatory collapse in its severe presentation,
Chikungunya can present with debilitating joint pain
which is not common in chikungunya.
Yellow fever is also predominantly endemic in Africa. It is less likely in
this case given the absence of any significant liver abnormalities. Also,
hepatomegaly can be picked up during examination in these patients.
Leptospirosis is predominantly spread by rodents. There is no clear risk
of exposure to its vector and it is also not usually associated with joint
pains. It is more commonly seen with myalgia and as the disease
progresses, liver and renal involvement start to become a prominent
feature.
Lastly, malaria is a common disease in both these countries. However,
anaemia and jaundice would be expected. Besides, the 3x negative
blood films are reassuring and useful to rule out malaria as the
underlying cause.

A 41-year-old man with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes mellitus
presents with a nodular lesion on the right-side of his face around the
angle of the jaw. One month ago he had a tooth extraction at the dentist.
The nodule is around 2 cm in diameter, raised and purple-red in colour.
On examination a sinus tract is seen in the middle of the nodule which is
draining a blood-stained fluid.
Microscopy of the discharge shows microscopic yellow granules.
What is the most likely causative organism?
explanation:
The correct answer is Actinomyces israelii. The patient's presentation of
a nodular lesion with a sinus tract draining blood-stained fluid and the
presence of microscopic yellow granules in the discharge are
characteristic features of actinomycosis, which is most commonly
caused by Actinomyces israelii. Actinomycosis is an indolent, slowly
progressive infection that often occurs following dental procedures or
oral trauma. The presence of microscopic yellow granules, also known
as 'sulfur granules,' further supports this diagnosis.
Tunga penetrans, also known as the chigoe flea, causes tungiasis, which
typically presents with pruritic papules or nodules on the feet. This
clinical presentation does not match the patient's facial lesion and
history of tooth extraction.
Klebsiella species are gram-negative bacteria that can cause a variety of
infections, including pneumonia, urinary tract infections, and soft tissue
infections. However, these infections do not typically present with
nodular lesions and sinus tracts containing sulfur granules.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is another gram-negative bacterium that can
cause various infections such as skin and soft tissue infections,
particularly in immunocompromised individuals. Although Pseudomonas
aeruginosa can cause skin lesions, it does not produce sulfur granules
nor form sinus tracts like those seen in actinomycosis.
Finally, Escherichia coli is a gram-negative bacterium commonly
associated with gastrointestinal and urinary tract infections. It can
occasionally cause skin and soft tissue infections but would not present
with the characteristic nodular lesion containing sulfur granules seen in
this patient.

A 75-year-old male with a long history of intravenous drug use is
admitted with fevers, rigors and back pain. Three sets of blood cultures
taken at admission grow positive for gram positive cocci in clusters. He
is suspected of having Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia and is
commenced on intravenous vancomycin.
Half an hour after the infusion is commenced, he is noted by the nurse to
be flushed. On examination, he is noted to have erythema over his neck,
face and trunk but denies any significant distress or discomfort.
His observations are as follow: blood pressure 125/70 mmHg, heart rate
85/min, temperature of 36.8ºC, respiratory rate of 18/min and oxygen
saturation of 98% on room air.
Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
Stopping the vancomycin infusion, administering 200mg of IV
hydrocortisone and informing the patient that he is allergic to the
medication
Stopping the vancomycin infusion and administering a single
dose of 0.5mcg intramuscular adrenaline
Stopping the vancomycin infusion until symptoms resolve and
then re-starting a slower rate
Stopping the vancomycin infusion and prescribing topical 1%
hydrocortisone cream to affected areas
Continuing the vancomycin infusion and administering 1000 ml
of 0.9% saline solution over 1 hour

admitted with fevers, rigors and back pain. Three sets of blood cultures
taken at admission grow positive for gram positive cocci in clusters. He
is suspected of having Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia and is
commenced on intravenous vancomycin.
Half an hour after the infusion is commenced, he is noted by the nurse to
be flushed. On examination, he is noted to have erythema over his neck,
face and trunk but denies any significant distress or discomfort.
His observations are as follow: blood pressure 125/70 mmHg, heart rate
85/min, temperature of 36.8ºC, respiratory rate of 18/min and oxygen
saturation of 98% on room air.
Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Stopping the vancomycin infusion, administering 200mg of IV hydrocortisone and informing the patient that he is allergic to the medication
Stopping the vancomycin infusion and administering a single dose of 0.5mcg intramuscular adrenaline
Stopping the vancomycin infusion until symptoms resolve and then re-starting a slower rate
Stopping the vancomycin infusion and prescribing topical 1% hydrocortisone cream to affected areas
Continuing the vancomycin infusion and administering 1000 ml of 0.9% saline solution over 1 hour
explanation:
Red man syndrome is associated with rapid intravenous infusion
vancomycin. It is a common adverse reaction of intravenous vancomycin
use and is a distinct entity from anaphylaxis due to vancomycin use.
Typical symptoms include redness, pruritus and a burning sensation,
predominantly in the upper body (face, neck and upper chest). Severe
cases can be associated with hypotension and chest pain.
The pathophysiology of red man syndrome is attributed to vancomycin-
related activation of mast cells with release of histamine.
The management of red man syndrome involves cessation of the
infusion, and when symptoms have resolved, recommencement at a
slower rate. In patients who are more symptomatic antihistamines can
be administered, and may require intravenous fluids if the syndrome is
associated with hypotension.
References:
Sivagnanam S, Deleu D, Red man syndrome. Crit Care. 2003
Apr;7(2):119-20
Bruneira FR, Ferreira FM, Saviolli LR, Bacci MR, Feder D, et al. The
use of vancomycin with its therapeutic and adverse effects: a review
Eur Rev Med Pharmacol Sci. 2015 Feb;19(4):694-700.

A 34-year-old man is referred to the medical admissions unit with joint
pain and swelling in his hands and feet. One month prior to his
attendance, he had developed an illness while travelling in Colombia,
which was characterized by fever, headache, rash and debilitating
polyarthralgia. His treating physicians noted mild hepatomegaly at the
time. He recovered well from this episode without intervention, except
for his ongoing musculoskeletal symptoms.
Examination reveals a small joint polyarthritis of the hands and feet.
Abdominal examination was unremarkable.
Serological testing is positive for an RNA virus.
What is the likely diagnosis?
Chikungunya virus
Dengue
Epstein Barr Virus (EBV)
Parvovirus
Zika virus
Question 127 of 287
A 34-year-old man is referred to the medical admissions unit with joint
pain and swelling in his hands and feet. One month prior to his
attendance, he had developed an illness while travelling in Colombia,
which was characterized by fever, headache, rash and debilitating
polyarthralgia. His treating physicians noted mild hepatomegaly at the
time. He recovered well from this episode without intervention, except
for his ongoing musculoskeletal symptoms.
Examination reveals a small joint polyarthritis of the hands and feet.
Abdominal examination was unremarkable.
Serological testing is positive for an RNA virus.
What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Chikungunya is the correct answer. This is an RNA alpha-virus
characterized by sudden onset fever accompanied by skin rashes and
joint pain followed by persistent rheumatic symptoms. In contrast to the
other diagnoses, which can all cause headache, fever and rash, the
polyarthralgia is said to be far more debilitating and it is most
Chikungunya can present with debilitating joint pain
associated with the development of persistent musculoskeletal
symptoms. Furthermore, hepatomegaly can be a feature of this
condition but this is not seen in Zika or dengue. While hepatomegaly is a
feature of EBV, this is a DNA virus and is less likely to cause persistent
musculoskeletal symptoms.
Zika virus is characterized by a pruritic maculopapular rash
accompanied by other symptoms such as fever, headache, conjunctivitis,
myalgia and arthralgia. It is an RNA virus but is much less likely to cause
persistent musculoskeletal symptoms.
Dengue is incorrect. This is another RNA arbovirus that causes fever,
rash and arthralgia in addition to other features such as
thrombocytopenia. However, hepatomegaly is not a feature and it is not
associated with the development of persistent arthritis.
Epstein Barr Virus (EBV) is incorrect. This is a DNA virus.
Musculoskeletal manifestations are less prominent.
Parvovirus is incorrect. This can cause rash, hepatomegaly and
polyarthritis but it is a DNA virus.

explanation:
Leptospirosis is caused by zoonotic spirochete bacteria, spread via
contact with infected animal urine. Animals such as rodents act as
reservoirs of infection, shedding the bacteria in their urine which
subsequently enter mucous membranes and broken skin. Freshwater
swimming and other watersports are associated with leptospirosis
infection. After an incubation period of 7 - 14 days, the disease presents
in a biphasic fashion: acute fever, malaise, headache, and abdominal
pain followed by severe systemic upset such as renal failure, pulmonary
haemorrhage, and hepatic failure. Thrombocytopenia is also seen
(suggested mechanisms include poor production by bone marrow and
immune-mediated platelet destruction). Serology is the most commonly
used test for the diagnosis of leptospirosis, however, antibodies may not
be present until after 7 days.
Serology is the most commonly used test for the diagnosis of
leptospirosis, however, antibodies may not be present until after 7
days
Leishmania brasiliensis is the unicellular parasite responsible for
cutaneous and mucosal leishmaniasis. Endemic in South America, this
disease presents with skin and mucosal ulcerative lesions and is spread
by the sandfly. Leishmaniasis is diagnosed by detecting Leishmania
parasites (or DNA) in tissue specimens. This patient had no such skin
lesions and no history of insect bites.
This patient's hepatitis serology demonstrates that she has been
exposed to hepatitis B (positive anti-HBc and anti-HBs) but has cleared
the virus (negative HBsAg). Hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) is an indicator
of viral replication and correlates with hepatitis B virus infectivity. This
would typically be measured if the patient had active hepatitis B. As this
patient is HepBsAg negative, this test is not necessary.
Schistosoma haematobium is a parasitic fluke endemic to areas of
Africa. The intermediate host is the freshwater snail; transmission risk is
increased by swimming in such bodies of water. Whilst acute infection
can cause a transient febrile illness (Katayama syndrome) the history
typically includes pruritis (swimmers itch) with eosinophilia.
Schistosomiasis is primarily a chronic disease with Schistosoma
haematobium causing urological manifestations such as cystitis or
obstructive uropathy. Examination of the urine for ova is the primary
method used to diagnose suspected Schistosoma haematobium
infections.
Treponema pallidum a sexually transmitted bacterial spirochete
responsible for causing syphilis. Primary syphilis is characterised by a
painless self-limiting genital ulcer (chancre) and lymphadenopathy
occurring 10-90 days after sexual transmission. Secondary syphilis
occurs following the haematogenous spread of the bacteria and can
present with a variety of symptoms including a widespread rash,
adenopathy, arthralgia, hepatitis, and alopecia. This classically presents
4-8 weeks after the presentation of the chancre. Whilst this diagnosis
should be considered given the patient's sexual history, there is no
mention of a genital lesion in the question stem, and the very short
period between the sexual encounter (8 days prior) and the onset of her
symptoms is not typical of secondary syphilis. The Treponema pallidum
particle agglutination (TPPA) assay is one of many tests that may be
used to detect specific anti-treponemal antibodies in serum. This is
usually only requested after a positive non-treponemal screening test in
the diagnostic workup of syphilis.

contact with his nephew, who was unwell and had a rash at the time. It
has since been confirmed that his nephew has measles. The patient is
concerned as he was not immunised against measles as a child.
Furthermore, he takes methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis.
He has no symptoms currently.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
Immunoglobulin
Measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine
Measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine and
immunoglobulin
Measles-only vaccine
No treatment
Question 130 of 287
A 46-year-old man telephones his GP for advice. Five days ago, he was in
contact with his nephew, who was unwell and had a rash at the time. It
has since been confirmed that his nephew has measles. The patient is
concerned as he was not immunised against measles as a child.
Furthermore, he takes methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis.
He has no symptoms currently.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine and immunoglobulin
explanation:
The most appropriate course of action, for a patient who is
immunosuppressed and does not have adequate immunity to measles,
is to administer immunoglobulin following exposure. Ideally, this should
be done within 72 hours, but can be done up until 6 days post-exposure.
For patients with normal immunity, who have not been fully immunised
against measles, the MMR vaccine should be administered within 72
hours of exposure.
Those exposed to measles can be given immunoglobulin to reduce
the risk of infection
Administering both the MMR vaccine and immunoglobulin is
inappropriate. This can invalidate the effect of the vaccine.
Giving the measles-only vaccine would also be inappropriate. This
patient should be given immunoglobulin. For a patient with normal
immunity, who is not fully immunised, the MMR vaccine should be given
rather than a measles-only vaccine.
No treatment is incorrect. Given this patient's clear exposure and history
of both immunosuppression and lack of immunisation against measles,
immunoglobulin should be given.

A 23-year-old man presents to the emergency department with
shortness of breath, fever and a cough. He has had a non-productive
cough for two weeks. Before this, he had felt unwell with muscle aches
and malaise. He went to his GP and was given amoxicillin but this has
made no difference and now he is feeling more breathless and unwell.
He has not been outside of the UK in the last year. He has no other
medical problems and takes no regular medications. His cough is non-
productive and comes in paroxysms which make him concerned.
On examination, there are a few bilateral crepitations, but the
examination is otherwise normal. His observations show fever and mild
hypoxia. Blood tests show mild anaemia and raised inflammatory
markers. A chest X-ray shows bilateral consolidation, but he improves
with IV co-amoxiclav and clarithromycin over a few days.
What is the most likely causative organism?
Klebsiella pneumoniae
Legionella pneumophila
Mycoplasma pneumoniae
Chlamydia psittaci
Coxiella burnetii
Question 133 of 287
A 23-year-old man presents to the emergency department with
shortness of breath, fever and a cough. He has had a non-productive
cough for two weeks. Before this, he had felt unwell with muscle aches
and malaise. He went to his GP and was given amoxicillin but this has
made no difference and now he is feeling more breathless and unwell.
He has not been outside of the UK in the last year. He has no other
medical problems and takes no regular medications. His cough is non-
productive and comes in paroxysms which make him concerned.
On examination, there are a few bilateral crepitations, but the
examination is otherwise normal. His observations show fever and mild
hypoxia. Blood tests show mild anaemia and raised inflammatory
markers. A chest X-ray shows bilateral consolidation, but he improves
with IV co-amoxiclav and clarithromycin over a few days.
What is the most likely causative organism?
explanation:
The correct answer is Mycoplasma pneumoniae. There are several hints
in this history and investigations to suggest Mycoplasma pneumoniae
as the likely cause. First of all, he is a young and fit patient who
describes a non-productive cough preceded by flu-like symptoms and
not responding to penicillins. Secondly, he has anaemia which may be
due to haemolysis, and finally there is bilateral consolidation on the
chest X-ray. Klebsiella pneumoniae is more typical in alcoholics,
Legionella pneumophila is associated with a history of foreign travel,
Chlamydia psittaci is associated with contact and exposure to birds and
finally, Coxiella burnetii is rare and associated with farm animal
exposure.
Mycoplasma pneumoniae
Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a cause of atypical pneumonia that often
affects younger patients. It is associated with a number of characteristic
complications such as erythema multiforme and cold autoimmune
haemolytic anaemia. Epidemics of Mycoplasma pneumoniae classically
occur every 4 years. It is important to recognise atypical pneumonia as it
may not respond to penicillins or cephalosporins due to it lacking a
peptidoglycan cell wall.

his GP as he presented with dysuria and a negative urine dipstick test. A
sexual health screen, including blood tests for HIV and syphilis serology,
are requested. What form of consent is required?
No consent
Implied consent
Verbal consent
Written consent
Written consent for HIV testing and verbal consent for sexual
health screening
Question 134 of 287
A 23-year-old gentleman presents to GUM clinic. He has been referred by
his GP as he presented with dysuria and a negative urine dipstick test. A
sexual health screen, including blood tests for HIV and syphilis serology,
are requested. What form of consent is required?
options: Written consent for HIV testing and verbal consent for sexual health screening
explanation:
The correct answer is verbal consent. Consent clearly is needed as an
investigation is done but since syphilis and HIV are transmittable
diseases consent needs to be specific towards each. This means that
the patient must be aware that they are being tested for HIV and syphilis
rather than just aware that they are having a routine blood test. Written
consent is not needed, and may discourage patients from having testing.
Source:
UK National Guidelines for HIV Testing 2008. London: British HIV
Association, 2008
(see page 10)

explanation:
Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is a herpes virus which commonly leads to
infectious mononucleosis. This presents, often in teenagers and young
adults with fevers, painful throat, lymphadenopathy and flu-like
symptoms. Although it can last longer the symptoms are usually self-
limiting within 2 weeks. Acute infection often leads to splenomegaly or
hepatosplenomegaly and although a transient hepatitis is common it
can lead to clinical jaundice.
Infectious mononucleosis
Infectious mononucleosis (glandular fever) is caused by the Epstein-Barr
virus (EBV, also known as human herpesvirus 4, HHV-4) in 90% of cases.
Less frequent causes include cytomegalovirus and HHV-6. It is most
common in adolescents and young adults.
The classic triad of sore throat, pyrexia and lymphadenopathy is seen in
around 98% of patients:
sore throat
lymphadenopathy: may be present in the anterior and posterior
triangles of the neck, in contrast to tonsillitis which typically only
results in the upper anterior cervical chain being enlarged
pyrexia
Other features include:
malaise, anorexia, headache
palatal petechiae
splenomegaly - occurs in around 50% of patients and may rarely
predispose to splenic rupture
hepatitis, transient rise in ALT
lymphocytosis: presence of 50% lymphocytes with at least 10%
atypical lymphocytes
haemolytic anaemia secondary to cold agglutins (IgM)
a maculopapular, pruritic rash develops in around 99% of patients
who take ampicillin/amoxicillin whilst they have infectious
mononucleosis
Symptoms typically resolve after 2-4 weeks.

A 69-year-old woman with diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis presents to
the clinic complaining of malaise. She takes metformin, sulfasalazine
and hydroxychloroquine daily and methotrexate once a week. She
volunteers at a care home near her home. On examination, she appears
frail, and her fingers and toes are deformed. She is alert, afebrile and
comfortable at rest. Her pulse rate is 70 beats per minute, BP is 120/80
mmHg, and respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute. On inspection of
her legs, you notice the following:
© Image used on license from DermNet NZ
What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this
patient?
options: Admit and treat with intravenous antibiotics
Order for an x-ray of the limb
Order for blood cultures and review with reports after one week
Prescribe oral antibiotics and arrange a follow-up visit for the next week
Prescribe oral prednisolone and arrange a follow-up visit
explanation:
The most appropriate next step is to admit and treat with intravenous
antibiotics. The image provided shows a swollen and erythematous right
lower limb. Differential diagnoses for a swollen limb include cellulitis,
deep vein thrombosis (DVT), lymphoedema, and fluid overload
conditions such as chronic heart failure. Cellulitis should be suspected
when there is a history of fever and malaise, with superficial bullae
potentially observed over the affected area. DVT typically presents in
patients who have risk factors (such as recent immobilisation, surgery,
or pregnancy) with unilateral limb oedema, erythema, and tenderness.
Lymphoedema often has an insidious onset and manifests as a slowly
progressive swelling of a limb; it is commonly observed in patients post-
lymph node dissection proximal to the affected area. Fluid overload
states usually present with bilateral pitting pedal oedema without
associated warmth or tenderness.
In this case, we are presented with a frail, immunocompromised woman
exhibiting symptoms of right leg cellulitis. These characteristics'frailty
and an immunocompromised state'are indications for in-patient
management according to NICE guidelines on admission criteria for
cellulitis. It is important to note that methotrexate is typically withheld
for patients who are being hospitalized with severe infections requiring
intravenous antibiotic therapy.
Ordering an x-ray of the limb is not correct. While cellulitis is diagnosed
clinically, an x-ray may be warranted only if there is strong clinical
suspicion of osteomyelitis in the underlying bone; otherwise, it does not
play a role in the management of cellulitis itself. Ultrasound (USG),
computed tomography (CT), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can
help exclude deeper tissue infections such as myositis or detect
abscess formation.
Ordering blood cultures and reviewing after one week is inappropriate
for this scenario. This patient has an acute infection necessitating
immediate antibiotic treatment. Blood cultures are indicated when
sepsis is suspected but should not delay empirical antibiotic therapy
aimed at preventing infection progression.
Prescribing oral antibiotics and arranging follow-up is incorrect for this
patient's presentation. Given her frailty and immunocompromised status,
she requires hospital admission for intravenous antibiotic therapy rather
than outpatient management with oral antibiotics, which are reserved for
Eron class I and II cases of cellulitis.
Prescribing oral prednisolone would be ill-advised here as it could
exacerbate the infection by suppressing the immune response instead
of treating it. Prednisolone may be indicated in patients experiencing
acute rheumatoid arthritis flares but is not applicable to this clinical
situation.

A 46-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a
history of dyspnoea, rhinorrhoea, and cough. She reports a low-grade
fever and general malaise. On systemic examination, the only notable
finding is an itchy vesicular rash distributed over her trunk. She takes no
regular medications and has no recent travel history. No constitutional
symptoms are noted.
Her vital signs are as follows: temperature 38.0°C, blood pressure
128/86 mmHg, heart rate 78 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation at
95% on room air.
A chest x-ray has been performed as part of her evaluation, shown
below:
© Image used on license from Radiopaedia
What is the underlying infection responsible for her condition?
explanation:
The chest radiograph reveals diffuse interstitial infiltrates scattered
throughout both lung fields, but predominantly located at the hila. There
is no sign of consolidation, which helps exclude other differentials.
Pneumonia can be a long-term complication of varicella infection as
chickenpox is transmitted via droplets. The presence of an itchy
vesicular rash should prompt consideration of varicella infection.
Varicella pneumonia typically develops 1-6 days after the onset of
cutaneous symptoms. While shingles exhibit a dermatomal distribution,
chickenpox is not restricted to dermatomes.
Aspergillosis typically affects immunocompromised individuals,
including those who are post-transplant or on immunosuppressive
therapy. In such cases, the chest X-ray might show widespread
pulmonary nodules with or without cavitation. However, aspergillosis
does not present with a vesicular rash.
Miliary tuberculosis (TB) could present with similar radiographic
findings; however, this would usually be accompanied by a history of
travel to TB-endemic regions or close contact with an individual
diagnosed with TB—none of which are evident here. Constitutional
symptoms are also associated with TB but are absent in this scenario.
Moreover, miliary TB does not manifest with a vesicular rash.
Renal cell carcinoma may lead to 'cannonball' metastases visible on
chest X-rays as large, well-circumscribed nodules within bilateral lung
fields, which differs from the diffuse calcifications observed here.
Patients may also have relevant medical or family history and typically
exhibit constitutional symptoms.
Sarcoidosis-associated rashes include lupus pernio or erythema
nodosum but do not have a vesicular character. This clinical feature
allows differentiation between sarcoidosis and varicella infections.

Efavirenz however can cause neuropsychiatric toxicity (due to variable

psychosis here. Normal LP excludes TB meningitis. Ethambutol causes
optic neuritis, so monitoring of visual acuity during treatment is
essential. HIV encephalopathy is possible but unlikely to present so
acutely and the temporal relation to Efavirenz introduction, in this case,
is the key.

explanation:
The candidate should have no difficulty in recognising that this patient
has meningitis. However, good knowledge of the epidemiology of
meningitis is required to answer the question completely.
The most common cause of meningitis in Saudi Arabia during Hajj is
meningococcal meningitis type A. It is also the leading cause of
epidemics of what is known as the meningitis belt in Africa along the

Type B and Type C are mainly responsible for sporadic cases of

His Glasgow Coma Score is 15/15. Neurological examination reveals

either eye. You notice needle track marks on the patient's forearm and an
erythematous wound in the patient's right antecubital fossa.
What is treatment would you give to the patient immediately?
explanation:
This patient has presented with typical features of botulism, which is
likely to have been contracted via the patient's wound in this case. He
has suffered from a descending weakness, initially affecting his bulbar
and pharyngeal muscles, then his upper limbs. If untreated this would
progress to involve his respiratory muscles and lower limbs. In contrast,
Guillain Barre Syndrome (GBS) presents with an ascending weakness
usually involving the lower limbs, then upper limbs then cranial nerves.
Both conditions show autonomic features and progress rapidly.
One particularly distressing feature of botulism is that it does not affect
GCS.
The immediate treatment of choice would be IV Trivalent antitoxin
immediately and general supportive measures.

A 24-year-old man attends the sexual health clinic complaining of
urethral discharge and dysuria following an episode of unprotected
intercourse. Examination of the external genitalia confirms purulent
discharge but no other abnormalities. There is no previous history of
sexually transmitted infection.
You undertake microscopy of the discharge which reveals many white
blood cells but no organisms. A urine sample is sent for nucleic acid
amplification tests (NAAT) for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria
gonorrhoea. You treat him empirically with a course of doxycycline for
presumed chlamydial infection.
He returns for review a week later. You note both NAAT results to be
negative. However, the patient tells you his symptoms have fully
resolved.
What is the most likely explanation?
Mycoplasma genitalium infection
False negative NAAT for Chlamydia trachomatis
False negative NAAT for Neisseria gonorrhoea
Herpes simplex virus infection
Urinary tract infection
