A 43-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a fever,
rash, and headache. He has recently returned from travelling around the
Solomon Islands. He has no past medical history of note.
On examination, he has a diffuse morbilliform rash and a dark, scab-like
lesion is noted on his leg. His temperature is 38.4ºC.
Given the likely diagnosis, what is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
Doxycycline is correct. The patient presents with a fever, headache, and
rash. These are common features of many illnesses in the returning
traveller. However, the dark scab-like lesion is more discriminating and in
the context of a patient returning from the Solomon Islands, this likely
represents the black eschar associated with scrub typhus infection. The
Solomon Islands from the southern tip of the 'Tsutsugamushi Triangle'
where scrub typhus is endemic. The treatment is with doxycycline.
Atovaquone-proguanil is incorrect. Also known as Malarone, this is an
accepted oral treatment for uncomplicated malaria. Malaria is present in
the Solomon Islands but a rash is actually uncommon in malaria and a
Doxycycline is typically used in the management of typhus
black eschar is not a feature.
Ceftriaxone is incorrect. This would be an appropriate treatment for
typhoid, which is a common cause of fever in returning travellers. A
black eschar is not a feature of typhoid infection.
Ciprofloxacin is incorrect. This would be an appropriate treatment if we
suspected anthrax. This is another cause of eschar. However, while a
patient with anthrax may be systemically unwell, a diffuse morbilliform
rash is not typical. Additionally, the eschar of anthrax may be associated
with some perilesional oedema and blister which are not mentioned
here.
Supportive management is incorrect. The mortality rate of scrub typhus
is 6% untreated. Management is with doxycycline.

A very difficult question. The timing of events is key.

important differential, especially in the context of HIV infection. All of his
findings on examination are consistent with COPD.
Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome is bilateral adrenal haemorrhage in
the context of meningococcal septicaemia.

Incubation is between 4-14 days. Typical symptoms include high fever,
headache, muscle aches, vomiting and may have meningitis and
jaundice.

deranged liver function. Acute hepatitis A infection is prevalent in Hong
Kong and incubation period is between 2 - 6 weeks but infection would
not explain the neurological symptoms.

explanation:
This patient presents with a history typical of tick-borne encephalitis.
Tick-borne encephalitis (TBE) presents as meningoencephalitis, caused
by a flavivirus infection of the central nervous system. This virus is
Treatment for tick-borne encephalitis is supportive
transmitted by the Ixodes tick, the activity of which is usually highest in
the summer months. The disease is endemic in Central and Eastern
Europe and the Far East (Russia, China, northern Japan). The disease
starts 4-28 days after being bitten by the infected tick and presents in a
biphasic fashion. After a few days of fever, fatigue, and myalgia, the
patient will have a symptom-free interval before progressing to central
nervous system dysfunction (meningitis/encephalitis/cranial nerve
palsies). Diagnosis is generally by CSF/serum serology for TBE-specific
antibody and management is supportive - aciclovir is given initially as an
empirical treatment but can be stopped when HSV/VZV is ruled out.
In this case, whilst the specific serology confirming the infection is not
given, the other investigations and history of a tick bite point towards
this diagnosis. He has a predominantly lymphocytic pleocytosis with a
raised CSF protein which is typical for viral CNS infections.
Whilst doxycycline appeared to help this patient initially, this coincided
with the symptom-free interval commonly seen in the biphasic illness of
TBE. Negative serology for Borrelia burgdorferi makes a diagnosis of
Lyme disease very unlikely. Therefore, another course of doxycycline is
not appropriate.
Continuing aciclovir is not necessary given that the CSF investigations
for HSV-1 and HSV-2 and VZV are negative.
IV immunoglobulin can be used for autoimmune/paraneoplastic
encephalitis but there is nothing in the stem to suggest that this is the
underlying pathological process.
Praziquantel is a drug used in the treatment of parasitic infections such
as schistosomiasis.
The management of TBE is supportive. Whilst it would be important to
identify the cause by performing further serological testing, this is not an
option.

thrombocytopaenia and leucopenia, strongly suggestive of dengue fever.

ingestion of contaminated water is possible, is to consider is also

had unprotected sex during her travel, gonorrhoea presents more
typically with a migratory arthritis and tenosynovitis with discharge.
Leucopenia is classical of dengue fever and does not necessarily
suggest immunodeficiency, possibly secondary to HIV.

The clinical picture here is of an acute pyelonephritis with fever, rigours
and tenderness over the renal angle. However blood analysis and
imaging suggest there is another entity at play that has predisposed the
patient to this.
S. mansoni and S japonicum, S. mekongi and S. intercalatum produce
eggs that can invade the bowel wall causing an intense inflammatory
reaction that gives rise to loose bloody stools. Eggs can also migrate to
liver through the portal venous system where they can elicit a
granulomatous fibrosing reaction. This can eventually lead to the
blockade of venous blood and flow. Portal venous hypertension results
which can give rise to varicies and upper gastrointestinal bleeding.
S. haematobium on the other hand leads to granulomatous inflammation,
ulceration of the vesicle and ureteral walls. Subsequent fibrosis can
cause bladder neck obstruction, hydroureter and hydronephrosis. These
changes can cause a chronic renal impairment and predispose to
secondary bacterial infection as well as squamous cell carcinoma.
In addition, all schistosome species can result in immune complex
deposition in the kidneys leading to a proteinuria and nephrotic
syndrome.

culture is performed and reveals extended-spectrum beta-lactamase

Ciprofloxacin
Amoxicillin-clavulanate
Ceftriaxone
Meropenem
Gentamicin
Question 221 of 287
A 65-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a high
fever, dysuria, and lower abdominal pain. He has a history of recurrent
urinary tract infections and was recently treated with ciprofloxacin. On
examination, he appears unwell with a temperature of 39°C. A urine
culture is performed and reveals extended-spectrum beta-lactamase
(ESBL)-producing Escherichia coli.
Which antibiotic is most appropriate for treating this infection?
explanation:
Meropenem is the correct answer because it belongs to the carbapenem
class of antibiotics, which are resistant to most beta-lactamases,
including ESBLs. This makes meropenem particularly effective in
treating infections caused by ESBL-producing bacteria such as E. coli in
this scenario.
Ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic that can be used for some
urinary tract infections but is not effective against ESBL-producing
organisms due to resistance issues, especially considering the patient's
recent treatment with ciprofloxacin.
Carbapenems (e.g. meropenem) are useful in the management of
ESBL-producing bacteria
Amoxicillin-clavulanate combines amoxicillin with clavulanic acid, which
inhibits some beta-lactamases but not those produced by ESBL
organisms. Therefore, it would not be an appropriate choice in this
scenario where the pathogen produces ESBL.
Ceftriaxone is a third-generation cephalosporin that would typically be
ineffective against ESBL-producing bacteria because these enzymes can
hydrolyse cephalosporins, rendering them ineffective.
Gentamicin, an aminoglycoside antibiotic, could potentially be active
against certain strains of E. coli; however, its efficacy can vary greatly
depending on local resistance patterns and it does not cover all potential
pathogens in complicated urinary tract infections like carbapenems do.

options: tonsillitis and rheumatic fever. Rheumatic fever is associated with erythema marginatum, an annular erythematous rash that appears on the trunk, upper arms and legs that spread outwards in a circular shape Clotrimazole
explanation:
This patient's rash is typical of erythema migrans given the 'bulls-eye'
appearance of a circular erythematous centre with a clear border and
outer erythematous border. Erythema migrans is typically associated
with Lyme disease, a zoonotic infection secondary to the spirochete
Borellia burgdorferi. It is spread by the bites of infected ticks. Associated
symptoms include fever, myalgia and fatigue. The rash can appear 1-2
weeks following a tick bite and can enlarge in size over time with central
clearing. The lesions are not typically painful or itchy.
Amoxicillin is correct. The typical first-line treatment for Lyme disease is
doxycycline. However, as this patient is pregnant, doxycycline is
contraindicated and amoxicillin is the next best treatment of choice.
Clotrimazole is incorrect. This is used in the treatment of fungal
infections including tinea corporis. Tinea corporis can present similarly
with a circular lesion and an erythematous outer border. However, the
lesions with ringworm are usually itchy with a scaly outer edge which is
not seen here.
Doxycycline is incorrect. This is the first-line management for lyme
disease. However, doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy due to the
risk of bone and teeth deformity. Therefore, the most appropriate option
would be amoxicillin.
Phenoxymethylpenicillin is incorrect. This is typically used in the
management of infections caused secondary to Streptococcal species
(e.g. Streptococcus pyogenes). Group A Streptococci such as
Streptococcus pyogenes have the potential to cause infections such as
with central clearing. However, this is very rare in adults and in developed
countries.
Prednisolone is incorrect. Corticosteroids can be used for several
inflammatory skin conditions including eczema and psoriasis. However,
these lesions are often multiple, exfoliative, scaly and itchy which is not
seen in this patient's presentation. Therefore, an alternative diagnosis
should be considered.

A 22-year-old man presented to his General Practitioner with an itchy
rash across his arms and legs. Symptoms had developed within the last
few days and were causing the patient significant discomfort and
preventing him from sleeping. The patient was a university student
currently enjoying his summer vacation. He reported returning from a
backpacking trip around Eastern Europe one week previously when he
had stayed mostly in youth hostels. Since his return he had been staying
in his parent's home. Interestingly, the patient had discovered on
Facebook that a similar rash had afflicted a friend he had made at the
end of his holiday.
He also worked part-time as a barman and denied coming into contact
with any unusual chemicals at work. He had not recently introduced any
new skin care products.
The patient had suffered from mild atopic eczema as an infant but had
no recent skin complaints or other past medical history. He took no
regular medications and had no known allergies. The patient smoked 10
cigarettes per day and drank roughly 40 units of alcohol each week.
On examination, the patient's arms and legs were covered with 2-5 mm
maculopapular lesions with a central haemorrhagic punctum. In several
places, several lesions were noted to be lying close together in a curve
formation. There were minor marks of excoriation associated with the
lesions. The patient's groin, abdomen, chest and back were free from
rash. There was no axillary, cervical or inguinal lymphadenopathy.
What organism is the likely cause for the patient's rash?
Sarcoptes scabiei
Leishmania donovani
Ancylostoma braziliense
Mycobacterium leprae
Cimex lectularius

explanation:
The patient has symptoms and signs of exposure to bed bug infestation.
In temperate regions, this is caused by the insect Cimex lectularius. A
rash develops up to 11 days after exposure due to an allergic reaction.
Bed bug infestation has increased in frequency over the past 10 years
with the patient likely exposed during a recent stay at youth hostel.
The other organisms are all potential causes of skin disease in the
returned traveller.
Sarcoptes scabiei (scabies)
Leishmania donovani (cutaneous leishmaniasis)
Ancylostoma braziliense (cutaneous larva migrans)
Mycobacterium leprae(leprosy)
Bed bugs
Bed bugs describe a variety of clinical problems including itchy skin
rashes, bites and allergic symptoms secondary to infestation with Cimex
lectularius.
Bedbug infestation seems to be an increasingly common presentation
within UK general practice. Bedbugs thrive in mattresses or fabrics, and
can be extremely difficult to eradicate. Topical hydrocortisone is suitable
to control itch, but definitive management is through a pest
management company and fumigation of the house.
Bed bug numbers may be controlled by hot-washing bed linen and using
mattress covers.

explanation:
The most important three differential diagnosis for a ring-enhancing
lesion in an HIV patient is CNS lymphoma, TB and Toxoplasmosis.
In this case the retinal necrosis in characteristic of ophthalmic
toxomplasmosis. Multiple lesion also favour toxoplasmosis. His poor
compliance with HIV treatment (as indicated by the low CD4 count and
the high viral load) suggest his compliance with co-trimoxazole is also
poor.

A 25-year-old woman is started on antiretroviral therapy for HIV. She
attends the GP 1 week later complaining of dizziness and nightmares.
She is unable to work due to feeling muddled and disconnected. Which
drug is responsible?
explanation:
Efaverinz is a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI) and
is frequently known to cause disturbing dreams and other cognitive
disturbances in 50% of patients in the first month of treatment.
The most concerning side effect of Abacavir is a hypersensitivity
reaction that can lead to fever, malaise, nausea and skin rash which can
be very severe. It is strongly associated with a specific allele at the
human leukocyte antigen B locus, HLA-B*57:01.
Lamivudine and Zidovudine are nucleoside analogue reverse
transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs). The NRTIs were the first class of
antiretroviral drugs developed. As with all drugs in their class, they can
cause a potentially fatal lactic acidosis & severe hepatomegaly with
steatosis when used alone or in combination with other antiretrovirals.
Tenofovir is a nucleotide analogue reverse transcriptase inhibitors
(NtRTI), it is a prodrug, the commonest side effects are gastrointestinal.

A 35-year-old man presents to the travel walk-in centre due to a week of
diarrhoea following a recent holiday to Brazil. He had a stool sample
sent for ova, cysts, and parasites which tested positive for Strongyloides
stercoralis.
What medication should be prescribed for the patient?
explanation:
Ivermectin is the drug of choice for strongyloidiasis which acts by
deactivating chloride channels which result in paralysis and death of the
parasite either directly or by causing the worms to starve.
Azithromycin is an effective antibiotic for Typhoid, Campylobacter and
often treatment of choice for traveller's diarrhoea. It is not effective for
treatment of Strongyloides.
Diethylcarbamazine is not used to treat Strongyloides. It is the treatment
of choice for Wuchereria bancrofti, Loa Loa, Toxocara canis.
Praziquantel is also not an effective treatment for Strongyloides. It is
used to treat Schistosoma haematobium, Paragonimus westermani and
Ivermectin is the drug of choice for treatment of strongyloidiasis
Clonorchis sinensis.
Triclabendazole is the treatment of choice for Fasciola hepatica (the liver
fluke) and is not the treatment of choice for Strongyloides.
Strongyloides stercoralis
Strongyloides stercoralis is a human parasitic nematode worm. The
larvae are present in soil and gain access to the body by penetrating the
skin. Infection with Strongyloides stercoralis causes strongyloidiasis.

A 36-year-old Somali male presents on the medical take with a severe
generalised headache associated with nausea and vomiting. He has
been living in the UK for the last 10 years. He was diagnosed with HIV 5
years ago and has been well maintained on therapy with an undetectable
viral load and a CD4 count of 500 cells/mm3.
He has a long history of headaches since the age of 10 which are
normally controlled with simple analgesia. Over the last 2 days he has
been suffering with a particularly bad attack which culminated in him
becoming aggressive and vomiting profusely. He was noted to have a
tonic-clonic seizure whilst in accident and emergency which resolved
with diazepam.
Clinical examination reveals a pulse of 78 beats per minute, a blood
pressure of 130/90, oxygen saturations of 98% on air and a temperature
of 36.8 degrees. There was no focal neurological defects.
A CT scan subsequently showed cystic and calcified lesions within the
brain and mild hydrocephalus.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
Tuberculous meningitis
Cryptococcal meningitis
Lymphoma
Neurocysticercosis
Human african trypanosomiasis
Question 231 of 287
A 36-year-old Somali male presents on the medical take with a severe
generalised headache associated with nausea and vomiting. He has
been living in the UK for the last 10 years. He was diagnosed with HIV 5
years ago and has been well maintained on therapy with an undetectable
viral load and a CD4 count of 500 cells/mm3.
He has a long history of headaches since the age of 10 which are
normally controlled with simple analgesia. Over the last 2 days he has
been suffering with a particularly bad attack which culminated in him
becoming aggressive and vomiting profusely. He was noted to have a
tonic-clonic seizure whilst in accident and emergency which resolved
with diazepam.
Clinical examination reveals a pulse of 78 beats per minute, a blood
pressure of 130/90, oxygen saturations of 98% on air and a temperature
of 36.8 degrees. There was no focal neurological defects.
A CT scan subsequently showed cystic and calcified lesions within the
brain and mild hydrocephalus.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Cysticercosis is caused by the larval stage of the tapeworm Taenia
solium. Clinical syndromes that can arise include neurocysticercosis
(NCC) and extraneural cysticercosis. In endemic areas NCC is an
important cause of adult-onset seizures.
Cysticercosis is transmitted by ingestion of T. solium eggs shed in the
stool of a human tapeworm carrier. Following ingestion, embryos
(oncospheres) hatch in the small intestine, invade the bowel wall and
disseminate hematogenously to the brain, muscle, liver and other
tissues. Cysts located in the brain result in neurocysticercosis and can
lead to hydrocephalus if they obstruct the outflow of CSF from the
ventricles. The condition can be chronic and develop over a protracted
period of time.
This question relies primarily on knowledge of the relevant condition and
your ability to think beyond the fact that the patient has HIV. While the
other options are all plausible you are given clues throughout the
question on which you can discount each one until you are left with the
correct answer.
The first hint is that his HIV was diagnosed early and is very well
controlled. This makes an opportunistic infection incredibly unlikely
therefore discounting crypotcocosis and TB meningitis. There are two
forms of human african trypanosomiasis both transmitted by the tsetse
fly, T.gambiense a chronic condition contracted in west africa and
T.rhodiesiense that is acutely progressive and contracted in east africa.
Given that he has been in the UK for 5 years we can discount
T.rhodesiense and the finding of calcified lesions on the CT would be
most unusual for T.gambiense.
This leaves us with lymphoma and neurocistercicosis, lymphoma will
generally present with progressive focal neurology over a period of time
and is unlikely to show calcified lesions in the brain.

A 42-year-old male from Bolivia presents with a 8 month history of
progressive fatigue, dyspnoea and intermittent chest pains. He is a
chronic smoker and during a recent severe episode of breathlessness
had consulted his GP who prescribed amoxicillin and prednisolone to
combine with his regular inhaler therapy. Shortly after this he
experienced a febrile episode which had lasted 7 days before resolving.
His breathlessness also worsened during this period.
On examination he has a temperature of 37.2 degrees, a heart rate of 98
beats per minute, a blood pressure of 110/70 mmHg and a respiratory
rate of 24/min. His jugular venous pressure was raised, there was lower
limb oedema to the mid shin and a pan systolic murmur heard best in
inspiration in the left parasternal region. An ECG showed a prolonged PR
interval.
What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
Ischaemic heart disease
Chronic pulmonary emboli
Chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy
Sarcoidosis
HIV
Question 233 of 287
A 42-year-old male from Bolivia presents with a 8 month history of
progressive fatigue, dyspnoea and intermittent chest pains. He is a
chronic smoker and during a recent severe episode of breathlessness
had consulted his GP who prescribed amoxicillin and prednisolone to
combine with his regular inhaler therapy. Shortly after this he
experienced a febrile episode which had lasted 7 days before resolving.
His breathlessness also worsened during this period.
On examination he has a temperature of 37.2 degrees, a heart rate of 98
beats per minute, a blood pressure of 110/70 mmHg and a respiratory
rate of 24/min. His jugular venous pressure was raised, there was lower
limb oedema to the mid shin and a pan systolic murmur heard best in
inspiration in the left parasternal region. An ECG showed a prolonged PR
interval.
What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Teasing out the infective aetiology in this question is the key to finding
the answer. Chagas disease can present as an acute illness or as a
chronic disease years after infection and is caused by the parasite
Trypanosoma cruzi.
Acute disease is usually asymptomatic but may manifest as a febrile
episode in association with a swelling over the site of inoculation (if in
the skin this is called a chagoma if through the conjunctiva of the eye
this is known as Romanas sign). In severe cases an acute myocarditis
can evolve with a secondary pericardial effusion.
Chronic disease begins to develop weeks or months after the initial
inoculation and in some cases does not present until years after the
infection (as in this case). Chronic disease can effect the heart causing
a biventricular cardiomyopthy with predominant right sided features as
well as varying degrees of heart block and conductive abnormalities due
to fibrous inflammation around amastigotes embedded in the heart
muscle. Chest pain can also be common and does not imply an
ischaemic component. Chronic disease can also effect the bowel
causing dilation.
The first clue in the case is that the patient is from an area where
disease is endemic. Secondarily there is an absence of ischaemic
related risk factors other than his smoking history and he is of a
relatively young age. Perhaps the biggest clue of an infective cause is
the febrile episode following steroids therapy. This likely represents a
relapse of acute infection which is common with immunosupression. At
this point you may be able to see trypomastigotes in the blood but they
soon disappear on resolution of the fever.
Chronic PE is also a possibility given the predominance of right sided
signs but does not explain the first degree heart block or fever following
steroid therapy.

A 25-year-old man reports feeling unwell with fever, generalised muscle
aches, headache and widespread rash 1 week after returning from
Thailand. On admission his chest X-ray is unremarkable. His urine dip
showed 1+ protein only and viral swabs are negative. Bloods are also
normal aside from low platelet count. On day 2 of admission his blood
pressure drops and repeat bloods show a further fall in platelets and
reduction in haemoglobin count. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
All plausible options and further history including prior vaccination,
sexual history and malaria prophylaxis would be helpful. The history and
deterioration are most likely due to dengue fever and subsequent
'dengue shock syndrome'. Measles would be unlikely at his age, malaria
does not classically cause a widespread rash and herpes simplex would
not cause a drop in the platelets. Gonorrhoea fits quite well and has a
similar incubation period (4-7 days) . The patient would have normally
have reported an isolated septic joint by this stage in the disease.
Retro-orbital headache, fever, facial flushing, rash,
thrombocytopenia in returning traveller → ?dengue
Dengue fever
Dengue fever is a viral infection that can progress to viral haemorrhagic
fever (other examples include yellow fever, Lassa fever, Ebola).

30 minutes for intracellular and extracellular compartments to
equilibrate. Assuming that the patients pre-dialysis bloods showed a
high-normal K+ (which would fit with her recent hyperkalaemia
presentation) then her total body K+ will be much higher than the post-
dialysis sample suggests. The bloods should be repeated to confirm this
but over-zealous correction of K+ in this situation can be dangerous.
Magnesium is important to correct in the presence of hypokalaemia,
however, we do not think this patient genuinely has low potassium.
Intravenous calcium gluconate and insulin/dextrose infusion are both
treatments for hyperkalaemia and therefore are not appropriate.

that he completed a 7-day course of ciprofloxacin for a UTI 2 weeks ago.

Urinalysis shows pyuria and positive nitrites, and microscopy shows

What is the most appropriate empirical treatment?
explanation:
Meropenem is the most appropriate choice for empirical treatment in
this high-risk case, given the patient's severe sepsis, recent ciprofloxacin
use, and underlying conditions (type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney
disease), which increase the likelihood of multidrug-resistant infections.
Starting with the most effective broad-spectrum antibiotic is crucial to
preventing clinical deterioration, persistent bacteraemia, or
complications such as septic shock, rather than using inadequate initial
coverage and escalating later. Meropenem provides reliable coverage
against resistant organisms, ensures effective tissue penetration—
especially in the kidneys and bloodstream—and can be appropriately
dosed for renal impairment. This approach allows for early infection
control while enabling de-escalation based on culture results, reducing
unnecessary carbapenem use and the risk of resistance development.
Cefepime is a broad-spectrum cephalosporin effective against many
Gram-negative organisms, including E. coli, but it lacks reliable coverage
against ESBL-producing bacteria, which are a significant concern in this
patient due to recent ciprofloxacin use and severe sepsis. Cefepime is
hydrolysed by many ESBLs, and in high bacterial burden infections such
as pyelonephritis or sepsis, it shows reduced efficacy due to the
‘inoculum effect’, where clinical failure rates increase in septic shock
compared to carbapenems. Given the patient's high risk of ESBL
infection, cefepime is suboptimal in this scenario.
Ceftriaxone, a third-generation cephalosporin, is commonly used for
UTIs but is contraindicated in suspected ESBL infections, as ESBLs
readily hydrolyse these agents. In this case, the patient’s severe sepsis,
recurrent UTIs, and recent ciprofloxacin use significantly increase the
risk of ESBL-producing organisms. Ceftriaxone is a less reliable choice in
this setting, particularly in septic shock, where inadequate empirical
therapy can result in increased mortality. While ceftriaxone may be
appropriate for community-acquired pyelonephritis without resistance
risk factors, it is not recommended for this patient due to his underlying
comorbidities.
Fosfomycin is typically used for uncomplicated lower UTIs, particularly
Carbapenems (e.g. meropenem) are useful in the management of
ESBL-producing bacteria
cystitis, but it is not suitable for complicated UTIs or sepsis. It has poor
tissue penetration and inadequate systemic coverage, achieving low
concentrations in the kidneys and bloodstream, making it ineffective for
treating pyelonephritis or sepsis. While it is active against some ESBLs, it
is inappropriate in this case, given the patient’s severe symptoms,
multidrug resistance risk, and haemodynamic instability.
Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside with strong activity against Gram-
negative bacteria, including ESBL-producing E. coli. It is often used as
part of combination therapy for urosepsis. However, it is not the best
choice as monotherapy due to poor tissue penetration, particularly in
renal infections, and the risk of nephrotoxicity, especially in a patient with
chronic kidney disease (CKD stage 3) and worsening renal function.
Additionally, aminoglycosides rely on concentration-dependent killing,
meaning they are less effective in critically ill patients with altered drug
clearance and sepsis-related volume distribution changes. Given this
patient’s septic shock and renal impairment, gentamicin alone is not an
appropriate empirical choice compared to meropenem, which provides
broader and more reliable coverage.

The most likely diagnosis, given the trip to a tropical region of Africa,
intermittent bloating and diarrhoea, and an elevated CRP, is Giardiasis.
Empirical treatment is often given, with either a course of metronidazole
or a single dose of 2g tinidazole. Food intolerances may persist,
particularly with respect to lactose, for some time after the initial
infection.
Amoxicillin and ciprofloxacin would usually be used for listeriosis and
campylobacter respectively, and neither infection is likely. Neither a
wheat free diet nor a lactose-free diet is indicated given the likelihood of
ongoing giardiasis, although many patients may suffer symptoms of
lactose intolerance post-giardiasis.

new vaginal discharge. She has been having unprotected sexual
intercourse with a new male partner over the past eight weeks. Her
nuclear acid amplification (NAAT) test was positive for Chlamydia and
negative for gonorrhoea infection. She is currently menstruating.
What is the first-line treatment of choice for this infection?
Amoxicillin
Azithromycin
Ceftriaxone
Doxycycline
Erythromycin
Question 244 of 287
A 24-year-old female presented to clinic with symptoms of dysuria and
new vaginal discharge. She has been having unprotected sexual
intercourse with a new male partner over the past eight weeks. Her
nuclear acid amplification (NAAT) test was positive for Chlamydia and
negative for gonorrhoea infection. She is currently menstruating.
What is the first-line treatment of choice for this infection?
explanation:
This patient has a Chlamydia infection. We know she is not pregnant as
she is currently menstruating. The first-line treatment for Chlamydia
infection is a 7-day course of doxycycline. Azithromycin was previously
preferred as a first-line treatment as it can be given as a one-off dose,
which increases compliance. However, recent evidence has raised
concern for co-infection with Chlamydia and Mycoplasma genitalium,
with growing resistance to macrolides. Therefore, doxycycline is now
recommended as first-line treatment in non-pregnant patients.
Amoxicillin may be considered as a treatment for Chlamydia in pregnant
patients. However, is not the first-line in this case.
Chlamydia - treat with doxycycline
Azithromycin is no longer considered first-line due to growing concerns
around resistance. Azithromycin is also considered as a treatment
option in pregnant patients with chlamydia infection.
Ceftriaxone is the first-line treatment for patients with Gonorrhoea, rather
than Chlamydia infection. This patient was negative for Gonorrhoea
infection on NAAT.
Erythromycin may also be considered as a treatment for Chlamydia in
pregnant patients. However, is not the first-line in this case.

migrated to the UK from Guinea, where she had lived since birth. She had
suffered from malaria as a child but had been fit and well since. She did
not smoke and drank 6-10 units of alcohol per week.

minute and blood pressure was 124/80 mmHg. Her chest was clear on

explanation:
This patient has presented with features of onchocerciasis, a disease
caused by the filarial nematode Onchocerca volvulus. The parasite is
transmitted by blackflies of the genus Simulium, which deposit the
parasites larva onto the skin when biting to extract blood. The adult
worm lives in subcutaneous nodules and produces larvae, which
become deposited in the skin and eyes. Disease manifests when the
parasite dies in tissues and releases Wolbachia endosymbiotic bacteria
into tissues, provoking a host immune response. This above patients
disease has manifested as river blindness, where the worms die in the
cornea and provoke chronic inflammation, eventually leading to clouding
of the cornea. Inflammation in subcutaneous tissues leads to a pruritic
rash and formation of a leopard-skin appearance over time. The worms
can be visualised by microscopy of skin snip biopsy. The treatment of
choice is ivermectin; DEC should not be used because rapid death of the
worms can exacerbate damage to surround tissues and even cause
complete blindness.
Helminths

A 27-year-old nurse attends the emergency department and reports she
has just suffered a significant needle-stick injury while caring for her
patient on the intensive care unit. While providing her patient personal
care with her colleague, she was injured in the hand by a wide bore stylet
needle previously used to introduce an IV cannula to her patient that had
not been placed in an appropriate sharps bin. The needle had been
visibly blood stained. The nurse had been wearing gloves and had
followed correct first aid procedure for needle-stick injuries.
The nurse was very concerned as the patient who had been the needle-
stick donor was receiving treatment for the acute neurological phase of
rabies. Review of the patients clinical notes (with the consent of the
patients next of kin) indicated that he had contracted rabies following a
dog bite two months previously in Pakistan. The diagnosis of rabies
encephalitis had been made following clinical review by infectious
disease experts and the detection of neutralising serum antibodies.
The nurse was previously fit and healthy with no significant past medical
history. She did not use any regular medications and had no allergies.
She was uncertain if she had had any previous vaccination against
rabies, although did recall having a course of injections 10 years
previously before she visited family in rural India.
What is the correct management of the needle-stick injury to prevent
transmission of rabies?
Rabies immunoglobulin and full course rabies vaccination
Booster course rabies vaccination
Rabies immunoglobulin
Full course rabies vaccination
No action required

patient on the intensive care unit. While providing her patient personal

not been placed in an appropriate sharps bin. The needle had been
visibly blood stained. The nurse had been wearing gloves and had
followed correct first aid procedure for needle-stick injuries.
The nurse was very concerned as the patient who had been the needle-
stick donor was receiving treatment for the acute neurological phase of
rabies. Review of the patients clinical notes (with the consent of the
patients next of kin) indicated that he had contracted rabies following a
dog bite two months previously in Pakistan. The diagnosis of rabies
encephalitis had been made following clinical review by infectious
disease experts and the detection of neutralising serum antibodies.
The nurse was previously fit and healthy with no significant past medical
history. She did not use any regular medications and had no allergies.
She was uncertain if she had had any previous vaccination against
rabies, although did recall having a course of injections 10 years
previously before she visited family in rural India.
What is the correct management of the needle-stick injury to prevent
transmission of rabies?
options: Rabies immunoglobulin and full course rabies vaccination
explanation:
This situation represents a difficult clinical decision. Humans are
considered to be an end-host for the rabies virus as inter-human
transmission is not documented outside of transplantation cases. For
that reason, only standard infection control precautions are
recommended for health-care workers when in contact with individuals
with rabies. However, the needle-stick injury described could foreseeably
lead to transmission of the virus and given the severe consequences of
rabies should be considered as possible rabies exposure.
The patient does not have a clear history of previous immunisation (the
history stated could also be consistent with hepatitis B vaccination for
example). Rabies immunoglobulin should be given to provide passive
antibodies at the site of exposure prior to the development of an
immune response. As far as possible, the dose (20 IU / Kg) should be
administered locally around the wound. In addition, post-exposure
vaccination should be provided, with the WHO currently recommending a
four dose schedule (given on days 0, 3, 7 and 14).
If an individual has been previously vaccinated then immunoglobulin is
not required and a two dose vaccination schedule (given on days 0 and
3) should be given.
Crowcroft N, Thampi N. The prevention and management of rabies. BMJ
2015;350:g7827.

A 52-year-old male presents with a cough, fatigue, fever, and shortness
of breath. He had been feeling unwell for around 6 months with recurrent
colds that he couldn't seem to shake off. Over this period he had lost
around one and a half stone in weight. He attributed this to a poor
appetite. His only past medical history was asthma. He had been a
widower for 7 years and was a keen wildlife photographer which had
allowed him to travel the world. His last trip had been to Africa 2 years
ago.
On examination he had a temperature of 38.2ºC, heart rate is 102/min
and regular, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg and saturations 92% air. He
had fine bibasal crackles on chest auscultation. Heart sounds were
normal. Arterial blood gas showed a type 1 respiratory failure. Chest x-
ray showed bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. He was treated with
intravenous antibiotics. After two days of admission, his condition
worsened and his type 1 respiratory failure worsened and he was given
continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP). The beta glucan test came
back negative. Urinary antigens were negative. The patient remarked that
he had noted that his vision in his right eye was blurred and he had noted
flashing lights and spots in the same eye.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
Pneumocystis pneumonia
CMV pneumonia
Fungal pneumonia
Legionella pneumonia
Asthma exacerbation

On examination he had a temperature of 38.2ºC, heart rate is 102/min
and regular, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg and saturations 92% air. He

intravenous antibiotics. After two days of admission, his condition

back negative. Urinary antigens were negative. The patient remarked that
he had noted that his vision in his right eye was blurred and he had noted
flashing lights and spots in the same eye.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This gentleman has CMV pneumonia and then developed CMV retinitis
on the background of an undiagnosed HIV infection.
CMV infection is typically unnoticed in healthy people but can be life-
threatening for those who are immunocompromised, which would
include transplant patients, cancer patients, dialysis patients, HIV-
infected individuals and those on immunosuppressants.
CMV pneumonia often presents with a cough, fever, malaise, poor
appetite, myalgia, shortness of breath and night sweats. CMV can be
detected using serology. The virus can also be cultured from urine, throat
swabs, bronchial lavages and tissue samples to detect active infection.
PCR testing can also be done and this can help monitor viral load.
Ganciclovir or valganciclovir are treatments for CMV infection. Foscarnet
or cidofovir are alternatives when patients are resistant to ganciclovir.
Foscarnet can cause nephrotoxicity and electrolyte disturbance.
CMV retinitis often presents with blurred vision, floaters, flashing lights,
eye pain, photophobia and can lead to blindness. CMV retinitis most
commonly develops when the CD4 count is less than 50cells/mL.
However, it can occur in 20-30% when then CD4 count is less than 100
cells/mL.

What recent infection could increase the risk of his current condition?
explanation:
Chickenpox is a risk factor for invasive group A streptococcal soft
tissue infections including necrotizing fasciitis
The correct answer is chickenpox. This patient has developed
necrotising soft tissue infection, most commonly due to infection with
group A streptococcus. Recent chickenpox is a recognised risk factor for
invasive group A streptococcal (iGAS) infections such as this.
Herpes simplex virus encephalitis is incorrect. This is a severe central
nervous system infection which does have complications including
stroke and epilepsy. It is not known to increase the risk of iGAS.
Influenza is incorrect. The main bacterial infection seen in the aftermath
of influenza is Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia.
Mumps is incorrect. It does have a range of complications including
encephalitis and pancreatitis, but an increased risk of iGAS is not
recognised.
SARS-CoV2 is incorrect. Infection with this virus can increase the risk of
secondary bacterial respiratory tract infections. Some treatments also
increase the risk of infections - for example, some areas saw increased
rates of invasive fungal infections like mucormycosis related to high-
dose corticosteroid use. An association with iGAS, however, has not
been described.

A 32-year-old man has been brought to the hospital with severe
shortness of breath.
Initial observations with the paramedics were taken. These included a
respiratory rate of 32/min, oxygen saturations of 72% on room air, a
pulse of 120/min, a blood pressure of 123/72mmHg, and a temperature
of 38.3ºC.
On examination in the emergency department, he is sat on the bed
leaning forwards. There is evidence of drooling and a vomit bowl full of
saliva is next to him. There is audible stridor from the edge of the bed.
Oxygen has now been applied and saturations are 90% on 15L.
A neck x-ray was performed due to concerns for a foreign body and has
shown a 'thumb sign'.
What is the most appropriate next step in management?
Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP)
Endotracheal intubation
High flow oxygen
Intramuscular adrenaline
Nebulised adrenaline

A 32-year-old man has been brought to the hospital with severe
shortness of breath.
Initial observations with the paramedics were taken. These included a
respiratory rate of 32/min, oxygen saturations of 72% on room air, a
pulse of 120/min, a blood pressure of 123/72mmHg, and a temperature
of 38.3ºC.
On examination in the emergency department, he is sat on the bed
leaning forwards. There is evidence of drooling and a vomit bowl full of
saliva is next to him. There is audible stridor from the edge of the bed.
Oxygen has now been applied and saturations are 90% on 15L.
A neck x-ray was performed due to concerns for a foreign body and has
shown a 'thumb sign'.
What is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation:
Endotracheal intubation may be necessary to protect the airway in
acute epiglottitis
The above scenario describes a severe case of acute epiglottitis.
Patients approaching extremis tend to lean forwards to aid their
breathing and may have pooling of saliva due to an inability to swallow.
The 'thumb sign' on the neck x-ray is indicative of an oedematous
epiglottitis. Given the significant desaturation in oxygen along with
audible stridor, the most appropriate intervention would be endotracheal
intubation.
Given the degree of obstruction in this case, urgent anaesthetic input
should be sourced due to the high likelihood that this patient will require
intubation. This should not be delayed to trial CPAP. It is also possible
that CPAP will lead to the displacement of the epiglottis and worsen the
obstruction.
High flow oxygen can be used in patients that have low oxygen
saturation who are otherwise stable. This would not be appropriate in
the above scenario given the stridor and a need to urgently secure the
airway.
Intramuscular adrenaline would be beneficial if this was stridor
associated with anaphylaxis, however, there is no evidence of this from
the scenario.
Nebulised adrenaline can be used in croup but is not a part of
management in epiglottitis.
Acute epiglottitis
Acute epiglottitis is rare but serious infection caused by Haemophilus
influenzae type B. Prompt recognition and treatment is essential as
airway obstruction may develop. Epiglottitis was generally considered a
disease of childhood but in the UK it is now more common in adults due
to the immunisation programme. The incidence of epiglottitis has
decreased since the introduction of the Hib vaccine.

elevated protein. The white cell count may vary according to HIV
status
Cryptococcus neoformans is correct. This patient has evidence of
meningitis given the history of fever, headache and neurological
dysfunction. The background of HIV suggests a likelihood of
immunosuppression. In immunocompromised patients, it is important to
consider alternative organisms that could cause this presentation rather
than just those that are most prevalent in the general population.
Looking at the lumbar puncture results from this patient, there is a
significantly raised opening pressure, elevated protein and low glucose.
The white cell count is only marginally raised and is predominantly
lymphocytic. It is important to remember that the white cell count in CSF
analysis can vary in patients with HIV depending on the severity of their
immunocompromise. Cryptococcus neoformans is the most common
fungal infection of the CNS in patients with HIV. It causes the lumbar
puncture findings seen with this patient's presentation and is, therefore,
the most likely causative organism.
Herpes simplex virus is incorrect. Viral meningitis can be seen in
immunocompromised and immunocompetent individuals with common
responsible viruses including enteroviruses (most common),
herpesviruses, mumps and measles. Viral meningitis produces a CSF
with elevated protein and a raised white cell count of mostly lymphocyte
predominance as seen here. However, it would not cause a raised
opening pressure and the CSF glucose is not reduced in patients with
viral meningitis making this an unlikely diagnosis.
Listeria monocytes is incorrect. Listeria monocytes is an important
organism to consider in patients with meningitic symptoms who are over
the age of 50 years. Although the majority of bacteria cause neutrophil-
dominant leucocytosis in the CSF, Listeria monocytes can also cause a
lymphocytic predominance. However, the raised opening pressure points
away from Listeria monocytes as the causative organism.
Neisseria meningitidis is incorrect. This is one of the more common
causes of bacterial meningitis. Whilst Neisseria meningitidis can cause
an elevated opening pressure, the white cell count is generally made up
of neutrophils rather than lymphocytes as seen in this scenario.
Streptococcus pneumoniae is incorrect. Like Neisseria meningitidis, this
is one of the most common causes of bacterial meningitis. However, the
lymphocyte-predominant white cell count on CSF analysis makes this
organism less likely to be responsible for this patient's presentation.

cause of his repeated treatment failures?

Question 251 of 287
A 30-year-old male with HIV and a viral load of 10^6 and CD4 dropping
from 500 to 300 cells/µl since his last visit. The above mentioned results
are taken while he is on his third line of therapy. What is the most likely
cause of his repeated treatment failures?
options: Co-infection with a new HIV strain
Superinfection with a new HIV strain
explanation:
By far the most common cause of treatment failure in HIV therapy is
treatment non-compliance.
Re-infection with new HIV strain can occur via co-infection or
superinfection. Co-infection is defined as infection with 2 strains either
simultaneously or within a brief period of time before infection with the
first strain has an established immune response. Arbitrarily, HIV
coinfection would occur within the first month or so of infection.
Superinfection is defined as infection with a second strain after the initial
infection and the immune response to it has been established.

explanation:
The diagnosis is paragonimiasis or lung fluke infection.
Background
Paragonimiasis is a common tropical infection, the presentation of
which can often be misinterpreted as tuberculosis. Patients classically
present with a productive cough of brown / red sputum (which can often
be mistaken for haemoptysis). Patients may also exhibit constitutional
symptoms, however, these are often less severe than in tuberculosis or
malignancy. Furthermore, paragonimiasis is often associated with an
eosinophilia.
Although more commonly associated with East Asia, paragonimiasis is
also prevalent in North East India, Africa and parts of the Americas.
Treatment of paragonimiasis is with praziquantel.

A 23-year-old white Caucasian left-handed male presents with a 24-hour
history of slurred speech. He is a 'frequent flyer' in the Emergency
Department with repeated admissions and known is a known user of
intravenous drugs and alcohol. His past medical history includes
depression and previously treated in adolescence for functional
neurological symptoms. He denies having had a drink for the past 2
weeks but used intravenous cocaine yesterday.
On examination, he is obviously unkempt and a lack of prominent veins.
There is an old abscess scar over his right femoral crease. His speech is
markedly slurred but he remains orientated to time and place. You also
note a significant loss of forehead creasing and facial weakness on both
sides of his face with normal facial sensation. In addition, his power his
4-/5 in shoulder abduction, shoulder adduction, hip flexion and hip
extension, with 5/5 power on all other movements. Reflexes were
present in biceps, supinator, patella and ankle, with absent triceps reflex.
Both plantar reflexes were downgoing. Sensation to cotton wool,
proprioception and pinprick was normal, with the patient reporting no
pain.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
Heavy metal intoxication
Guillain Barre syndrome
Botulism
Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP)
Myasthenia gravis

On examination, he is obviously unkempt and a lack of prominent veins.
There is an old abscess scar over his right femoral crease. His speech is

note a significant loss of forehead creasing and facial weakness on both

4-/5 in shoulder abduction, shoulder adduction, hip flexion and hip

present in biceps, supinator, patella and ankle, with absent triceps reflex.
Both plantar reflexes were downgoing. Sensation to cotton wool,
proprioception and pinprick was normal, with the patient reporting no
pain.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The patient has presented with bilateral cranial neuropathies and
symmetrical proximal weakness, in the context of intravenous drug use.
The descending pattern of weakness is atypical for Guillain-Barre
syndrome. The time course of within 8 weeks also rules out CIDP.
Myasthenia gravis is a possibility but there is no suggestion of
fatigability. The distinction between heavy metal intoxication and
botulism is difficult: intravenous drug users, particularly those sourcing
from Eastern Europe, who have been known to present with manganese
poisoning due to dirty constituents. Clinical features of course depend
on the precise metal involved but acute poisoning typically includes
encephalopathy, gastrointestinal upset and myalgia in addition to
peripheral neuropathy. Significant sensory neuropathy causing
neuropathic pain is commonly prominent. In the case of this patient, with
bilateral cranial neuropathies and symmetrical proximal weakness, in the
context of intravenous drug use, makes botulism most likely. Treatment
is with antitoxin, removal of the original source of infection in addition to
close monitoring of respiratory function.

Surgery is the correct answer. This man has septic shock secondary to
necrotizing fasciitis as evidenced by fever, hypotension, rash and pain
out of proportion to the clinical findings. Furthermore, he has evidence of
end-organ dysfunction (acute kidney injury). The most important
treatment for necrotizing fasciitis is surgical debridement of infected
tissue. All other treatments are considered adjunctive. Both recent
chickenpox infection and diabetes are risk factors for this condition.
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy is incorrect. There have been case reports of
this treatment being used for necrotizing fasciitis but it is not the
mainstay of treatment.
Intravenous flucloxacillin is incorrect. This antibiotic would be a good
choice for simple cellulitis but necrotizing fasciitis is a more severe
infection, typically caused by gram-negative, gram-positive and
anaerobic bacteria and therefore requires a broader antibiotic cover.
Intravenous immunoglobulin is incorrect. This can be used as adjunctive
Chickenpox is a risk factor for invasive group A streptococcal soft

treatment to antibiotics and surgery in severe skin and soft tissue
infections but is not initial therapy or most important.
Tazocin and clindamycin are incorrect. This is the correct antibiotic
choice for necrotizing fasciitis as it gives a broad cover against aerobic
and anaerobic organisms and clindamycin has the added benefit of
inhibiting toxin production. However, the literature on necrotizing fasciitis
is clear in regarding surgery as the most important intervention.

A 38-year-old man presents to the emergency department with fever and
shivering, occurring approximately every two days. He has returned from
India three weeks ago, having spent four months travelling. While he was
in India, he was treated for malaria with chloroquine. He has no other
past medical history and does not take any regular medications.
Observations:
Heart rate 88 beats/min
Blood pressure 120/77 mmHg
Respiratory rate 18 breaths/min
Oxygen saturations 98% on room air
Temperature 38.6ºC
On examination, the patient is diaphoretic. There is palpable
splenomegaly.
A thick and thin blood film confirms malaria.
What organism is most likely to be responsible?
Plasmodium falciparum
Plasmodium knowlesi
Plasmodium malariae
Plasmodium ovale
Plasmodium vivax
Question 258 of 287
A 38-year-old man presents to the emergency department with fever and
shivering, occurring approximately every two days. He has returned from
India three weeks ago, having spent four months travelling. While he was
in India, he was treated for malaria with chloroquine. He has no other
past medical history and does not take any regular medications.
Observations:
Heart rate 88 beats/min
Blood pressure 120/77 mmHg
Respiratory rate 18 breaths/min
Oxygen saturations 98% on room air
Temperature 38.6ºC
On examination, the patient is diaphoretic. There is palpable
splenomegaly.
A thick and thin blood film confirms malaria.
What organism is most likely to be responsible?
explanation:
P. vivax and ovale have hypnozoite forms, which can cause clinical
disease long after patients leave the endemic area or may cause
relapsing disease following treatment
Plasmodium vivax is the correct answer. The patient has a confirmed
diagnosis of malaria, having previously been treated for malaria within
the last six months. This suggests a relapse of disease. The two forms
of malaria that cause relapsing disease are Plasmodium vivax and
Plasmodium ovale. Plasmodium vivax is more common in India while
Plasmodium ovale is more common in Africa. Chloroquine is the typical
treatment in most countries. This medication acts on blood-stage
parasites only and does not act on hypnozoites. The only available drug
that can kill the hypnozoites is primaquine.
Plasmodium falciparum is incorrect. This type of malaria does not cause
relapsing disease.
Plasmodium knowlesi is incorrect. This form of malaria, which is
common in South-East Asia does not cause relapsing disease.
Plasmodium malariae is incorrect. This does not cause relapsing disease
and is a less common form of malaria. Additionally, it causes fever every
three days rather than every two days as in other forms of malaria.
Plasmodium ovale is incorrect. This can also cause relapsing disease.
However, it does so far less commonly than vivax malaria and is more
common in Africa rather than Asia.

An 82-year-old gentleman inpatient is reviewed on the ward round. He
originally presented with diarrhoea on a background of ulcerative colitis
flare and is managed with oral and rectal mesalazine. His bowel has
settled but he developed a rash around his left antecubital fossa, and he
has developed a temperature of 38.2ºC. On examination, his chest
sounds clear and his abdomen is soft, but the left antecubital fossa has
a tender and warm erythematous rash. Stool results show no growth,
abdominal and chest X-ray are clear but a MRSA swab from the nose is
positive. What is the most appropriate treatment?
Mupirocin and chlorhexidine
Benzylpenicillin
Tazocin
Vancomycin
Flucloxacillin
Question 259 of 287
An 82-year-old gentleman inpatient is reviewed on the ward round. He
originally presented with diarrhoea on a background of ulcerative colitis
flare and is managed with oral and rectal mesalazine. His bowel has
settled but he developed a rash around his left antecubital fossa, and he
has developed a temperature of 38.2ºC. On examination, his chest
sounds clear and his abdomen is soft, but the left antecubital fossa has
a tender and warm erythematous rash. Stool results show no growth,
abdominal and chest X-ray are clear but a MRSA swab from the nose is
positive. What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
The correct answer is vancomycin. This is a patient with a new fever and
the most obvious cause is cellulitis. Given that the location of the
cellulitis is in a location common for cannulation the most likely
explanation is iatrogenic cellulitis. This makes MRSA a much higher
likelihood and therefore the most appropriate treatment is vancomycin.
Mupirocin and chlorhexidine are used to eradicate MRSA when present
as commensal organisms. In non-iatrogenic cellulitis benzylpenicillin
and flucloxacillin are commonly used.

and has no sensation in her left little finger. There is a non-painful 1x4
cm lump two centimetres distal to her left medical epicondyle.
Urinalysis reveals ++ of protein and + of blood.
Blood sugar: 8.8 mmol/L
On the clinical information alone what investigation is most likely to
secure the diagnosis?
explanation:
With skin lesions and peripheral nerve involvement leprosy should
certainly be on a differential diagnosis. Other give away features here are
the anaesthetic skin lesions and nerve thickening. The erythema
nodosum like lesions and the joint, renal and conjunctival involement
indicate a type 2 reaction which occur in patients with lepromatous
leprosy (usually following treatment).
Skin biopsy in this case will reveal the diagnosis. This would save her the
potentially disastrous consequences of immunosupression.
Leprosy
Leprosy is a granulomatous disease primarily affecting the peripheral
nerves and skin. It is caused by Mycobacterium leprae.
Features
patches of hypopigmented skin typically affecting the buttocks,
face, and extensor surfaces of limbs
sensory loss

explanation:
The diagnosis here is leprosy. Leprosy can present along a spectrum
from borderline to leprotamous and can often be mistaken for
conditions like psoriasis, SLE and granuloma annulare. The key
distinguishing feature is the presence of anaesthetic patches that are
present in leprosy but none of the other condition. A full clinical
examination is not complete until sensation has been checked over the
skin lesions with a microfilament.
The presence of anaesthetic patches should prompt you to look for
other hallmarks of disease such as thickened nerves (often easiest to
feel are the median nerve in the wrist the common peroneal nerve
around the lateral head of the fibula and the ulnar nerve at the elbow.)
the loss of hair (in and around lesions and often in the eyebrows) and
the presence of neuropathy. Diagnosis is made by demonstrating acid
fast bacilli within a cutaneous nerve on microscopy.
The severe skin changes seen with leprosy are not caused by the
bacteria themselves but the bodys own immune response towards the
bacilli. As a result steroids would improve the physical appearance of
skin lesions but at the same time accelerate disease as the bacteria
proliferate unhindered. This corresponds to the case outlined above
where the patients neurological symptoms worsen yet the skin disease
improves on starting steroids.

explanation:
Repeat serological testing is the best method of confirming
Strongyloides stercoralis eradication following treatment. A post-
treatment to pre-treatment titre ratio of < 0.6 is taken to represent a good
indicator of treatment success.
Blood eosinophil count is also often found to decrease following
treatment although this method clearly lacks specificity given the
numerous other causes of eosinophilia.
Strongyloides stercoralis infection is often asymptomatic therefore
resolution of symptoms does not provide good evidence of successful
treatment. While stool microscopy is the gold standard diagnostic test
for strongyloidiasis it has a sensitivity of only 50 % making it an
unreliable tool to confirm eradication. Stool concentration techniques
are used in specialist laboratories to improve sensitivity of stool
microscopy for strongyloidiasis.
Greaves D, Coggle S, Pollard C, Aliyu S et al. Strongyloides stercoralis
infection. BMJ 2013;347:4610.

cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis and oesophagitis caused by either CMV

therefore, the best option.
HIV: seroconversion
HIV seroconversion is symptomatic in 60-80% of patients and typically
presents as a glandular fever-type illness. Increased symptomatic
severity is associated with poorer long-term prognosis. It typically
occurs 3-12 weeks after infection

A 28-year-old woman presents to the clinic with a 5-day history of
dysuria and increased vaginal discharge. She reports the discharge is
thick and yellow-green with a strong odour. She denies any recent
changes in her sexual partner. On examination, she is afebrile but shows
signs of cervical inflammation. A microscopic examination of the
discharge reveals the presence of gram-negative intracellular diplococci.
What is the most appropriate treatment for this case?
Intramuscular ceftriaxone
Intramuscular ceftriaxone with oral azithromycin
Oral cefixime with oral azithromycin
Oral ciprofloxacin
Oral metronidazole
Question 266 of 287
A 28-year-old woman presents to the clinic with a 5-day history of
dysuria and increased vaginal discharge. She reports the discharge is
thick and yellow-green with a strong odour. She denies any recent
changes in her sexual partner. On examination, she is afebrile but shows
signs of cervical inflammation. A microscopic examination of the
discharge reveals the presence of gram-negative intracellular diplococci.
What is the most appropriate treatment for this case?
explanation:
Intramuscular ceftriaxone is the most appropriate treatment for this
case. The clinical presentation, characterised by dysuria, a thick yellow-
green vaginal discharge with a strong odour, and signs of cervical
inflammation, in conjunction with the identification of gram-negative
intracellular diplococci on microscopic examination of the vaginal
discharge, strongly suggests gonorrhoea caused by Neisseria
gonorrhoeae. The recommended treatment is a single dose of
intramuscular ceftriaxone.
Intramuscular ceftriaxone with oral azithromycin was previously the
standard regimen for treating gonorrhoea. However, the current
Intramuscular ceftriaxone is the treatment of choice for Gonorrhoea
guidelines now recommend monotherapy with a single dose of
intramuscular ceftriaxone as there is a lower incidence of resistance
with ceftriaxone and increasing resistance with azithromycin.
Oral cefixime with oral azithromycin serves as an alternative option for
individuals who are needle-phobic or decline injections. Nonetheless, it
is not considered the first-line treatment.
Oral ciprofloxacin is not recommended due to increasing resistance
rates. It may be used if bacterial sensitivity to ciprofloxacin is known.
Oral metronidazole remains the first-line therapy for bacterial vaginosis
and Trichomonas vaginalis, both common causes of vaginal discharge.
However, given this case's clinical and microscopic evidence,
gonorrhoea is deemed the most likely diagnosis; thus, metronidazole is
inappropriate.

options: 2 months of rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol and pyridoxine
3 months of rifampicin, isoniazid and pyridoxine
explanation:
Latent tuberculosis treatment options:
3 months of isoniazid (with pyridoxine) and rifampicin, or
6 months of isoniazid (with pyridoxine)
This patient has latent TB as evidenced by a positive interferon-gamma
release antibody (IGRA) test and no other symptoms consistent with
active TB. NICE advises that treatment for latent TB should be with either
3 months of rifampicin, isoniazid and pyridoxine or 6 months of
isoniazid and pyridoxine.
This patient has either been immunised against Hepatitis B or previously
infected and therefore has a positive Hepatitis B surface antibody test
but a negative antigen test. If they had chronic hepatitis B they would
have a positive antigen test. Treatment of chronic hepatitis B includes
once-weekly injections of peginterferon alfa-2a, a recombinant
interferon, for 48 weeks or antivirals such as tenofovir or entecavir.
If this patient had a positive IGRA test and symptoms consistent with
active TB, they would require treatment for active TB with 2 months of
rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol and pyridoxine followed
by 4 months of rifampicin, isoniazid and pyridoxine.
6 months of rifampicin only can be used to treat patients with latent TB
but is not recommended by NICE guidelines. It could also be used if this
patient's wife had isoniazid-resistant pulmonary TB.

What should be provided to the patient urgently?
explanation:
This patient is suffering from botulism which, although rare, normally
presents following consumption of contaminated food (e.g. tinned) or as
The treatment of botulism - supportive care and botulism antitoxin
in this case IV drug use. The patient has the typical presentation of
flaccid paralysis with bulbar and ocular involvement, whilst maintaining
full consciousness and no sensory disturbance. The mainstay of
treatment is supportive with early antitoxin use which can neutralise
non-bound, circulating botulinum toxin.
This patient has most likely a diagnosis of botulism. Although this can
progress to cause respiratory issues the patient does not currently have
evidence of respiratory failure. Antitoxin should be given as a priority and
respiratory function monitored.
Broad-spectrum antibiotics can be considered if there is evidence of
wound infection with Clostridium botulinum otherwise there use is non-
beneficial and specific botulism antitoxin with supportive care are the
only management that will affect the course of the disease.
Plasma exchange is incorrect as this has no evidence for its use in
botulism.
To date, no effective vaccination to assist in the management of
botulism has been approved for use.

options: answer. The patient has tick-borne encephalitis. This is evidenced by the fact that she has returned from a region where the disease is endemic (Siberia) and has presented with a biphasic illness characterized by flu- Continue aciclovir and ceftriaxone

explanation:

Treatment for tick-borne encephalitis is supportive
like symptoms in the first stage and neurological dysfunction in the form
of meningoencephalitis in the second stage. Her lumbar puncture results
suggest a viral meningitis and her CSF testing reveal specific antibodies
against a flavivirus, which is the cause of tick-borne encephalitis. There
is no specific antiviral treatment for tick-borne encephalitis. Patients
need admission to hospital if neurological symptoms are present and
require supportive care in the form of analgesia, anti-pyretics, fluid and
electrolyte management and intensive care input if appropriate.
Continue aciclovir and ceftriaxone is an incorrect answer. We have
confirmed a diagnosis of tick-borne encephalitis. Ceftriaxone can be
stopped as the CSF results do not indicate a bacterial infection and
aciclovir can be stopped as we have a confirmed diagnosis that does not
benefit from specific anti-viral treatment. Aciclovir is indicated in cases
of meningo-encephalitis caused by herpes zoster and herpes simplex.
Continue aciclovir and stop ceftriaxone is incorrect. Aciclovir has no
benefit in the management of tick-borne encephalitis.
Continue ceftriaxone and stop aciclovir is incorrect. The CSF results
demonstrate a lymphocytic pleocytosis with a normal glucose, indicating
a viral meningitis. Ceftriaxone has no role in the management of viral
infections.
Stop ceftriaxone and aciclovir and start ganciclovir is incorrect.
Ganciclovir is predominantly used in the treatment of severe
cytomegalovirus infection in immunocompromised patients. It has no
role in the treatment of tick-borne encephalitis.
Tick-borne encephalitis
Carried by ticks hosted by native wildlife, tick-borne encephalitis is
actually caused by a virus (Flavivirus) and transmitted by the bite of an
infected tick.

Question 269 of 287
A 98-year-old lady presents with a fever and confusion and on initial
review is started on broad spectrum antibiotics. Despite five days of
therapy, her temperature is 38.9°C and her clinical condition seems to
have deteriorated. She has no relevant past medical history. The
diagnosis of urinary tract infection (UTI) is confirmed when urine
cultures confirm an extended spectrum B-lactamase (ESBL) producing
Escherichia coli (E. coli).
Following the failure to respond to the first-line agent, which antibiotic is
most likely to be effective?
explanation:
Extended spectrum B-lactamase (ESBL) producing organisms are
typically resistant to penicillins and cephalosporins and as such the
carbapenem class of antibiotics are typically first-line although
nitrofurantoin or fosfomycin are also frequently effective. ESBL
producers are most commonly Escherichia coli (E. coli) and Klebsiella
species.

Emergency Department with increasing confusion. His wife states that
his specialist has not started him on antivirals yet. He was diagnosed six
months ago. His past medical history includes tuberculosis that has
been successfully treated 10 years ago.
His wife stated also that he slept more than usual in the last week and

inoculation of Trypanosome) as a child, and heart failure and

explanation:
Listeria may be suggested by CSF showing a lymphocytic
pleocytosis, raised protein and reduced glucose
This patient clearly has clinical meningitis, as evidenced by his
headache, neck stiffness, photophobia and fever. A degree of confusion
suggests that there may also be some encephalitis. The correct answer
is Listeria monocytogenes. This diagnosis is suggested by the CSF
results showing predominantly lymphocytes, with reduced glucose.
Listeria meningitis tends to occur in neonates, pregnant women, the
elderly and the immunocompromised. It most commonly presents with
sepsis and meningism and is more likely than other bacterial causes of
meningitis to also cause encephalitis or focal neurological deficits.
Haemophilus influenzae is incorrect. This organism can cause
meningitis but it mainly does so in infants and children. The CSF would
be expected to contain predominantly neutrophils rather than
lymphocytes.
Herpes simplex virus is incorrect. HSV might explain why the patient is
encephalitic as well as meningitic and you would expect to see a
lymphocytosis in the CSF, but the CSF glucose would be normal not low.
Mycobacterium tuberculosis is incorrect. Tuberculous (TB) meningitis
could give a similar CSF picture as in this patient, but is less likely given
that the patient has no epidemiological risk factors for TB acquisition.
TB meningitis also tends to present less acutely.
Neisseria meningitidis is incorrect. In this case, you would expect to see
a predominance of neutrophils in the CSF. Lymphocytes can sometimes
also be present if there has been a delay between starting antibiotics
and performing the lumbar puncture (partially treated meningitis) but
this is not the case here where we are told that the lumbar puncture has
been done immediately after giving antibiotics.

explanation:
Leishmaniasis is spread through sand-fly vectors from animal reservoirs
and remains endemic through areas of Africa, Asia, South America and
the Middle East. Visceral leishmaniasis can cause hepatosplenomegaly,
spiking fevers, pancytopenia and with certain strains blackening of the
skin leading to the alternative name of black fever (kala-azar). The gold
standard for diagnosis would be the demonstration of amastigotes on
splenic or bone marrow aspirates.
Serological testing, such as DAT, is useful in the diagnosis of
leishmaniasis but it is not the gold standard due to lack of evidence
demonstrating consistently higher sensitivities and specificities along
with a regional variation of the parasites complicating this. They are
however highly useful in endemic areas where it is a cheaper, less
technically challenging and occasionally a readily available alternative.
Demonstration of parasites on bone marrow or splenic aspirate
remains gold standard for diagnosing visceral leishmaniasis
diagnosis of leishmaniasis unless an alternative or additional pathology
is suspected.
A stool sample is of no use in the diagnosis of leishmaniasis which is a
vector born disease transmitted through sandfly bites.
Blood cultures can be useful in demonstrating blood-born parasites in
immunocompetent hosts with sensitivity rates up to 60%. This, however,
remains below that of the current gold standard.

explanation:
This gentleman has developed cytomegalovirus retinitis treatment of
which should be with intravenous ganciclovir or its prodrug oral
valganciclovir.
CMV retinitis:
Presents in those who are HIV +ve with CD4 counts typically <200
cells/mm3.
Patients may be asymptomatic initially, but tend to present with a
gradual deterioration in their visual acuity and visual blurring.
Typical fundoscopic features described include the 'pizza pie'
fundus. Flame hemorrhages may also be seen.
Treatment is with intravenous ganciclovir or its prodrug oral
valganciclovir.
Intravenous pentamidine and oral co-trimoxazole are used to treat
Pneumocystis jirovecii (formely known as Pneumocystis carinii.
Oral pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine, plus folinic acid is used to treat
toxoplasmosis.

left forearm. The nodule has gradually enlarged and ulcerated over the

Biopsy of a draining lymph node
Montenegro skin test
Punch biopsy of the lesion for histology

Question 276 of 287
A 20-year-old law student had been backpacking around India for 2
months over her summer holiday. She spent time in a number of rural
and coastal areas and volunteered at a wildlife conservation project for 2
weeks. She took malaria prophylaxis throughout.
A few days before her return to the UK she noticed a small nodule on her
left forearm. The nodule has gradually enlarged and ulcerated over the
last 4 weeks to form a 4cm painless ulcer.
What is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Biopsy of a draining lymph node
Punch biopsy of the lesion for histology
explanation:
This patient has cutaneous leishmaniasis. This is a protozoal infection
mainly caused by Leishmania major, Leishmania tropica and Leishmania
aethiopica in Asia, Africa, the Middle East and the Mediterranean, and by
Leishmania braziliensis and Leishmania mexicana in Central and South
America. It presents classically with a slowly developing painless ulcer
at the site of a sandfly bite.
The most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis is punch
Cutaneous leishmaniasis is typically diagnosed using a punch
biopsy
biopsy of the lesion for histology. The biopsy should be taken from the
outer border of the ulcer and should be full thickness. The specimen can
be examined using Wright or Giemsa stains to look for amastigotes in
the tissue. Culture or PCR can also be performed on the tissue sample.
Biopsy of a draining lymph node is incorrect. You are unlikely to see
parasites in tissue samples outside of the ulcer itself in cutaneous
leishmaniasis, as the infection is limited to the ulcer only.
Montenegro skin test is incorrect. This is a test in which killed
promastigotes are injected under the skin, and the degree of induration
at the site is read 48-72 hours later. It is used in some South American
countries but is not recommended as the sensitivity is low and it cannot
differentiate between past and current infections.
Serology is incorrect. This is not used in diagnosing cutaneous
leishmaniasis because antibody levels are generally low, meaning that
the sensitivity of the test is low. The specificity is also variable and there
may be cross-reactivity with other infections.
Serum PCR is incorrect. PCR can be carried out on tissue samples from
the lesion but is not carried out on serum as there would be minimal or
no protozoal DNA in the circulating blood, so the sensitivity would be too
low.

This gentleman has a painless single penile ulcer which given negative

His syphilis serology shows a positive screening EIA and follow up TPPA

seroconversion on the RPR.
This gentleman is having unprotected intercourse and is HIV positive, so
high risk for syphilis even if he gives a history of a single long-term
partner. He also gives no history of past infection and so he should be
treated for syphilis with antibiotics. Given he has no allergies, the first
choice should penicillin G.
However, for clarification regarding diagnosis, he requires further testing,
the gold standard being syphilis PCR.

explanation:
